facts: The accused, a government contractor, was alleged to be involved in a large-scale economic fraud involving forged petroleum bills used to claim government money. Fake bills allegedly prepared by the first accused were used by various officials and contractors, including the accused, to claim crores of rupees from the exchequer. The first accused died under suspicious circumstances after giving detailed confessions.

The accused was apprehended carrying Rs. 32,11,000 in cash, suspected to be intended for a militant group. The accused was earlier granted bail for offences under the IPC. Later, serious sections under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act were added, and the national investigating agency sought the accused's re-arrest. The Special Court directed custody, rejecting the accused's prayer to continue on the earlier bail.

The petitioner, a government employee, alleged that they were brutally tortured and castrated in police custody by multiple officers due to their involvement in an agitation. The accused, then the officer in charge of a police station, was among those charged. The petitioner sought cancellation of the bail granted to the accused, alleging post-release intimidation.

The case involves custodial rape of a person by multiple accused, including police officials. The trial court convicted several of the accused under IPC sections for rape and related offences. The accused were on bail during the investigation and trial. After conviction, some of the accused were granted bail under suspension of sentence, which the prosecution challenged, seeking cancellation.

The accused and co-accused were charged with the murder of the deceased, who was allegedly beaten to death by one of the co-accused with the support of others, including the petitioner. The petitioners sought review of the High Court's earlier order rejecting bail, citing overlooked witness testimony and an entitlement under Section 437 CrPC based on their personal characteristics.

The accused, a juvenile, was implicated in a gang-related robbery and murder based on confessions made by co-accused. The accused had been in a juvenile protection home for almost a year. Previous courts denied bail citing societal risk and psychological harm. The High Court reversed this, applying the JJ Act's presumption in favour of bail for children.

The accused was arrested along with two others during a police chase, with 6.71 grams of heroin recovered. A forensic report confirmed the substance to be heroin. The accused had prior NDPS cases, but no details were provided. Bail was sought under Section 439 CrPC after the charge-sheet was filed.

The petitioners, who were police personnel, were accused of murdering a suspect in custody at a police station. The defence argued that no prima facie evidence existed for a murder charge and sought anticipatory bail, contending that the case should at most fall under Section 330 IPC. The court held that the investigation was still ongoing and applied the Supreme Court's ruling that anticipatory bail should not be granted in murder cases while the investigation is incomplete.

The accused was arrested in connection with a murder case and granted default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC due to failure by the police to file the charge-sheet within 90 days. The State later filed the charge-sheet and sought cancellation of bail under Section 439(2). The High Court cancelled the bail, which was challenged before the Supreme Court.

The case involved two murders linked to political rivalry in a state. The accused, a public representative, was named in both FIRs involving brutal killings using firearms. Despite prior denial of bail and involvement in multiple criminal cases, the High Court granted the accused bail based on good conduct during temporary release. The complainants challenged this grant of bail in the Supreme Court.

The accused was alleged to have conspired to murder the deceased by paying 'supari' (a contract payment for a killing) to the co-accused. After the accused's anticipatory bail application was denied, the accused absconded and surrendered only several months later. The accused allegedly failed to cooperate with the police. The case involves the joint recovery of blood-stained weapons, which allegedly links the accused to the crime.

The accused, previously convicted under Section 302 IPC, was on post-conviction bail. During this period, the accused was allegedly involved in the murder of the appellant's parent, the deceased. Despite being summoned under Section 319 CrPC, the accused evaded arrest. The accused's criminal antecedents and political influence raised serious concerns, including judicial interference and police non-cooperation. The Supreme Court cancelled the accused's bail and condemned the High Court's inaction.

The accused was charged in a case of murder committed in public in broad daylight, and multiple bail applications filed by the accused had been rejected. A High Court judge later granted bail to the accused, disregarding the judicial convention that successive bail pleas should be referred to the same judge who heard the earlier ones. The Supreme Court found that the delays in the trial were due to the tactics of the accused and that serious allegations of witness tampering had been ignored by the High Court.

The applicant, arrested in 2016, was accused in three NDPS cases involving conspiracy to traffic charas. No contraband was recovered from the applicant, and the arrest was based solely on statements recorded under Section 67 of the NDPS Act. Co-accused were granted bail. The trial was pending. The applicant was an adult and had spent more than four years in custody.

A spouse of one of the appellants died from burn injuries along with their infant child. Two dying declarations suggested the death was accidental, but the deceased's parent alleged dowry harassment. An FIR was lodged under Sections 498A and 304B IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The Sessions Court granted anticipatory bail, the High Court cancelled it, and the Supreme Court restored it.

The accused, a foreign national, was accused by their spouse of dowry harassment during the time the couple lived abroad. The spouse filed an FIR after returning to the home country. The trial court declared the accused a proclaimed offender, despite arguments that Section 82(4) CrPC was inapplicable to offences such as those under Sections 498A and 406 IPC. The accused was later arrested and applied for regular bail.

The accused and others were alleged to be involved in a murder case involving the stabbing of the deceased. The prosecution cited eye-witnesses, including the deceased's spouse and another individual. The Sessions Judge granted anticipatory bail to the accused. The State filed for cancellation of the bail, alleging misuse of judicial discretion.

The deceased died of burn injuries within two years of marriage. The FIR, lodged by the deceased's parent, alleged dowry harassment and illicit relations between the deceased's spouse and the spouse's sibling's spouse. A Sessions Judge granted bail to the in-law and the spouse's sibling. The High Court found that bail was granted without proper consideration of the dowry death context.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was charged under dowry death and related sections. The deceased died over a month after sustaining burn injuries. A dying declaration named the accused and 11 others, including a minor. The defence argued that the dowry allegations were vague, that the family had arranged prompt medical attention, and that the accused had no criminal history. Two co-accused had already received bail.

The deceased died by suicide within 8 months of marriage to the accused's child. The deceased had earlier written a note alleging dowry harassment by their spouse and in-law, the accused. The family alleged demands for a flat and abusive behavior. The accused, an in-law of the deceased, sought anticipatory bail citing age and health, but the court found credible evidence of harassment from statements and written notes.

The accused, the in-law of the deceased, was charged in a dowry death case after the accused's child's spouse (the deceased) died due to 85% burn injuries. While a dying declaration indicated that the deceased self-immolated, it also mentioned harassment by multiple family members. The deceased's parent filed an affidavit stating that the allegations in the FIR were incorrect. The Court found the accusations vague and granted bail.

The deceased, the spouse of the accused, died allegedly by poisoning within two years of marriage. The FIR alleged harassment for dowry of ₹50,000. Anticipatory bail was granted to the accused under suspicious circumstances by a Sessions Judge, whose child represented the accused while the Sessions Judge's parent was the Government Pleader. The High Court noted improper judicial conduct and a strong prima facie case of dowry death.

Wait, correcting the relationships: the original states that the Sessions Judge's son represented the accused while "the father" was the Government Pleader, where "the father" is ambiguous. Neutral rewrite:

The deceased, the spouse of the accused, died allegedly by poisoning within two years of marriage. The FIR alleged harassment for dowry of ₹50,000. Anticipatory bail was granted to the accused under suspicious circumstances by a Sessions Judge whose child represented the accused while the Sessions Judge was the Government Pleader. The High Court noted improper judicial conduct and a strong prima facie case of dowry death.

The accused was arrested after marrying a minor who became pregnant. The marriage was arranged under familial pressure. The accused was charged under IPC Section 376 and under the POCSO Act and the Child Marriage Act. The victim admitted that the marriage took place under family pressure. There was no specific allegation of sexual assault beyond marital cohabitation. The accused had been in custody for nearly six months when the High Court granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have abducted and sexually assaulted a minor. The FIR was filed two days after the alleged incident, and the victim later made a statement suggesting the victim had implicated the accused out of fear of the victim's parent. Medical records and CCTV footage were inconclusive, and there were inconsistencies in the victim's narrative under Section 161 CrPC.

The petitioner, the accused (accused no. 3), was arrested along with others for abducting and gang-raping a minor. The incident involved confinement and repeated sexual assault by multiple accused. The prior bail application had been rejected. Accused no. 1 later committed suicide in jail. The petitioner filed a fresh bail plea shortly after, citing no new material changes.

The accused was charged with abducting and sexually assaulting a minor with the help of a co-accused. The accused allegedly raped the victim after forcibly taking them in an autorickshaw, and the victim later attempted suicide. The Sessions Court granted the accused bail, citing the duration of custody and the accused's family role. The State sought cancellation of bail, citing ignored evidence, including the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC.

The petitioner was in a long-term relationship with the complainant, a person with a disability. The complainant alleged that the petitioner abducted them, staged a fake court marriage, and sexually assaulted them multiple times under the pretext of marriage. After the relationship ended, the petitioner began a new relationship, prompting the complainant to file an FIR. The petitioner sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest.

Based on information from an NGO, police raided a house and found minors who were allegedly trafficked for sexual exploitation. The accused was found in one room with a minor, who stated that the accused assaulted them and forced them into sexual activity. Condoms were recovered from the scene. The accused claimed innocence and cited the absence of any direct recovery from them, as well as the grant of bail to similarly placed co-accused.

The applicant was accused under IPC and POCSO sections for allegedly sexually assaulting a minor. The FIR included grave charges, but the defence argued that the accused was cooperating and posed no flight risk. The court considered legal precedent and imposed multiple conditions while granting anticipatory bail.

The accused were booked under sections of the IPC and the POCSO Act following an FIR that alleged sexual harassment and related offences. The defence argued that the allegations did not require custodial interrogation and that the accused were cooperative. The Court, relying on precedent, granted anticipatory bail with several conditions.

The petitioner was arrested for allegedly having sexual intercourse with a minor who stayed with them for several days. Although the petitioner claimed the relationship was consensual, the victim was a minor under POCSO. The FSL report showed no biological evidence, but the medical report confirmed an old hymen tear. The petitioner had a prior similar case in which they were acquitted because the victim turned hostile.

The accused was booked under IPC and POCSO sections for allegedly sexually harassing a minor. The FIR was filed several days after the alleged incident. The defence highlighted an amicable settlement with the complainant, a supporting affidavit, and no need for custodial interrogation. The court took note of these and granted anticipatory bail with conditions.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case involving allegations of attempt to rape and murder under IPC and POCSO provisions. Though a co-accused had been granted bail, the accused's antecedents became disputed. The defence claimed only one pending case, but the prosecution submitted that the accused had seven cases as per the case diary. The Court deferred decision pending clarification via affidavit.

The complainant, a doctor employed with a railway establishment, alleged that their superior, the applicant, sexually harassed them at the workplace through offensive remarks and misconduct. An internal committee dismissed the complaint for lack of evidentiary support. The defence claimed the complaint was retaliatory because of a transfer and emphasised the applicant's unblemished record. The High Court granted anticipatory bail, citing lack of prima facie evidence and legal precedents.

The applicant was accused of assisting in transporting the victim in a case involving sexual assault under POCSO and IPC sections. The FIR alleged that the applicant helped facilitate the victim's travel with the main accused. The defence argued that custodial interrogation was unnecessary and that the applicant was cooperative. The Court granted anticipatory bail with conditions.

The accused sought pre-arrest bail in a case where they were accused of sexually abusing a minor. The victim, in a Section 164 CrPC statement, directly implicated the accused. The defence argued that the victim visited the house voluntarily and that the accused was falsely implicated. The prosecution and Amicus Curiae strongly opposed bail, citing the victim's minority and credible testimony.

The accused, convicted under Section 376(1) IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act for raping a minor with a disability, sought suspension of sentence and bail during the pendency of their appeal. The accused had served five years of a ten-year sentence. The prosecution opposed the application, citing medical evidence and the gravity of the offence. The court reviewed the record and denied the request.

The applicant was accused of misbehaving with the victim, an adult, after the victim informed a relative about the applicant's actions. The incident took place on a certain date. The victim refused medical examination. The applicant had no prior criminal record and had been in custody since a couple of days after the incident.

The accused was arrested under IPC Sections 354-A, 452, 506, 34 and POCSO Act Sections 7/8 for alleged misconduct involving a child. The accused had been in custody since the date of arrest. The accused claimed false implication and sought bail on the basis of parity with a co-accused who had already been granted bail.

The petitioner, an adult and a student, is co-accused 3 in a case involving alleged sexual offences. The incident allegedly occurred in April of one year, but the complaint was lodged only about nineteen months later. No criminal history was noted, and co-accused 2 was already granted anticipatory bail.

The petitioner allegedly took offensive photographs of the deceased and used them to blackmail the deceased for sexual favours, leading to the suicide of a couple. The case was registered under IPC Sections 306 and 34. The petitioner sought anticipatory bail on grounds of parity with a co-accused who had been granted bail.

The appellant was convicted under Section 8 of the POCSO Act and sentenced to 3 years of rigorous imprisonment with a fine. The appellant was on bail during the trial and did not misuse it. After conviction, the sentence was temporarily suspended to allow the filing of an appeal.

The applicant was accused of assisting the main accused in kidnapping a minor who was allegedly sexually assaulted by the co-accused. An FIR was filed under sections of the IPC and the POCSO Act. The Court noted the applicant's limited role and the applicant's age.

The complainant filed an application seeking cancellation of the anticipatory bail granted to the accused in a case involving IPC Sections 354A and 506(1), and POCSO Sections 11 and 12. The accused had earlier been granted anticipatory bail by the Sessions Court.

The accused was charged under IPC sections relating to kidnapping and rape, as well as under the POCSO Act and the SC/ST Act. The victim initially did not name the accused and refused medical examination. Three months later, the victim underwent a medical examination, which implicated the accused. The accused had a prior similar case filed by the same victim, in which the accused was granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped and sexually assaulted a minor. The victim travelled with the accused across several cities and lived with the accused for about four months. Contradictions were found between the victim's statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC, and the victim's medical examination showed no injuries. The accused had no prior criminal record.

The petitioner alleged that the accused coerced them into a sexual relationship, many years earlier, under the false promise of marriage, and continued the relationship through threats and coercion. A charge sheet was filed under multiple IPC sections. Bail had been granted to the accused several years earlier, and the petitioner sought its cancellation citing ongoing threats and coercion.

The victim was allegedly kidnapped and gang-raped by the accused and others, but the initial statements and the FIR did not contain allegations of rape. Allegations of gang rape appeared only in the statement under Section 164 CrPC, which was recorded 5 months later. The accused claimed to have saved the victim earlier and to have informed the police. The court noted the delay, the contradictions, and the lack of any criminal history of the accused.

The applicant was convicted under IPC Section 376(2)(n) and Sections 4 and 6 of the POCSO Act and sentenced to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment. The applicant applied for suspension of sentence and bail pending appeal. The court noted the seriousness of the offense and absence of bail during trial.

The accused was arrested under multiple sections of the NDPS Act for allegedly procuring and financing drug use for another person. The central narcotics agency alleged that the accused facilitated and financed drug procurement through intermediaries. The accused's bail plea was earlier rejected by the Special Court, citing Section 27A. The High Court found no material showing the accused's active involvement in drug trafficking or harbouring under Section 27A.

The accused and others were arrested with 41.1 kg of ganja in a vehicle. The charge sheet was filed within 180 days but without the Chemical Analyzer report. The accused claimed default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC, arguing that the charge sheet was incomplete under the NDPS Act.

A minor was repeatedly raped and sexually assaulted by multiple accused over a period of several months. The assaults were committed under threats involving a video. An FIR was filed shortly after the last of the assaults. The accused were arrested shortly thereafter. The complainant named each accused and provided detailed instances of assault.

The victim, a minor, was allegedly sexually assaulted by the accused, a relative, during a week-long stay at the accused's house. The FIR was filed over a month later, after a family dispute. Medical reports showed no evidence of assault.

The complainant, a student and youth leader of a political organisation, alleged that the accused, a police constable, developed a relationship with the complainant under the promise of marriage and later sexually assaulted the complainant. An FIR was registered under IPC Sections 376, 420, 506 and provisions of the Atrocities Act. The accused sought anticipatory bail after a Sessions Court rejected it.

The accused and the victim, who was a minor, were in a romantic relationship. On a certain date, they eloped, allegedly married in a temple, and stayed together for about two weeks until they were found. The accused was arrested and charged under sections of the IPC and the POCSO Act. The prosecution claimed kidnapping and rape, while the defence argued it was a consensual elopement.

The accused, the chairman of an unregistered child shelter, was alleged to have sexually abused several minor inmates over a period of years. An FIR was lodged following a complaint by the Child Welfare Committee, which was based on reports made by the children. The charge sheet included offences under the IPC and the POCSO Act. Some of the victims turned hostile, while others remained to be examined.

The petitioner sought cancellation of bail granted to their spouse, the accused, in a case involving charges of rape and sexual assault on their child. The petitioner alleged pre-bail threats, procedural violations, and misuse of judicial process. The court noted no post-bail violations and dismissed the cancellation petition.

The petitioners, including two of the accused, sought anticipatory bail in relation to an FIR for offences including cruelty and later gang rape. The complainant alleged severe mistreatment and sexual abuse by their in-laws and an unidentified person who claimed to perform spiritual rituals. The complainant's statement under Section 164 CrPC led to the addition of Section 376D IPC. Interim bail was granted earlier but later challenged.

The accused was charged with raping a minor, leading to the minor's pregnancy and childbirth. The victim made conflicting statements, implicating both the accused and another person, referred to here as the co-accused. A DNA report excluded the accused as the biological parent of the child, and surprisingly also indicated that the victim was not the biological parent of the child. The trial court had earlier denied bail.

The petitioner, who is co-accused 2, allegedly videographed the sexual assault of a minor by co-accused 1 and helped circulate the video. The victim was coerced by co-accused 1 into accompanying them, and the assault was recorded and later shared. The petitioner was arrested and remained in judicial custody for over 6 months before applying for bail.

The victim was coerced by co-accused 1 into accompanying them, and the assault was recorded and later shared. The petitioner was arrested and remained in judicial custody for over 6 months before applying for bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a registered crime under IPC sections 354, 452, 294, 506 and sections 7/8 of the POCSO Act. The victim, a minor, gave a statement implicating the accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2015 and had a prior criminal record. The chargesheet had already been filed at the time of the hearing.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case involving the trafficking and repeated sexual assault of a minor. The minor had gone missing for almost five months and was later recovered. Although the victim and the victim's parents turned hostile during trial, the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC directly implicated the accused. The accused has been in custody since an earlier date, as stated in the record.

The accused was arrested on a date in 2020 for housebreaking and theft under IPC Sections 379 and 457. The State opposed bail citing eight prior similar theft cases against the accused. The accused claimed false implication and requested release due to continued detention.

The accused was arrested in a case involving theft and sale of vehicles with forged engine and chassis numbers. The prosecution alleged that the accused, who owned a garage, played a role in modifying the vehicle identification numbers. Multiple co-accused had already been granted bail by the trial court and the High Court.

Based on information received, police raided the house of the accused and recovered 1068 kg of dried ganja in 27 containers. The accused was not present during the raid. The accused was granted anticipatory bail by the Special Judge, which the State sought to cancel.

Some time ago, the child of the appellant was shot and later died of the injuries. The FIR implicated the accused. Despite serious allegations, the Sessions Court granted anticipatory bail to the accused. The complainant challenged the order.

An interim bail was granted to an accused under IPC Section 376 and POCSO Section 4 without issuing the mandatory notice to the complainant. The complainant, a minor represented through their parent, filed a petition seeking cancellation of the bail. The court noted widespread non-compliance with the law requiring notice to the complainant in such cases.

The petitioner challenged the preventive detention order against their child, who was accused of sexually assaulting a minor. The detenu had been released on bail and had no prior criminal history. The detention order was based solely on this one FIR and alleged future risk to public order.

An adult accused was alleged to have repeatedly sexually assaulted a minor victim. The FIR was filed on the complaint of the victim's parent. The Trial Court granted regular bail, misinterpreting the applicable provisions of the POCSO Act. The victim testified in court supporting the allegations. The High Court found the grant of bail improper and cancelled it.

The complainant alleged that their minor child was kidnapped and sexually assaulted by the accused multiple times in a city. The accused was granted bail during investigation. The complainant later sought cancellation of the bail order, claiming the trial court had ignored vital evidence including the victim's statement and medical report.

The accused was booked under IPC Section 376AB and the POCSO Act for sexually assaulting a minor child aged below the age of twelve. The accused was granted regular bail by the Special Court. Subsequently, a preventive detention order was issued by the state citing public order concerns. The accused challenged the detention order in a writ petition.

The accused was alleged to have facilitated the smuggling of high-quality counterfeit Indian currency from a foreign country to India. The accused allegedly arranged visas and tickets for couriers, funded logistics, and maintained transaction records. Counterfeit currency was recovered from a co-accused. A national investigation agency charged the accused under provisions of the IPC and the UAPA.

The accused was arrested after an altercation with an official. The Magistrate granted the accused bail, but the accused was not released and was subsequently re-arrested under Section 151 CrPC. A sub-divisional officer allegedly manipulated court records to show that bail had been rejected, and the accused's detention was extended illegally. The High Court found gross misconduct and awarded compensation.

The appellant was accused in a series of bomb blasts in a town in 2006, which killed 31 people and injured over 300 people. A national investigating agency took over the investigation from earlier investigating agencies and filed a supplementary chargesheet naming the appellant among others. The bombs were allegedly planted in bicycles at sites with a large population of a particular community, allegedly as part of a larger conspiracy.

While posted as a judge, the judicial officer granted bail in an NDPS matter involving 3 kg of opium, ignoring the fact that an earlier bail application had been rejected by another judge. No reasons were recorded for deviating from the earlier decision. A second accused was denied bail shortly after. These contradictory orders led to questions about the officer's integrity and the officer's compulsory retirement.

The accused, a juvenile at the time of the offence, was accused under Section 302 IPC in a case registered at a police station. The Juvenile Justice Board determined the accused's age and referred the accused for trial as an adult. The bail application before the Children's Court was rejected, leading to an appeal under Section 101(5) of the JJ Act.

The accused and the co-accused were convicted under Sections 302, 364, and 201 IPC. While the co-accused was later granted bail during appeal, the accused's subsequent bail applications were rejected due to a legal conflict over whether parity applied and which bench had jurisdiction to decide repeated bail pleas. The matter was escalated to a Full Bench for resolution.

On a certain date in 2006, four bomb explosions occurred in a town in a state, killing 31 people and injuring over 300. The initial investigation attributed the explosions to members of an organisation. Later, a central investigating agency reinvestigated and charged a different set of accused, including the appellant, alleging an extremist conspiracy.

The accused, a juvenile, was accused in a murder case under Section 302 of the IPC and was taken into custody. The Juvenile Justice Board assessed the accused and ordered trial as an adult due to the heinous nature of the offence. The accused's bail application before the Children's Court was rejected. The accused challenged the order under Section 101(5) of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015.

On a certain date in 2006, four bombs exploded in a town in a state, killing 31 people and injuring over 300. Initially, a state anti-terror squad and a central investigating agency investigated the case and charged members of a particular group. Later, a national investigating agency took over the investigation and filed a supplementary chargesheet against the accused and others, alleging a different conspiracy.

The accused was booked along with three co-accused under Section 302 IPC. Earlier bail applications of the accused and some co-accused were rejected. Some co-accused were later granted bail. The accused filed a third bail application claiming parity with the co-accused.

The accused was arrested for illegal arms possession. The recovery included multiple pistols, foreign arms parts, and forged licenses. The investigation revealed links with multiple co-accused, and sales of illegal arms to anti-national groups. The accused was managing a gun shop illegally and was found to have deposited large sums in accounts linked to co-accused involved in arms smuggling.

The accused was arrested for allegedly abducting and raping a minor. The FIR included charges under IPC Sections 363, 366, and 376. However, during the investigation, the victim and the victim's parent gave statements not supporting the prosecution case.

The complainant purchased a property in a city in 2018. The complainant's spouse, who was suffering from a psychological disorder, allegedly sold the property using a forged power of attorney. The accused was the beneficiary of this forged sale deed. Multiple FIRs were filed, including for criminal trespass and forgery. Anticipatory bail granted earlier to the accused was challenged by the complainant.

The accused, who ran an educational institution, allegedly issued fake degrees, diplomas, and certificates without proper authorization, duping numerous students. The certificates spanned various courses and durations. After initially providing an undertaking to refund the money, the accused failed to comply. Despite the High Court denying bail, a Magistrate erroneously granted it.

The accused was detained under the COFEPOSA Act for allegedly smuggling 2.4 kg of gold from a foreign city to another city in the country by concealing it in their sandals. The accused admitted to previous instances of smuggling and to connections with other persons in two other cities. The accused's electronic devices revealed detailed chats, voice notes, and transactions linked to a gold smuggling network.

The accused, a juvenile, was alleged to be involved in a case concerning the death of the accused's in-law, the deceased, due to alleged dowry-related bride burning. The deceased had been married six months earlier and reportedly suffered 95% burn injuries. A dying declaration implicated the accused. The Juvenile Justice Board assessed the accused's age and mental maturity, and transferred the case for trial as an adult.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was charged under Sections 304B, 306, 498 and 114 IPC along with provisions of the SC/ST Act. The deceased committed suicide within four months of marriage. The allegations included harassment over dowry and pressure to obtain a flat. However, the FIR and supporting materials did not indicate specific acts or instigation attributable to the petitioner. The court noted the accused's five-month custody and the absence of any direct role in the deceased's decision to take their own life.

The accused, a juvenile, was accused under Section 302 IPC in a case registered at a police station. The Juvenile Justice Board determined the accused's age and referred the accused to be tried as an adult. The accused's bail application was rejected by the Children's Court in a district, prompting the present appeal.

On a certain date in 2006, multiple bomb blasts took place in a town, killing 31 people and injuring over 312 people. Initially, members of an organisation were accused and later released. A central investigating agency reinvestigated the matter and named new accused, including the accused in this case, who allegedly planted bombs along with co-conspirators. Bicycles used in the blasts were traced to purchases made under false names.

The applicant, an advocate, was accused by a law student who was interning with them of sexually assaulting the student over an extended period. The complaint alleged administration of poison and forced abortions. The first bail application was rejected. The applicant filed a second bail application citing a fabricated case due to personal disputes.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case investigated by a national investigating agency involving illegal funding for a banned terrorist organisation. The accused was alleged to have helped arrange large sums of money for the procurement of arms. The accused was initially granted interim bail on health grounds, but this was later cancelled after an appeal by the investigating agency.

The case involved the murder of the victim, allegedly due to rivalry over illegal sand mining. According to the FIR and eyewitness accounts, one accused held the victim while a co-accused shot the victim, and another accused assaulted the complainant. The High Court had granted anticipatory bail citing alibi and lack of direct evidence, but the Supreme Court found the High Court had ignored significant eyewitness testimony and investigation gaps, and thus cancelled the bail.

The accused, along with several others, was charged in connection with a 2002 train burning incident, specifically a fire on a passenger train near a railway station in a town. The case involved serious allegations under the IPC, the Indian Railways Act, the Prevention of Damage to Public Property Act, and subsequently under POTA. The petitioners argued mistaken identity, lack of direct involvement, and political bias in their implication.

Bomb blasts occurred in a town in a state, killing 31 people and injuring 312. Initially, certain persons were charged, but later a central investigating agency alleged that a different group of persons was responsible. The four appellants were arrested for allegedly planting the bombs, based on the agency's fresh investigation.

The accused, a district-level office-bearer of a political party, was alleged to have led a group that blocked a highway and caused damage to public property. The accused was initially granted bail, which was later cancelled by the Sessions Court. The High Court reviewed this cancellation.

A central investigating agency for serious corporate fraud investigated a large corporate fraud involving a credit cooperative society and a group of companies. The accused, along with others, allegedly siphoned public funds through shell companies using forged documents and accounting frauds. Multiple bailable and non-bailable warrants were issued because the accused was evading appearance before the court.

The accused was facing charges under IPC Sections 376 read with 511 and 354. The accused was earlier granted limited anticipatory bail by the High Court. After the accused's regular bail application was rejected by the Magistrate and the Sessions Judge refused to hear the case on maintainability grounds, the accused approached the High Court under Section 439 read with Section 482 CrPC.

The accused allegedly misappropriated Rs. 50,00,000 and Rs. 4,08,500 from the account of a newspaper organisation. Handwriting evidence implicated other staff, but the court found a prima facie case against the accused. Earlier anticipatory and regular bail were denied, and this was a repeat application after the charge sheet was filed.

The accused was implicated in a motorcycle theft case and sought anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC. The case was based solely on a co-accused's confessional statement under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The court noted the offence was punishable with imprisonment of up to 7 years and cited the Supreme Court's Arnesh Kumar guidelines to protect against unnecessary arrest.

The accused, along with others, allegedly kidnapped a minor and subjected the minor to rape. The victim made a statement under Section 164 CrPC, corroborating the allegations. Bail was granted by the lower court without proper evaluation.

The case involves multiple murder incidents registered under different FIRs, in which groups of accused were released on bail by the same Sessions Judge despite earlier rejection of their bail applications by another Sessions Judge and even by the High Court. In some cases, bail was granted without any new circumstances or justification. The victims were killed with multiple injuries inflicted by weapons such as sticks, spears, and axes.

A bank manager was stabbed multiple times late at night and later died. The prosecution alleged that the accused and co-accused ambushed and fatally assaulted the victim with sharp weapons. There were two eyewitnesses and a dying declaration. Bail had earlier been granted to the accused by a Sessions Court, but this was challenged by the State.

During a riot in a city, a mob of 2000–3000 people allegedly attacked the house of a public representative, looted documents and valuables, and set the house and vehicles on fire. The accused was arrested and charged with rioting, dacoity, arson, and other offences. Multiple charge sheets were filed against various accused involved.

The accused was arrested for allegedly assisting the chief of a banned organisation in converting extorted money collected from levies into legitimate funds through shell companies. The accused was a co-director in firms allegedly used to channel terror funds and was allegedly involved in hawala operations. The funds were linked to terror financing under the UAPA. The accused's prior bail applications were rejected by both the High Court and the Supreme Court.

A person was shot dead in 2013 while on a morning walk. A central investigating agency later arrested several individuals, including the accused, alleging that the accused helped conduct reconnaissance and provided escape route guidance. The case involved charges under the UAPA and the IPC.

The accused was alleged to have attempted to kidnap and rape a minor near the house of the victim's relative. The victim was later rescued by relatives. Medical evidence and eyewitness accounts failed to conclusively support the rape charge.

The accused was alleged to have travelled to a foreign country to join a proscribed terrorist organisation for the purpose of engaging in armed activities. The accused was arrested upon returning to the country in 2014 and remained in custody for over six years while facing trial under the UAPA and Section 125 of the IPC. The prosecution alleged that the accused intended to conduct terrorist activities in the country, including plans to target a police headquarters in a city.

The victim alleged that the accused took them in a car under threat, dropped the victim's relative, and drove the victim to another location where the accused allegedly compelled the victim into marriage and had sexual intercourse on the pretext of marriage. The next day, the accused dropped the victim at a village and refused to marry the victim.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a minor. The FIR was lodged by the minor's relative after the minor did not return home. Later, the minor, in a statement under Section 164 CrPC, denied any kidnapping and stated that they had left home voluntarily due to family issues.

The victim, a minor, was allegedly made to elope by a co-accused with a promise of marriage. The victim was later sexually assaulted by the co-accused and left in the custody of the present bail petitioners. The petitioners brought the victim to a police station, and an FIR was registered under various sections of the IPC and the POCSO Act.

The accused was arrested in connection with a theft that occurred in a city, where valuable gold jewelry and other items were stolen from a locked house. During investigation, the accused and other co-accused admitted to multiple thefts, including this one. Police records show the accused is a habitual offender with previous theft charges, and also cases under the Arms Act and Gangsters Act.

The accused was implicated in a kidnapping case in which the victim was abducted and a ransom of Rs.5 crores was demanded. The victim later returned and gave statements identifying the accused. The defence argued that the accused was not named in the FIR and put forward a plea of alibi, claiming to have been in a city elsewhere at the time of the incident.

The accused was charged with rape under Section 376 IPC along with other offences. The FIR was registered by the complainant after a delay. The accused had been in custody for over 18 months. The statement under Section 164 CrPC did not directly support the prosecution's version.

The complainant alleged that the accused kidnapped the complainant's minor child, who failed to return from school. The minor was later recovered from the accused's residence. The FIR was filed 22 days after the incident. The minor claimed to have voluntarily gone with the accused and married the accused. An FSL report indicated that the minor was under 18 years of age at the time.

The accused was charged with kidnapping and sexually assaulting a minor, who allegedly eloped with the accused. The minor was recovered after being kept in illegal confinement for several days, during which the minor stated that they were sexually assaulted. The prosecution emphasized the seriousness of the charges because the victim was a minor.

The petitioner was alleged to have assisted in the elopement and stay of a minor who was allegedly kidnapped and sexually assaulted by the main accused. The petitioner's role was limited to accompanying the main accused and helping arrange a place to stay. The victim claimed kidnapping and lack of consent for physical relations.

The minor victim was allegedly kidnapped by the main co-accused with help from the accused. The victim had been communicating with the main co-accused and expressed a desire to marry them after attaining majority. An FIR was lodged by the victim's parent, and the accused was arrested. Investigation revealed contradictions between the parent's complaint and the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC.

The appellant, who was the complainant, lodged an FIR alleging that two persons, sent by the accused, abducted the victim at gunpoint and kept the victim confined for eight days. The victim escaped and narrated the events, implicating the accused. The High Court granted bail to the accused, which was later challenged in the Supreme Court.

The complainant's child, a minor, was sexually assaulted by multiple accused, including the petitioner, who allegedly raped the minor, recorded videos, and blackmailed the minor. The assaults occurred while the minor was alone at home during the COVID-19 lockdown. Accused No.2, the petitioner, was arrested and sought anticipatory bail.

The accused, an adult student, was involved in kidnapping a minor relative of the accused, along with a person with whom the accused was in a relationship and others, in order to demand ransom. After taking the child on an outing, the accused handed the child over to the co-accused, who demanded ₹1 crore as ransom. The accused was later caught red-handed along with others while collecting the ransom.

The complainant, a college student, alleged that the accused, who had a relationship with the complainant's parent, sexually assaulted the complainant in one year and again several years later. Anticipatory bail had been granted earlier to the accused. That grant was challenged on the grounds that proper custodial interrogation was not allowed and that the Sessions Court erred in evaluating the complaint.

The petitioner was accused of sexually assaulting a minor in an earlier month of the same year, with whom the petitioner was allegedly in a romantic relationship. The minor had earlier been sexually assaulted by their relatives (accused no.1 and no.3), who were granted bail. The petitioner was arrested later that year and remained in custody until bail was granted.

The victim alleged that they were sexually assaulted by the applicant and other co-accused under threats and blackmail involving nude photos. The incidents allegedly began in a particular month in 2019 and continued until early 2020. The FIR was filed more than a year later, about 15 months after the alleged events. The defense highlighted inconsistencies in the victim's accounts and the lack of evidence such as the nude photos.

The accused was convicted under sections of the IPC and the POCSO Act for assisting in a sexual assault committed by a co-convict. The victim testified that the accused closed the door, thereby aiding the co-convict. An appeal followed the conviction. The accused had spent over 1 year and 5 months in custody against a 3-year sentence.

The petitioner, accused of separate instances of sexual assault on a minor within a 24-hour period along with co-accused, was arrested on a certain date. The victim claimed multiple assaults by different individuals. Co-accused 2 was previously granted bail; the petitioner sought parity and challenged the inconsistencies in the victim's account.

The complainant alleged that the accused, a known acquaintance, had forcibly established physical relations with the complainant on multiple occasions and blackmailed the complainant using intimate videos and photos. The FIR includes charges of sexual assault, criminal intimidation, and wrongful confinement. The accused did not cooperate with the investigation, and non-bailable warrants were issued.

The victim, a minor staying in a government hostel, alleged that the accused, a relative of the victim, repeatedly raped the victim at a relative's home. A pregnancy resulted, and a DNA test was conducted. The accused was arrested and has been in custody since.

The case involves allegations from several years earlier, in which the victim left home and was later married to another person, allegedly facilitated by the accused. The victim explicitly denied any sexual relations with the accused and stated that only the other person was involved. The FIR was filed several years after the alleged incident. Co-accused persons with more direct roles in the assault had already been granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have disrupted a public celebration and participated in a group assault causing head injury to the victim. A person also alleged misbehavior by the accused, though no sexual assault was reported. The co-accused had already been granted bail. The accused had no prior criminal history and had been in custody since a date in 2023.

The petitioner was accused of repeatedly raping a minor, who later became pregnant and delivered a child. The alleged acts took place while the accused's spouse was away for childbirth, and with the assistance of the accused's sibling. The complaint was filed after the minor's pregnancy was discovered by the minor's parent. Investigation was completed and the charge sheet was filed, but DNA testing was still pending.

The accused was alleged to have sexually assaulted a minor. The victim alleged forced undressing, threats, and sexual abuse. Initial medical reports showed post-anal injuries, though later reports were inconclusive. The accused, as petitioner, denied the allegations and pointed to the lack of conclusive medical evidence. The victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC was detailed and accusatory.

The complainant, an adult who is married, alleged that the accused, a neighbour, had persistently harassed the complainant and attempted to force a sexual relationship. On the day of the incident, the accused ambushed the complainant on the way from school, tore the complainant's shirt, and touched the complainant inappropriately. The complainant reported the incident to the complainant's family and local authorities. The police recorded the complainant's statement and collected the torn shirt as evidence.

The petitioner was accused, along with their child, of sexually assaulting the victim by taking turns inside the victim's house. The petitioner was charged under the IPC and the SC/ST Act. However, the DNA report did not match the petitioner, raising doubts about the prosecution's case.

The petitioner was arrested for allegedly engaging in paid sexual activity with a minor, which was facilitated by another person. The victim disclosed the incident during a police inquiry into an unrelated theft. The police arrested the petitioner based on the victim's identification and phone call records. The victim had alleged similar acts against multiple individuals, but only three were arrested.

The victim, an adult, alleged that the accused, a member of the armed forces, had sexual relations with them in a hotel in a certain month of 2021 under the pretext of marriage. They had been in contact since the previous year. The FIR was filed several months after the alleged incident, following the accused's refusal to marry the victim. The accused had already joined the investigation by the time of the bail hearing.

The petitioner, who was related to the complainant's parent as an adopted sibling, allegedly played a role in facilitating the complainant's elopement with the complainant's in-law relative, the main accused, who later allegedly committed sexual assault. The petitioner parted ways with the main accused midway through the journey. The main allegations of rape were against the main accused, who was the complainant's in-law relative.

The appellant was in a consensual relationship with a minor and allegedly had sexual intercourse with the minor. A complaint was filed by the victim's parent. The appellant was arrested several months before the appeal, and the appellant's bail application was initially rejected. On appeal, the High Court noted the consensual relationship and found no need for continued custody.

The accused was convicted for conspiring to open fictitious accounts and divert compensation meant for victims of a riot. The accused was found guilty under Sections 467, 468, 471 read with 120B IPC and sentenced to 5 years of imprisonment. The appeal seeks suspension of sentence during pendency.

The petitioner was accused of kidnapping and raping a minor. The petitioner had already been granted bail in connection with the foundational offences. The current anticipatory bail application arose after additional sections of the MPDVPK Act were added. The Court considered the pandemic and the lack of flight risk while granting bail.

The petitioner was in custody for over four years in a kidnapping case under IPC Sections 364A, 120B, and 34. The kidnapped minor did not identify the petitioner during trial, though the minor identified a co-accused, who has already been granted bail.

The petitioner was accused under IPC Section 366A/34 for allegedly being involved in the enticement of the informant's married child. The main allegation of kidnapping was against a co-accused who has already been granted bail. The petitioner had been in custody since a date in an earlier year and had no similar past criminal record.

The petitioner was accused of kidnapping the informant's sibling with intent to murder or secretly confine them. An earlier anticipatory bail plea had been rejected, and despite parity arguments, the Court found no grounds to revisit its prior decision.

The petitioner was accused of kidnapping a minor along with co-accused. The minor, in their statement under Section 164 CrPC, did not support the prosecution. There was a 24-day delay in filing the FIR, and the petitioner had no prior criminal record. Co-accused with similar allegations were previously granted bail.

The accused was charged with kidnapping, wrongful confinement, and rape of a minor under the IPC and the POCSO Act. The victim later returned home and did not support the prosecution. Key witnesses, including the victim's family, turned hostile. The accused had been in custody for 4 months before being released on bail.

The accused was charged with kidnapping and sexually assaulting a minor over a period of two months. The victim and the victim's parent later denied the accusations, testifying that the victim had gone away voluntarily. It was revealed that the victim and the accused married after the victim attained majority, and they were living together with a child.

The appellant was convicted for defrauding compensation meant for victims of a riot by creating fictitious accounts and diverting funds. The appellant was sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment under various IPC sections for conspiracy, cheating, and forgery. The appellant sought suspension of sentence during appeal.

The accused, convicted for the abduction and murder of the deceased, sought interim bail to attend a sibling's wedding. The accused was serving a life sentence and had a prior history of misuse of bail during another murder case. The accused argued familial obligations, but the State and the complainant opposed the application, citing flight risk and threat to witnesses.

The accused was implicated based on the disclosure of a co-accused, from whom 1.925 kg of Ganja leaves were recovered. The petitioner was not caught at the spot. The accused argued that Ganja leaves are not covered under the NDPS definition and that the implication was retaliatory due to a complaint made by the accused's sibling against the police. The accused was arrested and the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The petitioner, accused of aiding in the kidnapping of a minor for ransom, was identified in the Test Identification Parade and implicated through a recovered mobile phone and SIM card. The accused was also involved in a prior NDPS case. The ransom demand and communication were made using a SIM card activated through a third party. The bail petition was a successive one, filed after earlier rejections.

The accused was alleged to have masterminded a large-scale liquor scam in a state involving senior bureaucrats and politicians. The case involves illegal commissions, fake holograms, and diversion of liquor, causing a loss of over ₹2100 crores to the state. The Directorate of Enforcement initiated a money laundering case under the PMLA. The petitioner had been in custody for several months and challenged their prolonged detention and double arrest in related ECIRs.

The petitioners were convicted of murder and related charges under Sections 148, 307, and 302 read with Section 149 IPC, and sentenced to life imprisonment. They applied for bail under Section 389(1) CrPC after completing five years of actual sentence. The court considered their eligibility in light of a precedent on suspension of sentence and bail pending appeal, and found no disqualifying factors such as offences of exceptional gravity.

The petitioner was arrested with 35 Buprenorphine injections and 35 Avil injections. The petitioner claimed the recovery was planted and attempted to invoke Rule 66 of the NDPS Rules, 1985, arguing personal medical use. The court held that there was no documentary proof or prescription to support this claim.

The petitioner was arrested in an NDPS case involving 425.5 kg of ganja recovered from a truck. The petitioner claimed to be a helper with no knowledge of the contraband. A previous bail application was rejected on merits. The petitioner again sought default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC, which was rejected as premature since only 90 days had passed out of the 180-day limit under the NDPS Act.

The accused was arrested for possession of 100 Etizolam tablets, a commercial quantity under the NDPS Act. The accused had no prior criminal antecedents and had spent over a year in custody. The defense invoked Article 21 and relied on precedents of prolonged custody where bail was granted despite the Section 37 NDPS bar.

The accused, a foreign national, was arrested at an airport carrying a large quantity of Diazepam tablets. The accused admitted to the possession in a statement under Section 67 NDPS Act. The High Court granted bail, holding that it was not proven that the substance matched the NDPS Schedule. The customs authorities appealed, citing the Central Revenue Control Lab report and the Section 37 bar on bail.

The accused was arrested under the NDPS Act. The accused's bail plea was rejected by the Sessions Court and the High Court under Section 37 of the NDPS Act. The accused later claimed a right to default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC due to delay in filing the charge sheet. However, the charge sheet was filed several months after the arrest, before the accused asserted this right.

The accused was caught at a police checkpoint with 199 bottles of a cough syrup containing Codeine Phosphate and Triprolidine Hydrochloride. The prosecution argued that the quantity exceeded the threshold for commercial quantity under the NDPS Act. The accused challenged the applicability of the NDPS Act, citing therapeutic use limits and exemptions under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

The petitioner, a forwarding agent, was arrested in 2012 for alleged involvement in the export of 151.980 kg of ketamine. The petitioner was charged under multiple sections of the NDPS Act. The petitioner's bail applications had been repeatedly rejected over the years. The petitioner argued that they had been in custody for over 9 years and that the trial was yet to conclude. The prosecution opposed bail, citing the commercial quantity involved and prior statements recorded under Section 67 of the NDPS Act.

The accused was apprehended by police in a city based on a tip-off and was allegedly found in possession of 1.017 kg of charas in a plastic bag. The accused was arrested under Section 8/21 of the NDPS Act. The accused claimed false implication due to enmity with a local political family, and pointed to the lack of independent witnesses despite the arrest occurring in a busy area.

The petitioner was accused in a dowry death case after the petitioner's child's spouse, the deceased, died due to 90% burns within months of marriage. Allegations included harassment and dowry demands. The prosecution cited witness statements and pending investigation against the co-accused. The defence argued that the deceased did not accuse the petitioner in the dying declaration and that efforts to record the deceased's statement before a magistrate failed.

The applicants, who are in-laws of the complainant (a sibling of the complainant's spouse and that sibling's spouse), were accused under IPC sections related to dowry harassment. They claimed false implication based on omnibus allegations without specific acts. The prosecution opposed bail citing Rs. 65 lakh given as dowry. The Court applied the Arnesh Kumar precedent to avoid unnecessary arrest.

The accused was charged in connection with the murder of the informant's spouse. The deceased was allegedly last seen with the accused, who had taken the deceased to drink liquor. A torch found at the murder site was identified as belonging to the accused. Based on these facts, the accused's earlier bail application was rejected.

The deceased died under suspicious circumstances within two years of marriage, after repeated dowry demands, including a motorcycle and a car. The deceased was found hanging, but the post-mortem revealed ante-mortem injuries and signs of strangulation. An FIR was filed by the deceased's sibling against the deceased's spouse and in-laws, alleging continued harassment and eventual murder. The Sessions Court denied bail, but the High Court granted it to the in-laws, which was challenged by the complainant.

The deceased died of burn injuries within two years of marriage. The deceased had been harassed for dowry demands, including a scooter and a refrigerator. Witnesses testified to repeated cruelty. The deceased had told family that they were being mistreated and was hesitant to return to the marital home. The deceased died the day after returning with their spouse following a quarrel.

The deceased committed suicide about a year after marriage. The deceased's family alleged that the deceased faced harassment and physical abuse by their spouse and in-laws due to dowry demands. Despite the deceased's complaints and detailed statements from family and a close friend, the accused were granted bail and anticipatory bail by the Sessions Court, which the petitioner challenged in this case.

An anonymous letter alleged that the petitioner and others assaulted three individuals suspected of theft, resulting in the death of one person. The body was allegedly burned to destroy evidence. The petitioner was named as the first accused and was absconding.

The deceased, the spouse of the co-accused, died by hanging on a certain date. The deceased's family alleged that the deceased was harassed for dowry by the spouse and in-laws, including the accused. The prosecution alleged that the accused threatened the deceased's sibling one day before the incident. The court granted bail to the accused, noting the lack of injury, the omnibus nature of the allegations, the accused's age, and the prior grant of bail to a co-accused.

The accused was convicted under multiple IPC sections, including murder. The accused filed a writ petition under Article 32 seeking premature release after serving over 30 years in custody, including remission. The case was part of a larger batch involving 512 life convicts from a state. The petitions challenged a restrictive policy, framed in a particular year, that required convicts to have reached a minimum age threshold for release.

The accused, a prominent leader of an institution, was accused of conspiring to murder a manager of an institution. The murder was allegedly due to repeated allegations made by the deceased against the accused. After arrest and the rejection of bail by the High Court, the Supreme Court granted bail. The accused sought transfer of the trial outside the state, citing threats to a fair trial.

A journalist, who was the spouse of the petitioner, was shot dead in a town allegedly at the behest of the accused. The petitioner sought transfer of the accused from a jail in that town to a jail in another city, citing the accused's influence and the threat this posed to a fair trial. The accused had a history of serious criminal charges and convictions, and had influence over the jail and the local administration.

The appellant was accused of criminal conspiracy in the murder of another person. The FIR was filed several months after the incident, based on a statement by a person with a history of serious criminal conduct. Earlier, a discharge had been granted after the investigation found no evidence. Anticipatory bail granted by the Sessions Court was later cancelled by the High Court, and the Supreme Court overturned that cancellation.

The complainant's parent was shot dead near a place of worship by accused individuals, allegedly at the behest of the accused, who was lodged in jail at the time. It was revealed that the accused hatched the conspiracy using a mobile phone from jail and was in contact with the co-accused.

The victim allegedly died in a car accident during a trip with their spouse (respondent No. 2). The victim's parent lodged an FIR alleging that it was a premeditated murder. The investigation was transferred to a central investigating agency, which cited reports from a medical institute, a technical institute, a forensic science laboratory, and a road research institute suggesting strangulation and a faked accident. The accused was arrested and later granted bail by the High Court, which was challenged in the Supreme Court.

The respondent obtained a loan of over Rs. 2 crore from a bank for purchasing equipment but diverted the funds through fraudulent means using fake accounts. Investigation revealed that the accused routed funds to multiple accounts linked to the accused's residence and to the accused personally.

In a year, members of a banned insurgent organisation ambushed a police patrol in a state, killing four police officers and looting arms. The accused was later named as an accused on the basis of alleged financial and logistical support to the group. A search of the accused's house revealed unexplained cash and alleged links to other criminal cases.

The accused, the proprietor of an ice factory, was alleged to have committed electricity theft after an inspection revealed that the factory was operating despite being sealed. A first information report was registered, followed by a complaint under the Electricity Act. Anticipatory bail was initially granted to the accused, but the Special Judge later imposed a condition requiring a deposit of Rs. 25 lakhs, which was challenged.

The accused, a hospital staff member, allegedly misappropriated Rs. 1,11,430 collected under a hospital welfare society scheme. The accused had earlier secured bail using allegedly forged documents, which were later found to be fabricated according to forensic analysis.

The accused was alleged to have snatched a mobile phone and cash from another person using a knife. While the accused's bail application was pending in the High Court, the accused filed a fresh bail application before the Sessions Court and obtained bail there, without disclosing that the earlier application was pending in the High Court. The High Court later discovered this and addressed the procedural misconduct.

The accused, a non-executive director in two companies, was alleged to be involved in laundering proceeds of crime derived from a company through intermediary companies and downstream investments. Although the accused allegedly controlled entities that received funds, no direct charges were framed in the predicate offences, and most of the co-accused were not arrested.

The case stemmed from a dispute involving the removal of fence poles during an attempt to widen a pathway. The accused allegedly assaulted the complainant and removed property. Initially, a charge sheet for minor offences was filed, and the accused were granted bail. Later, further investigation added charges of theft and other offences, and the authorities sought cancellation of bail.

The accused was a key managerial person in a group of companies alleged to be involved in large-scale economic fraud through shell firms and benami companies. The accused allegedly misappropriated funds amounting to hundreds of crores from depositors of a cooperative society using fictitious transactions, creating a complex web of companies to siphon and launder money.

The accused was convicted for kidnapping and murdering a child as part of an alleged human sacrifice. The child's body was found in a gunny bag. Investigation linked the accused to the kidnapping and to the recovery of the murder weapon based on the accused's confessional statement.

The appellant was convicted in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor child for a ransom demand of one crore rupees. An earlier bail plea had already been rejected in an earlier year. A fresh interlocutory application for bail pending appeal was filed but denied again based on the same grounds.

The appellants were convicted for the brutal kidnapping and murder of a child whose body was mutilated. Their bail applications had been rejected earlier on two separate occasions, the first several years before the second. Despite long incarceration, the court refused bail due to the heinous nature of the crime and the ongoing appeal process.

The accused, a retired police officer, along with their sibling, allegedly defrauded the spouse of a deceased constable and illegally ran a petrol pump using the spouse's name. They were also involved in a separate case involving assault on a public servant and attempt to murder. Multiple bail pleas were filed, including default bail, which was ultimately cancelled due to procedural abuse and legal infirmity.

The accused was alleged to have committed rape of a minor child in an earlier year and was initially tried under adult criminal law. After years of incarceration, the accused was declared a juvenile based on their age at the time of the offence. Despite repeated bail denials by lower courts, the High Court intervened after the accused had spent over 5 years in custody, which exceeded the maximum period for which a juvenile can be held.

The accused was granted anticipatory bail in a case involving allegations of assault, hurling bombs, and creating voter intimidation in the run-up to local body elections. The complainant alleged fraud and suppression in securing bail, including failure to disclose prior bail rejections. Additional criminal cases were also pending against the accused.

Two directors of a company were accused of running a large-scale collective investment scam. They allegedly used forged sale deeds and shell companies to defraud investors, diverting funds worth thousands of crores to sister concerns and overseas entities. Despite having cooperated earlier, they were accused of attempting asset sales during custody.

The accused was arrested for alleged involvement in the kidnapping of a minor for ransom. The accused was found in a city with the child along with a co-accused. The complainant had received a ransom call from the accused's number. The prosecution alleged that the accused threatened to kill the child if the ransom was not paid.

The accused was charged in a child kidnapping case in which the accused's spouse and another co-accused allegedly abducted a child and demanded ₹5,00,000 as ransom. The child was later found in the accused's custody at a shrine. The accused was arrested and was in judicial custody with their two minor children, and was five months pregnant at the time of the bail plea.

The accused was alleged to have caused the dowry death of their spouse, the deceased. The deceased's parent, the complainant, alleged harassment for property and dowry. The accused was granted bail in a year several years earlier by presenting forged school documents to show that the marriage was over seven years old, which would undermine the presumption under Section 304B IPC. A later inquiry confirmed that the certificates were forged and that the actual marriage had taken place just over six years before the death.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped an infant from a hospital by exploiting the parent's temporary absence. CCTV footage confirmed the accused's involvement. The act caused public panic. The accused was initially denied bail by the Chief Judicial Magistrate but was later granted interim bail by the Sessions Judge. Before the interim bail expired, a preventive detention order under the Public Safety Act was passed against the accused, which the accused challenged in a writ petition.

The accused and their spouse, a childless couple, were accused in a case involving the abduction of a child. While the High Court denied bail citing illegal adoption procedures, it noted that the motive was not malicious. The Supreme Court observed that the appellant had already spent over 16 months in custody and granted regular bail without commenting on merits.

The accused and the co-accused allegedly kidnapped a minor from the custody of the minor's parent and demanded ₹5,000 as ransom. The accused was arrested and remained in custody. A charge sheet was filed and trial proceedings were ongoing.

The accused was granted anticipatory bail in a certain year on the basis of a police report that falsely stated the accused had no criminal antecedents. Later, it emerged that the accused had been involved in over a dozen serious criminal cases. The court found that the bail had been obtained fraudulently through police collusion and ordered its cancellation, directing the senior police authority of the state to take disciplinary action against the responsible police officer.

The accused, who was married, allegedly promised marriage to the complainant, who was divorced and worked as a performer, and had a sexual relationship with the complainant. After the accused failed to fulfil the promise, the complainant filed an FIR under Sections including 376(2)(n). Bail was initially granted based on an affidavit-cum-compromise, which was later challenged as forged. The trial court cancelled bail citing fraud, but the High Court found no legal proceedings proving forgery or violation of the bail terms.

The accused was alleged to have murdered the victim, with whom the accused allegedly had an illicit relationship. The accused had previously been convicted under Section 307 IPC for an earlier attempt to kill the same person and was out on bail. The State sought cancellation of the bail granted in the murder case, alleging suppression of the prior conviction and fraud upon the court.

A judicial officer was disciplined for granting bail to, and discharging, the main accused in a ₹9.7 lakh bank fraud case within 10 days. The High Court held that the officer acted with undue haste and without due consideration of the seriousness of the charge, raising doubts about the officer's integrity and judicial conduct.

The accused was granted regular bail by a High Court in a case involving forgery and fraud, where the case against the accused was based on statements of co-accused. Later, a different judge of the same High Court cancelled the bail, citing national security risks due to misuse of fake documents. The Supreme Court found this improper, as there was no evidence of misuse of bail, violation of its conditions, or fraud in obtaining bail, and the trial was already underway with witnesses examined.

The accused was charged in connection with the dowry death of their spouse, the deceased, who allegedly died by suicide due to sustained harassment. The FIR was filed by the deceased's parent, and a suicide note implicating the accused was recovered. Earlier, the deceased had also lodged a dowry harassment FIR against the accused several years before. The accused had been in custody since December of the year 2020 and the first bail application had already been rejected.

The complainant alleged that their spouse, the accused, and in-laws harassed them physically and mentally for dowry, both in the country and during their stay abroad. Despite a prior settlement and assurances by the spouse not to repeat such conduct, the complainant was again abused when they returned to live with the accused in a city. The accused allegedly retained the child's birth certificate and passport to harass the complainant.

The deceased was married to the accused in a certain year. The deceased allegedly faced sustained dowry-related harassment from their spouse and in-laws, including beatings and demands for a car. On a certain date the following year, the deceased set themselves on fire and later died from burn injuries. An FIR was registered under Sections 498A/304B/34 IPC. Two of the accused died during trial; the remaining accused, who are an in-law and a sibling-in-law of the deceased, stood trial.

The accused was alleged to have harassed their spouse for dowry, including physical abuse, forced medication during pregnancy, and coercive demands for money. The spouse allegedly consumed poison and later died. The spouse's dying declaration, recorded on video, named the accused and the accused's parent. The incident occurred within a year of the marriage and was preceded by sustained abuse and monetary demands.

The accused was named along with other in-laws in a dowry death case concerning the accused's sibling-in-law, the victim. The FIR alleged repeated dowry demands, physical abuse, and harassment. The victim was allegedly murdered by a gunshot fired by three co-accused. The accused was alleged to have committed harassment and abetment, but was not alleged to have been directly involved in the firing.

The victim, who was married to the accused's child, died by suicide within six months of marriage. The victim's parents alleged that the victim had been subjected to harassment and beatings due to inadequate dowry. A suicide note expressing affection to the victim's spouse was found, but the court noted that it could reflect emotional distress arising from harassment. An FIR was registered under Sections 498A and 304B IPC based on statements by the victim's parents.

The accused was charged with abetting the suicide of their spouse, who allegedly took their own life due to being harassed for suffering from psoriasis and tuberculosis. The complaint, filed by the victim's parent, alleged verbal and emotional abuse, though not dowry-related. The accused took the victim to the hospital and informed the family after the suicide. The accused had been in custody and the charge sheet had been filed.
