The accused and their spouse were accused of physically and mentally harassing their child's spouse for dowry. The complainant alleged assault and illegal retention of dowry articles. Despite prior promises not to harass the complainant again, the in-laws allegedly instigated further abuse. Specific allegations were made in the FIR and in statements recorded under Section 161 CrPC.

The victim died by suicide while residing with their spouse in a state, allegedly due to dowry harassment. The victim's in-law, the accused, resided separately in a different state. The FIR and statements by the victim's family accused the in-laws of earlier dowry-related harassment. The accused sought anticipatory bail, fearing arrest.

The deceased died by suicide while staying at their parental home. The deceased's parent alleged that after the marriage, which took place a few months earlier, the deceased faced dowry harassment by their spouse and in-laws, including the accused (a sibling of the deceased's spouse), particularly after the accused came to stay for maternity. The police registered a case under Sections 498A and 304B IPC. The deceased left a suicide note, but it did not mention harassment by the petitioners.

The accused was alleged to have physically and mentally harassed their spouse for dowry, leading to the spouse's suicide by consuming pesticide. The victim had previously reported a demand for ₹50,000 and repeated abuse. The charge sheet alleged sustained harassment and included multiple family members. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2020.

The complainant alleged that after marriage, they were harassed by their spouse and in-laws, including the accused, for dowry. The harassment included physical assault and repeated demands for money and gold. On multiple occasions, the complainant was sent back to their parental home. The FIR was registered under Sections 498A, 504, 506 IPC and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act.

The complainant alleged that after the marriage, which took place in a particular month of 2021, the complainant was harassed by their spouse, the accused, and the accused's family for dowry. The allegations included serious physical abuse, such as throwing chilli powder and inflicting burns with a lighted cigarette. Despite these claims, no medical report was produced. The accused sought anticipatory bail after the Sessions Court rejected the application.

The accused was arrested in connection with the death of their spouse, who allegedly died by hanging within 24 hours, with the allegation being that the death was due to dowry harassment. Statements under Section 161 CrPC recorded from the deceased's family accused the accused of sustained harassment. Although three witnesses were examined, the statements of key witnesses (the deceased's family) remained pending due to procedural delay in the issuance of summons.

The accused persons, who are spouses of each other and the in-laws of the deceased, were booked after the deceased committed suicide, allegedly due to dowry harassment. The FIR was lodged by the deceased's parent, implicating the deceased's spouse and vaguely suggesting that demands were made at the instance of the in-laws. The accused couple had been living separately from the deceased since a partition several years earlier.

The accused was charged with abetting the suicide of their spouse, who died within a year of marriage. The prosecution alleged consistent dowry-related harassment by the accused and the accused's family. A prior complaint by the deceased was on record, and witnesses gave specific statements implicating the accused in dowry demands and mental and physical abuse.

The accused was alleged to have repeatedly harassed their spouse for dowry, including through physical assaults and threats. A panchayat was convened shortly before the spouse's death, at which the dowry demands were reiterated. Four days later, the spouse was found dead by hanging at the matrimonial home. The postmortem showed ligature marks and additional injuries. The accused has been in custody since 2021.

The accused, a sibling of the deceased's spouse, was alleged to have harassed the deceased for dowry, which allegedly led the deceased to commit suicide by hanging. Although there were claims that the accused and the accused's parent visited and harassed the deceased, the accused was residing separately in a different town, while the deceased and the deceased's spouse had moved to another city three months before the incident.

The deceased, the spouse of a person, died by suicide by jumping into a pond along with their child, who survived. Allegations were made that the deceased's in-laws ill-treated the deceased and did not converse with them, causing emotional distress. The FIR was filed under Sections 304B and 306 IPC against the deceased's in-law (the parent of the spouse), the deceased's sibling-in-law, and another sibling-in-law. However, the complaint lacked specific details of dowry harassment and the death note contained no incriminating material.

The accused was arrested in connection with the death of their spouse, who allegedly died by suicide while two months pregnant. The FIR, registered under Sections 498A and 304B IPC and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, accused the accused and their family of dowry harassment. The accused sought interim bail citing the critical heart condition of their parent and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

The accused was arrested for the dowry death of their spouse, who died by hanging. The prosecution alleged harassment for dowry based on a statement by the deceased's parent, who claimed the deceased had informed them of such harassment shortly before the death. The accused claimed false implication and highlighted the lack of prior complaints and their cooperation in the funeral proceedings.

The accused was arrested for the alleged dowry death of their spouse within 14 months of marriage. Initial applications for bail had been rejected, but after 16 months in custody and examination of material witnesses including the doctor, the accused's bail plea was reconsidered. The postmortem indicated natural causes related to anemia and heart/lung failure, and not homicide.

The accused was alleged to have harassed their spouse for additional dowry, which allegedly led the spouse to kill their child and then commit suicide. There were no prior allegations during their ten-year marriage. The accused was arrested and remained in judicial custody after the charge sheet was filed.

The complainant's child was married to accused No.1 in an earlier year. The FIR alleged that the complainant's child was frequently harassed for dowry by their spouse and in-laws. The complainant's child died several years later under suspicious circumstances. A complaint was filed against eight persons, later reduced to five, accusing them of dowry harassment leading to the death, alleged to be either suicide or murder. Accused Nos.2 to 4 sought bail after being in custody since a date several years earlier.

The accused and the accused's parent were alleged to have harassed the complainant for ₹6,00,000 as dowry since the beginning of the marriage, which took place several years earlier. The complainant was eventually driven out of the matrimonial home and lodged a complaint after counselling failed. The complainant and the accused have a young child. The accused sought anticipatory bail, claiming that the allegations were false and that the accused intended to resume married life.

The accused was charged under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act by their spouse, who alleged harassment and dowry demands by the in-laws and support from the accused. The accused's anticipatory bail was denied by lower courts. The Supreme Court considered the accused's appeal and used the occasion to address misuse of arrest powers in dowry-related complaints.

The accused was charged in a vehicle theft case involving a car stolen from a town in a state and later sold as scrap in a city in another state. The accused was identified based on confessional statements made during interrogation, and the accused also admitted involvement in other car thefts at different locations. The court noted that the accused was a habitual offender with multiple theft cases registered against them.

The accused was arrested in connection with the death of their spouse, the deceased, under Section 304B IPC, with allegations of cruelty and dowry harassment. The defence claimed the charge sheet lacked original documents and cited the grant of bail to a co-accused. However, the prosecution emphasised the gravity of the charges and the accused's role as the deceased's spouse.

The accused was charged in connection with the suicide of their spouse. The deceased initially survived a hanging attempt but died eleven days later in hospital. The deceased had complained to their parents multiple times over a period of about two years, several years before the incident, about dowry demands. A day before the suicide, the accused allegedly called the deceased's parents and threatened to kill the deceased if they did not take the deceased back. Witnesses supported this version, and there were inconsistencies in statements about the dowry amount.

The spouse of the applicant committed suicide by setting themselves ablaze within one year of marriage. The prosecution alleged sustained dowry demands and physical abuse by the deceased's spouse and in-laws. While the co-accused had been granted bail, the applicant remained in custody since several years earlier. The prosecution's key witnesses had not yet been examined.

The accused was arrested for the suicide of their spouse, the deceased, who allegedly hanged themselves due to sustained dowry-related harassment and physical assault by the accused and the accused's in-laws. The incident occurred within three years of marriage. Witnesses, including the deceased's parent and a relative, provided statements implicating the accused in harassment and dowry demands of ₹3,00,000.

The petitioner was in custody in a dowry harassment case alleging physical abuse, denial of food, abandonment, and further dowry demands. Three petitions from separate districts involved similar facts. Lower courts denied bail, but the High Court noted the non-grievous nature of the allegations and that the accused had been in custody for months. The Court emphasized that such cases should typically be resolved at the Magistrate or Sessions level.

The accused was alleged to have murdered their spouse by setting the spouse ablaze due to dowry demands. Though there was a dying declaration suggesting accidental death, the prosecution produced letters written by the deceased alleging ongoing dowry-related torture and threats. The accused avoided arrest and filed successive anticipatory bail applications.

The deceased was married to the applicant's child and died by suicide by hanging while pregnant, within two years of marriage. The prosecution alleged continuous dowry harassment and beatings by the applicant and other in-laws, with six antemortem injuries found during postmortem. After the incident, the applicant absconded and was arrested over a year later after a reward was declared.

The deceased was married to the accused's sibling and faced continuous dowry-related harassment from their spouse and in-laws, including the accused. After giving birth to a child, the deceased died by alleged strangulation at the matrimonial home. The death was initially treated as suicide, but later medical reports and investigation indicated homicidal strangulation. Earlier, regular bail was granted to the accused, but it was later cancelled after the addition of IPC Section 302.

The deceased committed suicide allegedly due to physical and mental harassment by their spouse and in-laws, including demands for dowry. An FIR was registered under Sections 306 and 498A IPC, the Dowry Prohibition Act, and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The complainant later submitted an affidavit expressing no objection to anticipatory bail for the in-laws.

The accused was charged under Sections 498A and 304B IPC after their spouse died by hanging within three years of marriage. The allegations included dowry demands of ₹5 lakh. No prior complaints had been made by the deceased or the deceased's family. After investigation, charges were dropped against other family members and only the accused was charge-sheeted. The accused had been in custody for several years, since 2020, and no witnesses had been examined by the trial court.

The accused was arrested following the death of their spouse, the deceased, who was found hanging from a tree. Initially, the deceased's parent and grandparent did not accuse anyone, but later, the deceased's other parent filed a complaint alleging that the deceased was harassed for dowry. The co-accused were already granted bail. No prior complaints or suicide note existed, and the deceased had voluntarily returned to the matrimonial home.

The accused, along with their parents (co-accused 1 and co-accused 2), was accused by their spouse, the complainant, of cruelty, harassment for a dowry demand of ₹2 crore, and outraging modesty. An FIR was lodged and a charge-sheet was subsequently filed. The applicants filed for anticipatory bail, citing false allegations, separate living arrangements, and the non-requirement of custodial interrogation. The prosecution opposed the application on the grounds of evasion and the issuance of a proclamation under Section 82 CrPC.

The High Court took suo moto cognizance to examine whether bail granted to the two accused persons should be cancelled, noting that they were granted bail while a co-accused's bail was rejected. The co-accused had serious criminal antecedents involving dacoity and robbery, unlike the present respondents. The court found no allegation of misuse of bail by the respondents.

The accused was alleged to have drugged and rendered unconscious eight persons staying at a hotel in a town, and to have stolen their mobile phones and ATM cards. The accused had used a fake identity card and fled the scene. The accused was later arrested in a similar case in another city. CCTV footage, room keys, and toxicology reports substantiated the accused's involvement.

Within a few days in an earlier month, the complainant and a friend were diverted by an auto-rickshaw driven by the accused to a different location in a city, where two rear passengers threatened them with a knife and robbed them of mobile phones, cash, and digital payment transfers. The applicant was arrested three days later and charged with armed robbery under provisions of the IPC and the Arms Act. The accused had prior cases, but was acquitted or granted bail in some.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a violent incident in which a car was snatched at gunpoint, followed by a police chase and an exchange of fire. During the encounter, some co-accused were injured and later died. The accused fled but was later apprehended with arms. The accused disclosed involvement in various robberies and violent crimes across several states.

The complainant alleged that while resting in their truck, four persons, including one carrying a pistol (later found to be a toy), entered, beat the complainant's helper, and robbed ₹4 lakhs. CCTV footage showed the getaway vehicle used by the accused. The owner of the car confirmed that the accused had taken the vehicle. ₹80,000 was recovered from the accused.

The accused filed for release claiming to have been a juvenile at the time of the offence, which was committed in 2006. To prove their age, the accused submitted a baptism certificate and school certificates. However, the court noted that the accused had a history of 13 criminal cases and had previously misused bail by committing another offence involving a bomb blast. The submitted documents were suspected to be forged, and the accused's parent was even tried for this but acquitted for lack of proof.

The accused was arrested in a case involving theft and robbery in which ₹1.85 lakhs and ornaments were allegedly looted. Out of the alleged loot, only ₹6,200 was recovered from the accused. The Court noted that the accused had no prior criminal record and observed that statements of the co-accused were improperly used to deny bail at the Sessions level.

The complainants alleged that on a certain day in 2020, the accused and co-accused attacked them with weapons, looted a mobile phone and a gold chain, and assaulted them. The accused claimed the incident stemmed from a confrontation during threshing of wheat, where the complainants, allegedly intoxicated, attacked them. The initial inquiry by police found the robbery claim to be false, and bailable offences were first registered. Later, under pressure, Section 395 IPC and other provisions were added.

In an earlier month of 2019, the applicants allegedly attacked the complainant with weapons and attempted to set the complainant on fire using petrol and a matchstick, in an apparent gang-related assault arising from prior enmity. The applicants had been granted bail earlier but violated the bail conditions and engaged in further criminal activity. The bail was subsequently cancelled. Although a settlement was claimed, the applicants' criminal background was cited as a hindrance to granting fresh bail.

Several months before the arrest, the accused and others allegedly assembled with weapons near a road in a locality, intending to commit robbery. Upon seeing patrolling police, the accused fled, and only two persons were caught on the spot. Items such as iron rods, ropes, and knives were recovered from the vehicle. The accused was arrested much later, around one and a half years after the incident. The accused sought bail citing parity with co-accused who had already been released.

The accused was charged with conspiring in, and participating in, a robbery at the office of a finance company. The accused had been in custody for over two years and three months. Earlier bail applications by the accused had been rejected by the High Court and by the Supreme Court, with the latter granting liberty to reapply after six months. Only one witness had been examined during this time, and the trial was delayed because the co-accused were being tried in another court.

At a certain point in June 2022, the complainant was lured to a toll booth by co-accused 2. There, the accused and another co-accused abducted the complainant, forced the complainant to consume alcohol, assaulted the complainant, and then demanded ransom from the complainant's parent for the complainant's release. The accused was arrested about nine days later and remained in custody.

The accused was arrested during a police raid, following a robbery complaint made the previous day involving theft of gold and silver ornaments. The accused was caught along with two co-accused on a motorcycle. While no items were recovered directly from the accused, the co-accused were found with weapons and stolen property. The prosecution claimed that the accused was habitually involved in similar robbery cases.

The accused was arrested after a country-made pistol, two live cartridges, and a stolen motorcycle were recovered from their possession. The accused had been in custody for several years since their arrest and had multiple past criminal records related to theft and robbery.

The accused was arrested several years earlier for alleged robbery under Sections 392 and 397 IPC. Despite having multiple prior criminal cases, the accused was acquitted in three separate Sessions Trials. The bail plea cited prolonged incarceration and COVID-19-related delays in the trial proceedings.

The accused was alleged to have been involved in a home invasion and robbery in which the victim was killed and the victim's spouse was injured. The accused was not named in the FIR. A witness later claimed to have seen the accused begging near the house a day before the incident. The defense argued that the recovery was not independently corroborated and that the key witness later retracted. The accused had no criminal history prior to this case.

The accused was charged in a robbery case registered at a police station. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2022. An earlier bail plea had been rejected, but the accused renewed the application, citing that the victim had already been examined and had not identified the accused during testimony.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a road robbery case registered at a police station. The accused had been in custody since November of the previous year. Charges were framed several months later, and a co-accused had been granted bail earlier. The accused renewed the bail plea, affirming there was no suppression of facts and offering full cooperation with the trial proceedings.

The applicant was arrested in 2021 for alleged involvement in a robbery case under Section 394 IPC. The applicant's name was not mentioned in the FIR. The charge-sheet had been filed and the trial was expected to take time. The applicant agreed to conditions including a monetary deposit to Legal Aid Services.

The accused was arrested following a police raid based on secret information about an assembly of criminals. The arrest took place several years before the present proceedings. From the accused's possession, a loaded country-made pistol and three live cartridges were recovered. The accused had three prior criminal cases involving dacoity and robbery.

The accused allegedly attempted to rob a bracelet from a child at a hospital in a city. The accused was apprehended by hospital staff on suspicion and identified by the complainant. The accused was in custody, and the charge-sheet was already filed by the time of this bail application.

The accused was arrested along with the co-accused while fleeing from the scene after allegedly committing robbery in a shop. Although the co-accused had been granted bail, the accused was found to have 12 prior criminal cases. The accused's earlier bail request was rejected several years earlier, and this was a renewed application.

The accused was apprehended by police while riding a motorcycle, and a country-made loaded pistol with two live cartridges was found in their possession. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2017. Although a co-accused was granted bail, the accused's prior criminal history involving two robbery cases led to the rejection of the bail plea.

The accused was alleged to have committed a highway robbery in a case registered at a police station and was named in witness statements. An earlier bail application of the accused was rejected, and the trial court was instructed to expedite the trial. Later, the accused had been in custody for about two years without charge being framed, which formed the basis for the renewed bail plea.

The accused was alleged to have committed a robbery, in a case registered at a police station. Initially, the accused was charged under Section 392 IPC, but the charge-sheet was later submitted under Section 395 IPC. An earlier bail application was denied because of a recovery made from the accused. However, a co-accused was later granted bail, and the accused applied again, citing parity with the co-accused.

The case involves the robbery and murder of a person. The accused was implicated based on a confessional statement, which led to the recovery of looted articles and a bloodstained knife. The accused had been in custody for approximately nine years at the time of the bail application.

The accused was convicted along with others for a pre-planned bank robbery of ₹12 lakhs involving armed assault, vehicle tampering, and firing to create terror. After conviction, the accused repeatedly sought temporary bail citing their child's illness. Despite bail rejections, the accused secured parole through political influence and misrepresentation. The High Court later suspended the parole, declaring it unlawful.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case involving gang rape and robbery. The accused was identified as the principal offender and has been in custody since a date in 2022. The offences included serious charges under the IPC and the POCSO Act. The trial is ongoing.

On a date in March 2022, the complainant was intercepted by two armed persons in a car and robbed of ₹2,15,000. The complainant was later hospitalized and filed a police complaint. Investigation linked the accused and the co-accused, who were already in custody in another case, to the robbery. Although the money was not recovered, their involvement was supported by the seizure of the car and by confessional statements. Both had prior criminal cases involving dacoity and robbery in various places across a state.

The accused was convicted for murder and robbery in a case involving the killing of a student, the victim. The body was found concealed under cow dung at a place in a village. Witnesses, including an approver, stated that the accused and the co-accused beat the victim to death in a tin shed. The accused was sentenced to life imprisonment under Section 302 and one year under Section 392. The accused applied for bail pending appeal after over 10 years in custody.

The applicant was accused of murdering a person with multiple stab wounds and committing robbery at the victim's residence. The FIR, initially registered under Section 307 IPC, was later updated to include Sections 302, 394, and 411 IPC after the victim succumbed to the injuries and missing items were reported. A bloodstained weapon was recovered from the accused's possession, and the co-accused had named the accused in a confessional statement.

On a night in late October 2022, the accused and a co-accused impersonated police officers and stopped a vehicle at a circle in a city. They demanded documents and ₹20,000 from the complainant and the complainant's friends. When the complainant refused, the accused threatened them with a knife. The real police arrived, and the accused and the co-accused were apprehended while a third accomplice escaped. A knife was seized from the accused.

In the early hours of a day in August 2022, at around 2:00 a.m., the accused and others were found near a petrol bunk with rods, ropes, a knife, and chilli powder, allegedly intending to commit robbery. Police apprehended five accused while others fled. No actual robbery occurred and no vehicle was proven to have been stopped. The accused was denied bail by the Sessions Court but applied again on the grounds that other co-accused had been granted bail and the accused's prior cases were minor.

On a certain date in 2021, police received information about five suspicious persons at a road in a city. They were apprehended with weapons including a knife, a jambe, chilli powder, and monkey caps. The accused, along with the co-accused, admitted they were preparing to commit robbery or dacoity. The accused was arrested and remained in custody, with no prior criminal antecedents.

The accused was arrested in connection with an FIR registered for offences of kidnapping and robbery under the IPC and the Gujarat Police Act, along with provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The complainant later filed an affidavit indicating an amicable resolution of the matter and raised no objection to the grant of bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a bank robbery case registered at a police station. While no weapons or stolen money were recovered from the accused, eleven mobile phones were seized. The accused had been in judicial custody at the time of the bail application. The co-accused had already been denied bail.

The accused was arrested in April 2020 in connection with a robbery involving ₹3,000. The accused was booked under Section 392 IPC and a state law relating to the prevention of dacoity and related offences. The defense argued false implication and delay in trial due to the pandemic. The court took note of Supreme Court directions for prisoner release amid COVID-19.

The accused was alleged to have committed robbery of a tempo and had been in jail since late 2020. The accused's first bail application was rejected, and this was the second application, citing long detention and trial delay, with no charges framed yet.

The accused and co-accused allegedly robbed Rs. 52,000 and a mobile phone from the complainant's shop and threatened further extortion. The FIR was delayed, and the applicant has been in jail since a date more than a year before the present application. The accused claims to have been falsely implicated because of their professional work.

The accused, along with co-accused, allegedly broke into a home at night, assaulted the residents, and stole gold ornaments and cash. The complainant identified the accused. The accused was implicated based on a co-accused's statement and is alleged to be a habitual offender involved in multiple robbery and murder cases across states.

The case involves a bank robbery in which the accused was apprehended. Unlike a co-accused who was granted bail, the accused was identified in a Test Identification Parade, and cash was recovered on the accused's statement.

The accused was arrested for allegedly attempting to commit dacoity in a bank in a city, along with other co-accused. The accused has been in jail since an earlier date, several years before the present application. The charge sheet has been filed.

The accused and co-accused allegedly robbed a vehicle carrying 40 quintals of areca nut and Rs. 1,75,000 in cash after intercepting it with deadly weapons. The incident occurred on a certain date and the FIR was registered the next day. The accused were later identified and the robbed goods were recovered based on voluntary statements.

The complainant withdrew Rs. 1,01,500 from a bank and, while walking with their parent, a person on a bicycle collided with the complainant, causing the complainant to fall. Another person then stole Rs. 1,00,000 from the complainant's pocket. The accused were arrested based on a co-accused's voluntary statement.

The accused was arrested in connection with an alleged attempted robbery at a school in a city in a state. The prosecution claimed that the accused and others planned the act and assaulted police during their intervention. The defense argued that the accused had no role in causing injuries and had no criminal record. Injuries to the victims were minor and caused by blunt weapons.

The accused is charged in a robbery case in which the victim was allegedly drugged using a stupefying substance. The accused has been in custody for over 393 days, has no criminal antecedents, and charges have not yet been framed due to procedural delays.

The accused was arrested in connection with a bank robbery case and had been in custody since a date in early 2023. Their involvement was alleged on the basis of statements made by co-accused persons, with no recovery made and no test identification parade conducted.

The accused was charged in a case involving the brutal murder of a person with multiple stab wounds, along with a related robbery. The evidence included the recovery of a scissor allegedly used in the crime and stolen money recovered from the accused's bag. The accused had previously been denied bail. Bail was later granted after the co-accused, who allegedly played a more direct role, was granted bail.

The petitioner was convicted of attempting to murder a person by shooting them during an armed robbery. The petitioner was sentenced under IPC Sections 398 and 307 read with Section 34, and Sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act. The petitioner has been in custody since 2021 and has 15 prior criminal cases. The petitioner's bail plea during appeal was rejected by the trial court and again by the High Court.

The applicant was accused of committing a robbery of Rs. 9.5 lakhs along with two co-accused (co-accused 1 and co-accused 2). Rs. 1.28 lakhs were recovered from the applicant. The applicant's first bail application was rejected, and the second one was based on co-accused 2 having been granted bail. However, only Rs. 9300 had been recovered from co-accused 2.

The petitioner was accused of robbing Rs. 9,500 and a mobile phone from a food vendor along with a co-accused. While the co-accused was caught at the scene, the petitioner fled with the cash. The petitioner was arrested two days later, and a portion of the stolen cash and the phone were recovered. The petitioner had been in custody for 9 months before being granted bail.

The appellant was convicted under IPC Sections 302, 394, and 120B for participating in a murder committed during a robbery. The appellant had already served over four years in custody and sought bail during the pendency of the appeal. The earlier bail pleas of the appellant were rejected twice.

The applicant was arrested in a robbery case involving Rs. 4,000, clothes, a mobile phone, and an ATM card. The applicant was not named in the FIR, but Rs. 3,000 and a phone were later recovered from them. The recovered phone was not identified by the informant. The applicant had been in jail for several years, since 2016, and no progress had been made in the trial proceedings due to COVID-19. The co-accused had already received bail.

The applicant was arrested in a murder and robbery case and has been in custody since 2016. The applicant was allegedly apprehended at the scene with a weapon. While the co-accused were granted bail, the applicant's previous bail application was rejected in 2019. The trial has not progressed significantly due to COVID-19.

The accused was apprehended by police while an associate allegedly fired upon the officers and escaped. Upon arrest, one country-made pistol, four live cartridges, and a magazine were recovered from the accused. The accused had been in custody for eight months at the time of the bail application and had four prior criminal cases.

The accused, a juvenile, was denied bail by both the Juvenile Justice Board and the Sessions Judge. The accused had been in custody for over a year and was accused in a case registered at a police station under the Arms Act. The accused also had three other pending cases involving robbery and murder under IPC Sections 393, 394, 302, and Arms Act Section 27.

The accused had been in custody since April 2016 in connection with a case registered at a police station under IPC Sections 399 and 402 and Arms Act Sections 25(1-b)A, 26, and 35. The accused had five prior cases, mostly for robbery. This was the accused's fourth bail application.

The accused was implicated in a case registered at a police station under Sections 399 and 402 IPC and provisions of the Arms Act. Police, acting on secret information, raided a location where a group was allegedly planning a robbery. One person was caught with arms and named the accused as a co-conspirator. The accused claimed false implication and said they worked as a canteen worker.

The informant was carrying ₹6,00,000 to deposit in a bank when they were looted by criminals. The FIR was filed against unknown persons, and later the accused was named during investigation. Based on the accused's confessional statement, recovery of the looted money was made from the accused's possession, and the accused could not justify its ownership.

The petitioner, who is co-accused 3 in the case, was arrested in connection with a crime for planning to commit dacoity. A weapon and rope were recovered from the accused's possession. The charge sheet had been filed. The accused also had a previous robbery case registered in a police station.

Police officers on patrol near a railway underbridge in a city found seven individuals near a vehicle, carrying clubs and iron rods. The individuals were apprehended and disclosed that they had gathered from another state to commit dacoity. Weapons, cash, and mobile phones were seized, and the case was registered suo moto by a police officer.

The accused was arrested in 1991 with 5,100 grams of opium found in an attache case while travelling by bus. The accused filed multiple bail applications, with the third one prompting a legal reference on the applicability of CrPC provisions to NDPS bail.

The respondent was found in alleged possession of approximately 400 kg of poppy straw. The Special Judge had denied bail, but the High Court granted it, citing lack of exclusive possession and no criminal history. The Supreme Court held that the High Court failed to consider the stringent requirements under Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

The accused was arrested with 1 kg of opium. The charge sheet was filed 44 days late, and the accused was not produced before a Special Court within 15 days as required under the NDPS Act. The accused applied for default bail on these procedural grounds. Two other co-petitioners in connected matters had similar procedural delays related to Section 36-A(1)(b).

The accused was allegedly found with 814 grams of cannabis (charas) near a bridge during a police patrol. The accused was arrested after allegedly throwing a bag containing the substance upon seeing the police. Investigation was complete and the case was pending for prosecution evidence.

The accused, a key accused in a large financial company fraud case prosecuted by a central investigating agency, was arrested several years before the present application. The charges involved fraudulent financial activities under the Companies Act and the IPC. The trial was delayed significantly, with cognizance taken only several years after the arrest, and over 60 witnesses were listed. The accused remained the only accused still in custody and was suffering from multiple serious medical conditions.

The accused was named as a co-accused in a narcotics case based on the disclosure statements of two arrested individuals who were found with 38 cough syrup bottles and 250 intoxicant tablets. The accused was arrested four months later, and phone records showed contact between the accused and the arrested individuals. No drugs were recovered from the accused's possession. The accused had two other FIRs involving NDPS sections.

The accused was arrested based on a disclosure by the co-accused, who was caught with 65 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup. During investigation, the accused made a disclosure leading to the recovery of 60 more bottles and Rs. 10,000. The accused had been in custody for over a year at the time of decision and had no prior criminal record.

Based on a chance recovery from the co-accused, 600 tablets and 144 capsules of controlled medicines were recovered. The co-accused disclosed that the contraband belonged to the accused, who was arrested and has remained in custody since then, a period of over a year. The accused has four prior NDPS cases, but most involved intermediate quantity. In the current case, the recovered quantity is commercial.

The accused was arrested with 45 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup found during a chance recovery. The quantity seized was commercial, and the State claimed compliance with all statutory NDPS procedures. The accused had no prior criminal record and was in custody for 1 year and 8 months at the time of judgment.

Police, acting on prior information, seized 1800 tablets (225g) of Alprazolam from the accused. The accused was charged under Section 22(c) of the NDPS Act. The accused had no prior criminal record and had been in custody for nearly 1 year and 11 months at the time of the bail order.

The applicant was allegedly involved in a narcotics case involving concealment of drugs in car compartments. The prosecution relied on statements from two witnesses, one of whom died and the other of whom turned hostile, and on a confessional statement by a co-accused. The applicant had been in jail for over six years and sought bail on grounds of parity and changed circumstances.

The accused was arrested in an earlier year in connection with an NDPS case involving the seizure of 25 kg of Mephedrone, allegedly linked to the accused's factory, run through a company. The case relied on statements recorded under Section 67 of the NDPS Act and on indirect links through the co-accused. No contraband was recovered from the accused personally, and multiple co-accused had already been granted bail.

Some time earlier, police intercepted a vehicle driven by the accused, who was travelling with the co-accused. Upon search, 7.5 kg of poppy juice was recovered from the vehicle. Both were arrested and charge-sheeted under the NDPS Act.

The accused was arrested for transporting 2 quintals and 17 kg of poppy husk. During a police chase, the accused allegedly fired at a police constable, injuring them. A country-made pistol and 7 live cartridges were recovered from the vehicle. The FIR was lodged by a police officer in charge of the police station, and a charge-sheet was eventually filed after judicial extensions.

The accused was arrested after being found seated in the back seat of a car in which 39,500 tablets of Tramadol Hydrochloride were recovered. The co-accused were allegedly involved in procurement and transportation of the contraband. The prosecution alleged conscious possession, but the defence highlighted the accused's lack of knowledge and role.
Police intercepted a vehicle driven by co-accused 1, with the accused seated beside them. Upon search, 7.5 kg of opium was recovered. Both were arrested and charge-sheeted under NDPS Act provisions.

Police stopped a mini truck on a certain date and recovered 102 grams of Charas from under the seat, allegedly in the possession of the driver, who is the accused. The accused attempted to flee and was arrested. The accused has been in custody since then.

The accused was charged in an NDPS case involving the transportation of poppy-straw. Although no contraband was found in the accused's possession, the prosecution alleged that financial transactions linked the accused to co-accused persons who transported over 450 kg of poppy-straw. The accused had prior NDPS cases pending.

Some time ago, 50 bottles of Codeine Phosphate-based cough syrup were seized from the main accused, who named the accused as the seller. Bank records confirmed a payment of ₹9,600 from the main accused to the accused. The accused claimed to be a licensed drug dealer and sought interim bail during the pendency of a reference to a larger bench on whether such cough syrups are covered under the NDPS Act.

The accused was alleged to have participated in the murder of the informant's child by firearm, allegedly in revenge for a prior killing. The accused was not present at the scene of the shooting, and the police had already filed a charge-sheet.

The accused, a compounder, allegedly connived with a co-accused to kidnap the complainant's child and demand ₹20 lakh as ransom. The child was unharmed and returned safely. The FIR was filed and the applicant was arrested the same day.

The accused was alleged to be involved in the murder, by firearm, of the informant's child, allegedly arising from past enmities. The accused was not present at the scene of the firing. Investigation was complete and a charge-sheet had been submitted. The informant had a hostile history with the accused.

On an unspecified date in 2020, a newborn child was abducted from a hospital in a city. CCTV footage showed the accused and a co-accused taking the child in a car. Investigation revealed that the child was handed over to others as part of an illegal adoption for money. The child was recovered safely.

The accused, acting as guarantor, was alleged to have conspired with bank officials and others to fraudulently secure and misuse a ₹4 crore loan using forged documentation and diverted funds. Investigations revealed multiple similar frauds connected to the accused, with the bulk of the loan funds routed to entities under the accused's control.

The accused, a partner at an audit firm, served as statutory auditor of a company during the years in which the company falsified its accounts, inflating cash and bank balances and misleading shareholders. The accused was alleged to have failed to perform due diligence and to have misrepresented the financial statements, thereby contributing to one of the country's largest corporate frauds.

The accused, who operated a business dealing in building materials, was alleged to have defrauded a co-operative bank through manipulated deposit slips and ledger entries, causing financial discrepancies. The alleged fraud involved unexplained differences between bank deposit slips, passbooks, and journal entries, pointing to collusion with bank officials.

The accused, facing trial under Sections 21/61/85 of the NDPS Act, applied for interim bail claiming that their spouse required surgery and needed their assistance. The prosecution opposed the plea, citing the accused's criminal history of 21 prior cases and NDPS-related offenses. The court had previously denied regular bail.

The accused was implicated after 575 grams of heroin was found hidden in shock absorbers in a parcel destined for a foreign country. The accused was linked to the case through statements of a co-accused, call detail records, and the recovery of shock absorber tools and packaging material from the accused's residence. The accused was arrested and remained in judicial custody.

The accused was alleged to have been found in possession of 500 grams of heroin. The accused's first bail application was denied due to the commercial quantity involved. In the second application, the independent public witness denied witnessing any recovery, and discrepancies were found in police documents. The court found these developments crucial enough to reassess bail.

The accused was intercepted at a railway station with 16.4 kg of ephedrine hydrochloride concealed in quilts. The accused admitted in a voluntary statement to involvement in trafficking. Charges were framed under Sections 9A and 25A of the NDPS Act. The trial had progressed slowly, and the accused had been in custody for several years since their arrest.

A parcel containing 677 grams of ketamine was intercepted at a courier company facility in a city. The parcel was linked to the accused through the co-accused's disclosure, recovered packing materials, photocopies of fake IDs, and mobile phone data. The accused was arrested at their residence, where similar materials and ₹5.84 lakh in cash were found. Phone data showed communications with the co-accused and parcel tracking.

The accused was arrested after 5 grams of heroin were recovered from a hotel room where the accused stayed with a co-accused. The accused's disclosure led to the interception of a 980g heroin parcel. The accused was linked to multiple co-accused involved in trafficking via courier. The prosecution cited messaging application chats, co-accused statements, and recoveries of identity documents as evidence.

The accused was arrested following the interception of 10 kg of heroin from two co-accused, who named the accused as a member of a syndicate. The accused was later traced and arrested in a state. While no contraband was recovered from the accused directly, ₹1.29 lakh in cash was found. Call detail records and transcripts showed regular contact with the co-accused and discussions related to drug supply.

Based on a tip-off, narcotics officers intercepted a scooter carrying the co-accused and the accused. The co-accused was driving and the accused was the pillion rider. 8 kg of heroin was recovered from the co-accused's bag. The accused was identified by the informer as the trader supplying the narcotics. No recovery was made directly from the accused.

The accused was apprehended along with co-accused 1 and co-accused 2 while travelling in an auto-rickshaw. Two bags containing a total of 38.33 kg of Ganja were recovered: 14.13 kg near the accused and 24.20 kg near co-accused 1. The prosecution alleged conspiracy supported by mobile call records. All three were charged under Section 20(C)/29 of the NDPS Act.

The accused was arrested on a certain date in 2016 at a road in a city with 1.5 kg of Charas. The accused was charged under Section 20(ii)(c) of the NDPS Act. The defence raised concerns over the absence of public witnesses and procedural lapses in the submission of the sample to the forensic science laboratory. The accused remained in custody for over 6 years, with trial delays partly due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

The accused was arrested based on the disclosure of the co-accused, who was caught with 1 kg of heroin. The co-accused claimed to have purchased the heroin from the accused. Voice samples of both the accused and the co-accused were sent to a forensic science laboratory, and expert analysis indicated a probable match. No contraband was found on the accused.

On an earlier date, the accused, a foreign national, was apprehended near a metro station with 46 packets of charas totaling 475 grams. The accused was caught handing over one packet to the co-accused in exchange for money. The investigating agency arrested both individuals and seized the contraband. The accused admitted to supplying drugs and was charged under Sections 8, 20(b), and 29 of the NDPS Act.

The accused, a professional in the hospitality industry, allegedly conspired to defraud a company after business disputes arose. The accused devised a scheme with a co-accused to issue fake discount coupons through an advertising firm without the complainant's consent, intending to cause massive losses to the company while earning a personal commission. The accused admitted their role during police interrogation.

The accused was arrested along with their spouse for allegedly delivering 1 kg of heroin to the co-accused, who was later found with another 2 kg of heroin. The co-accused identified them through photographs. No direct recovery was made from the accused. The accused's counsel argued that the accused merely accompanied their spouse and pointed to the accused's health issues and repeated compliance with the conditions of interim bail.

The accused, an employee of a well-known person, was arrested under the NDPS Act based on statements linking the accused to the procurement of Ganja and Charas for the employer and another person through other co-accused. No contraband was recovered from the accused. The prosecution invoked Section 29 (conspiracy) and Section 27A (financing illicit traffic). The accused was alleged to have received drugs on the instructions of others but was not a consumer or dealer.

The accused was arrested by a central narcotics enforcement agency in a case related to the drug angle arising from the investigation into the death of a well-known person. The accused was alleged to have procured drugs through a network involving several co-accused and to have arranged payments through various means. The case involved the recovery of a commercial quantity of LSD from a linked co-accused and digital evidence of drug facilitation.

The accused, a house-help employed by a well-known actor (since deceased), was arrested under multiple sections of the NDPS Act on the basis of statements made by co-accused persons linking the accused to the procurement of ganja and charas for the deceased. No contraband was recovered from the accused. The accused was alleged to have received deliveries on the instructions of co-accused 1 and to have made payments using the debit card of co-accused 2.

The accused was arrested during a raid conducted on a certain date in 2019 for possession of Mephedrone, a psychotropic substance, along with the co-accused. The raid was conducted around 1:15 AM and resulted in recovery of contraband. The defense argued non-compliance with Section 42 NDPS Act, as the raid occurred between sunset and sunrise allegedly without proper authorization.

In an earlier year, an infant was kidnapped while playing with the infant's parent in a locality in a city. The accused was arrested along with seven others. As per the prosecution, the infant was kidnapped by co-accused 1 and co-accused 2 and passed through a series of intermediaries, and was eventually recovered from co-accused 3. The accused's alleged involvement was based on disclosure statements indicating that the accused met other co-accused during the chain of custody.

The accused was arrested in connection with the kidnapping and trafficking of a child. The FIR was initially registered against unknown persons. During investigation, the accused and three co-accused were apprehended. Allegedly, the accused and co-accused 2 kidnapped the child and took the child to the residence of co-accused 3. The child was subsequently rescued.

The accused was arrested in 2021 after being found with a red bag containing five plastic packets of brown sugar weighing 500 grams, valued at ₹7.5 lakhs, during a police raid at a hotel. The accused attempted to flee but was apprehended on the spot. A prior bail application had been rejected based on the commercial quantity involved.

The accused was arrested in December 2020 after a co-accused, who was found with 5g of Mephedrone, disclosed the accused's involvement. The accused was then apprehended in an auto-rickshaw and found with 52g of Mephedrone. The accused remained in custody for over 3 years. The accused's prior bail applications had been rejected. In this third application, the accused raised the issue of non-compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act for the first time.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a child born from the complainant's second marriage and taken the child to a foreign country. The complainant alleged that the child was unlawfully removed from the complainant's custody. The FIR invoked kidnapping and cheating provisions. Other co-accused had already been granted bail.

A minor child, an infant of six months, was kidnapped by a person named as an accused and was later recovered from the house of a co-accused (co-accused 1). The accused was not named in the FIR, but was implicated through the statement of another co-accused (co-accused 2), who claimed that the accused connected co-accused 2 with co-accused 1. The prosecution alleged that the accused facilitated the kidnapping. The accused had no prior criminal history and had been in custody since a date in the year 2023.

The accused was arrested after being intercepted in a vehicle with a co-accused and was found in possession of 40.5 kg of ganja. The accused persons were informed of their rights under Section 50 NDPS Act and samples were collected. A charge sheet was filed. The co-accused was later granted bail on technical grounds. The accused had been in custody for over 3.5 years at the time of this second bail application.

The accused and the co-accused were arrested for kidnapping a child and demanding a ₹50 lakh ransom. The child was rescued based on GPS tracking and a call made by co-accused 4. Investigation revealed that the accused, a neighbour of the complainant, had shared information with the others and helped plan the kidnapping. The accused was arrested following a co-accused's voluntary statement. One accused remains absconding.

The accused was alleged to have received a kidnapped newborn from co-accused 1 and co-accused 2. The kidnapping was allegedly planned by co-accused 3, a hospital sweeper, on the instructions of the accused, who had been promised money by another person. The child was recovered from the accused's rented accommodation.

The accused, a person of foreign origin, was arrested in October 2020 for alleged possession of cocaine and ecstasy, based on substances seized in a police trap. The initial forensic report suggested that the NDPS Act applied. However, a corrigendum from the forensic laboratory later clarified that the substances were Lidocaine, Tapentadol, and Caffeine, none of which fall under the NDPS Act. The court noted a violation of Article 21 due to prolonged wrongful incarceration.

The case involves the kidnapping of a child of very young age (a minor). It was alleged that one accused kidnapped the child at the behest of another co-accused and handed the child to the applicant, who allegedly agreed to sell the child to a third person for ₹70,000. Instead of cash, property documents were given. The child was eventually rescued from the third person. The applicant was arrested as Accused No.2 based on statements of co-accused.

The accused was charged along with two others of kidnapping a child aged under two years (an infant). The child was recovered from co-accused 1, who has already been granted bail, along with co-accused 2. The first informant later turned hostile in court and did not support the prosecution case. The accused had no criminal record and had been in jail since a date in the previous year, which was over a year before the bail application.

The complainant alleged that their child, a minor aged under three, disappeared while playing, and suspected the accused of being involved, as the accused had earlier threatened the complainant. The accused was not named directly but was suspected due to the previous threats. The child had not been recovered at the time of the bail hearing.

The accused was arrested after police recovered 900 grams of Charas from their possession during a raid near a public ground. The accused was alleged to have intended to sell the contraband. Despite a prior withdrawal of a bail plea, the accused had been in custody for over three years with no progress in the trial.

Two highly educated adults (co-accused 1 and co-accused 2, referred to together as the accused) were allegedly influenced and manipulated by a person posing as an astrologer (co-accused 3). They reportedly left their homes to stay with that person, fell under their influence, and began using ganja. A raid led to the arrest of the accused along with co-accused 3 under the NDPS Act. The parents of the accused sought interim bail and permission to shift the accused to a rehabilitation center, citing the low quantity of 14.9 grams and the absence of any prior criminal record.

The accused was found in a car at a state border with the co-accused and a kidnapped minor child. The prosecution alleged that the accused played a role in human trafficking. The accused claimed that the co-accused had taken them along on the pretext of going for a visit, and that they had no knowledge that the child had been kidnapped. There was no evidence connecting the accused to a kidnapping syndicate.

The accused was alleged to have entered a cowshed and attempted to commit rape on the victim, who was present there with a cow. Upon the victim's outcry, a witness arrived, prompting the accused to flee. Saliva was found on the victim's shirt. The accused was arrested after absconding and had prior FIRs registered against them in earlier years.

The accused, a director of a pharmaceutical company, was arrested after 500 kg of Tramadol powder was seized from a container at an inland container depot. The consignment had been misdeclared as Sildenafil Micro Granules and was headed to a foreign country. The authorities alleged intentional concealment, forged documents, and lack of a proper export license. The accused was present at the scene and identified the mislabeled drums. Investigation revealed deliberate misdeclaration, tampering with CCTV, and deletion of chats with the intended importer.

On a certain date, police seized 38 vials of codeine-based cough syrup and 250 Carisoprodol tablets from a motorcycle driven by the co-accused, with the accused as pillion rider. The vehicle was registered in the accused's name. The accused was arrested and incarcerated under the NDPS Act. The forensic science laboratory confirmed the presence of Codeine Phosphate and Carisoprodol in commercial quantity. No recovery was made from the accused's person, and the accused was not involved in any other case.

The accused was implicated in a heroin trafficking case from a particular year involving 56 kg of heroin allegedly smuggled by foreign nationals by sea into the country. The accused was not named in the original FIR but was added on the basis of a supplementary charge sheet, which alleged the accused's prior involvement in a similar operation the previous year, in which 15 kg of heroin was successfully received. The prosecution highlighted the accused's key role in planning, financial transactions, boat hiring, and communication with overseas dealers. No contraband was recovered from the accused's possession in the present case.

The accused was arrested in August 2019 after police recovered 375.054 kg of poppy straw from the accused's shop and adjoining godown in a city. Multiple bail applications of the accused were earlier rejected. The present application was based on prolonged incarceration and medical grounds, including cardiac disease and diabetes, along with trial delay. The prosecution argued that medical care was provided in jail and that the trial was actively progressing.

The accused was implicated in a case from the year 2022 involving the smuggling of 56 kg of heroin from a neighbouring country to India by sea. The accused was not named in the FIR but was later arrested on the basis of statements and call records. It was alleged that the accused had previously, in the preceding year, rented out a boat to the same group of accused persons for trafficking 15 kg of heroin. In both instances, the accused allegedly accompanied the group near the coastal waters of the neighbouring country. The prosecution highlighted financial transactions and a lack of fishing activity as indicators of complicity.

On the basis of a tip-off, a central narcotics enforcement agency seized a parcel at a courier company's facility in a city. The parcel contained 677 grams of Ketamine hidden inside handbags. The parcel had been booked using fake documents. Upon investigation, co-accused 1 implicated the accused, from whose home matching packaging material, a fake identity card, and ₹5.84 lakhs were recovered. Forensic analysis confirmed communication between the accused, co-accused 1, and another co-accused (co-accused 2).

During a patrol, police found the accused in possession of 190 Etizolam tablets, weighing 25.56 grams in total. The tablets were seized after the accused was seen throwing a polythene bag containing them on the ground. The forensic science laboratory confirmed the tablets were Etizolam, which qualifies as a commercial quantity under the NDPS Act. At the time of the bail application, the accused had been in custody for 1 year and 11 months. Although the accused had prior FIRs, one ended in acquittal and another in a sentence for a non-commercial offence.

The accused was arrested in an earlier year during a raid by a central narcotics enforcement agency at a restaurant in a city. The accused was found seated with a co-accused, who was carrying 5.8 kg of Methamphetamine. An additional 1.86 kg was later recovered from another co-accused. Although no contraband was found directly on the accused, the agency alleged conscious possession based on the accused's presence and call detail records linking the accused to the co-accused.

The accused was implicated in a case registered under multiple NDPS sections following the seizure of brown sugar and approximately 1000 YABA tablets from the co-accused, who was apprehended near a shop in a locality. During the investigation, the accused's involvement surfaced, and the accused was arrested. Although initially remanded to judicial custody, the Special Judge later released the accused on interim bail, which was extended multiple times despite allegations of a connection to the narcotics trafficking.

The accused was arrested after police received information that the accused was transporting a large quantity of Charas in a vehicle. Upon inspection in the presence of an Executive Magistrate, 8.190 kg of Charas was recovered from the speaker box and rear lamps of the vehicle. A charge sheet was filed, and six material witnesses were examined. The defense argued non-compliance with Section 42 NDPS Act and prolonged incarceration.

The accused, a senior police officer, was alleged to have colluded with a police inspector (the co-accused) in facilitating narcotics trafficking. Based on reports by a Special Investigation Team constituted under court orders, the accused was alleged to have knowingly promoted and protected the co-accused, who was involved in multiple offences under the NDPS Act. The reports highlighted the accused's role in promotions, falsified clearances, and possible laundering of drug proceeds through real estate.

The accused and the co-accused were found cultivating 7000 kg of opium poppy on government land. They were booked under Sections 8/16 of the NDPS Act. The prosecution did not file the chargesheet within 60 days. The petitioners claimed entitlement to default bail under Section 167(2)(a)(ii) CrPC.

The accused was arrested in June 2024 along with two others while travelling in a vehicle containing 30 soap boxes filled with 339 grams of heroin. Another vehicle, suspected to be escorting the consignment, was also seized. The accused was charged under Sections 21(c)/29 of the NDPS Act. The bail plea challenged the sampling method of the contraband under the 2022 NDPS Rules, arguing non-compliance and procedural lapses.

Based on informer input, 2.25 kg of morphine and Rs. 2 lakh were recovered from a car owned by the accused and driven by the co-accused. The accused was arrested and charged under Sections 8/21/25/29 of the NDPS Act. Bail was sought on the grounds of procedural lapses in sampling under Section 52-A, no prior criminal antecedents, and parity with a co-accused who had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested with 40 grams of Yaba tablets, an intermediate quantity. The accused was charged under Sections 22(b)/29 of the NDPS Act and Section 14 of the Foreigners Act for illegal stay in the country. After over 5 years and 5 months in custody, only one prosecution witness had been fully examined. The accused invoked Section 436A CrPC citing excessive undertrial detention.

The FIR originated from a secret tip-off about co-accused 1, who was arrested with 1050 Tramadol tablets. Based on co-accused 1's disclosure, co-accused 2 was identified, and from co-accused 2 the police seized 115,350 intoxicant tablets, 51 kg of poppy husk, and ₹1.77 lakh. Co-accused 2 named several others, including their own parent, their sibling, and the accused (the petitioner), alleging that they sourced the contraband from another accused. The accused was arrested, and no recovery was made from the accused. Only 2 of the 19 prosecution witnesses had been examined at the time of the bail hearing.

On a certain date, the accused was found travelling in a taxi near an airport during a police naka when a search led to the seizure of 60g of wet ganja, 1330 Spasmo Proxyvon Plus capsules, and 120 tablets of Ultracet (Tramadol Hydrochloride). The accused was arrested, and the contraband was seized in the presence of a Magistrate. The substances were later confirmed by the forensic science laboratory as containing commercial quantities of psychotropic drugs. The accused was alleged to have sold the contraband to local youth and has remained in custody since the filing of the charge sheet, which was filed within about three months of the seizure.

The accused was named by a co-accused in a disclosure statement as someone who had previously purchased poppy husk. No recovery was made from the accused. The accused was arrested and had been in custody since then, a period of over two years by the time of the bail hearing. Out of 34 listed prosecution witnesses, none had been examined at the time of the bail hearing. The Court noted that there was no corroborative evidence aside from the disclosure.

A truck carrying 2520 kg of poppy husk was intercepted and two persons were arrested. In a disclosure statement, those two persons named the accused, alleging the accused's prior involvement in transporting poppy husk. No recovery was made from the accused. The accused was arrested later. The investigation also revealed a separate case involving heroin and weapons against another co-accused. The accused was in custody for over 5 months and no prosecution witnesses had been examined.

The accused was linked to a case registered several years earlier in which 5.5 kg of morphine was seized from a co-accused. The accused was named in a Section 67 NDPS statement as a regular recipient. The accused was arrested several years after the seizure following a production warrant. The prosecution relied solely on Section 67 statements without independent corroboration. The accused had already secured bail in three other NDPS cases, two of which also lacked recoveries.

A co-accused was apprehended with 600 loose intoxicant tablets and, in a disclosure statement, named the petitioner as the supplier. The petitioner was arrested later, and no recovery was made from the petitioner. The petitioner had prior convictions and was an undertrial in other NDPS cases. Only 1 out of 10 prosecution witnesses had been examined.

The accused was arrested in a month of 2020 while driving a truck loaded with 315 kg of ganja. The accused claimed to be a professional driver recruited by a third party. Co-accused 1 and co-accused 2 were arrested with additional ganja shortly thereafter. Call detail records, disclosure statements, and bank transactions formed the basis of the prosecution's case.

Some time earlier, the accused was apprehended at an airport in a city after arriving on a flight from abroad. A trolley bag in the accused's possession was found to contain 2.22 kg of cocaine hidden in a concealed compartment. The accused confessed to smuggling the contraband on the instructions of another person, citing financial distress. The confession led to the arrests of co-accused. The charge sheet was filed, but the trial had not commenced, and co-accused 2 and co-accused 3 had already been granted bail.

The accused was implicated in an NDPS case following the seizure of 414 kg of poppy husk from a vehicle. The accused was arrested on production warrants from custody in a related NDPS case and was named on the basis of the disclosure of a co-accused and call records. No recovery was made from the accused. The accused had been convicted in an earlier NDPS case. Only 9 of 40 prosecution witnesses had been examined in over a year of custody.

Following the arrest of three individuals and the recovery of 150 kg of poppy husk, co-accused 1 disclosed that the contraband was to be delivered to the accused, who had deposited Rs.1,32,000 in co-accused 1's bank account. Based on this disclosure, the accused was nominated as an accused. The State produced a list showing the accused's involvement in over 20 prior cases, including convictions under the Excise Act and one NDPS conviction.

The accused was named in a disclosure statement by a co-accused in a case involving the seizure of 50,000 Tramadol tablets. The accused allegedly supplied the tablets at the behest of another individual. No recovery was made from the accused, who was arrested nearly three years after being named, following interim bail proceedings. The accused was declared a proclaimed offender before surrendering voluntarily. None of the 18 prosecution witnesses had been examined by the time of bail.

A person was apprehended with 100 Tramadol SR 100 tablets near a school in a town. Based on that person's disclosure, the petitioner was named as a co-accused, though no recovery was made from the petitioner. The petitioner later joined the investigation and was released on personal bond by the investigating officer.

A person was apprehended with 100 Tramadol SR 100 tablets near a school in a town. Based on that person's disclosure, the petitioner was named as a co-accused, though no recovery was made from the petitioner. The petitioner later joined the investigation and was released on personal bond by the investigating officer.

On a certain date, the NCB seized 3.860 kg of opium from a vehicle and arrested two persons, co-accused 1 and co-accused 2. Co-accused 1 escaped custody but was apprehended several days later along with the accused and another associate. The accused was implicated based on a co-accused's disclosure and call detail records showing contact. No contraband was recovered from the accused. The accused remained in custody since July 2023, and none of the 23 prosecution witnesses had been examined.

Police intercepted a car driven by the accused near a junction in a town in a state, acting on credible information. Four bags containing a total of 108 kg of ganja were recovered from the car. The accused confessed to transporting the ganja to a city for sale. The accused was arrested the following day and has remained in custody since then. The co-accused were later charge-sheeted, with one declared an absconder. Nine out of twenty witnesses had been examined by early 2025.

The accused was named in the disclosure statement of a co-accused, who had been arrested for supplying 34.39 grams of opium. The co-accused claimed to have procured the contraband from the accused. The petitioner had prior convictions in two NDPS cases and sought anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC.

The accused was arrested as one of the two passengers in a truck from which 56 kg of poppy husk was recovered. The accused had been in custody for more than 1 year and 8 months and had no criminal antecedents. Although charges were framed several months after the arrest, no prosecution witness had been examined as of the date of the bail order.

Based on intelligence inputs, the police intercepted a car at a check post. The accused and two co-accused were arrested with a total of 21 kg of ganja: 10 kg was recovered from the accused and 5.5 kg each from the other two. Each person had a separate bag, and three separate mahazars were prepared. The defence argued that each person had only an intermediate quantity, but the court held that the accused were in conscious possession of the entire consignment.

The accused was apprehended by police based on a secret tip-off while riding a motorcycle, and 310 grams of heroin was recovered from their possession. The petitioner alleged false implication and procedural inconsistencies in the Section 50 NDPS notice and consent memo. The accused remained in custody for over 1 year and 11 months without any witness being examined in trial.

The accused was named as a supplier of intoxicating tablets based on the disclosure of a co-accused, who was arrested with 410 loose tablets under the NDPS Act. Although not present at the scene, the accused was implicated based on statements and nominated in the FIR.

The accused was arrested after being found in possession of 260 grams of heroin during a personal search conducted on the basis of secret information. The accused had been in custody for over one year and five months when charges were framed, and none of the 11 listed prosecution witnesses had been examined at the time of the bail hearing. No other criminal case was pending against the accused.

The accused was arrested for possession of 48 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup and 200 Nitrazepam tablets during a police naka check. The total codeine exceeded permissible therapeutic limits and was categorized as commercial quantity under the NDPS Act. The accused has been in custody for 248 days and claimed prolonged incarceration as a ground for bail.

The accused was arrested for possession of 1500 tablets of Tramadol Hydrochloride (Colovidol-100 SR) without a valid permit or license, along with a co-accused who has since passed away. The accused had been in custody for over 1 year and 6 months, with no witnesses examined out of 18 cited, and no other case pending against them.

The accused was previously granted bail in an NDPS case, despite alleged involvement in the possession and trading of illicit psychotropic substances. The accused was later found to be involved in two additional NDPS cases while on bail, leading the State to file for cancellation of bail.

The accused was arrested for possessing 1450 tablets of Tramadol Hydrochloride, amounting to 577.94 grams, which is classified as commercial quantity under the NDPS Act. The accused remained in custody for over 2 years and 5 months, with only 2 out of 8 witnesses examined. No other NDPS case was pending against the accused.

The accused was arrested along with co-accused for transporting heroin and methamphetamine worth over Rs. 1.47 crore. A central investigating agency filed charges beyond the 180-day statutory period under the NDPS Act without a valid extension, and the court had earlier failed to inform the accused of their right to default bail. The co-accused were already granted default bail.

The FIR was filed after the informant's child was found missing from their bed late at night. The kidnapped child was later recovered from the co-accused. The accused's name appeared only in the co-accused's confessional statement. The accused was taken into custody and had no prior criminal record.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped and murdered their sibling's child, a minor, in an earlier year. The child was lured, drugged with sleeping pills, forcibly administered a harmful substance, and smothered. Physical evidence, including drugs and the child's belongings, was recovered from the accused's house. The prosecution presented circumstantial evidence, including mobile call records, linking the accused to the crime.

The juvenile accused was charged with the brutal murder of their parents and sibling, allegedly committed to access money. The accused stayed with the bodies for two days and afterward used the parent's retirement money. The accused had previously shown problematic behavior, such as stealing and running away.

The accused was implicated in a kidnapping case in which a child was abducted and a ransom was demanded. The accused was alleged to have provided the vehicle used in the crime and was not named in the initial FIR. A revolver and cartridges were recovered from the accused's room. The accused had been in custody since a date in December 2020.

The accused, a juvenile at the time of the offence, was accused of murdering an elderly person during a robbery in 2016. The accused allegedly entered the deceased's house on the pretext of asking for water, hit the deceased with a steel pan, smothered the deceased, and robbed the deceased's valuables. The accused was arrested using technical surveillance after using the deceased's mobile phone with a SIM card belonging to the accused's parent. The accused had previously been involved in a murder case in the preceding year, in which the accused was acquitted under Section 302 IPC but convicted under Section 364A IPC.

A minor child was kidnapped for ransom and later recovered from the house of the accused. The accused was initially granted default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC due to failure to file a charge sheet within 90 days. After the charge sheet was submitted alleging the graver offence under Section 364A IPC, the Sessions Court cancelled the accused's bail. The accused challenged this cancellation under Section 482 CrPC.

The accused was granted bail in a case involving allegations under IPC Sections 306 and 498A.
