The complainant later sought cancellation of bail on the grounds that the accused was influencing their child, who is a witness, through video calls by making disparaging comments about the child's maternal relatives. Simultaneously, the accused sought relaxation of the bail conditions to visit their ailing parents in a city.

The applicant was implicated based on a co-accused's statement in a kidnapping case involving a minor child. The child was recovered the next day but not from the applicant's possession. The applicant is not named in the FIR and has been in custody since a date several years earlier.

The petitioner was previously granted bail in a case involving the murder of a person. A second FIR was later filed accusing the petitioner of kidnapping and attempting to traffic the deceased's minor child. The petitioner claims the second FIR is a duplicate for the same incident.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a large-scale financial fraud involving the transfer of government funds into firms allegedly operated by the accused's sibling using the accused's name. The prosecution claims that the accused's bank accounts were used in the transactions. The accused had been in judicial custody for over a year, and the chargesheet was voluminous with many witnesses.

The petitioner was accused of handling proceeds of crime linked to a company through a web of other companies, while acting as a non-executive nominee director. The funds were allegedly laundered through layers of intermediary firms over a period of several years. The petitioner was arrested under the PMLA and, according to the facts, had never been named in the original ECIR or in the predicate offence chargesheets.

The accused, acting as an auto-rickshaw driver, along with others, allegedly diverted passengers from their intended route and robbed them at knife-point of mobile phones, Rs. 500 each, and funds via a digital payment app. The incident occurred in March 2022, and the accused was arrested shortly after. The accused had multiple prior FIRs for theft and assault.

The accused and others were arrested for allegedly smuggling over 160 kg of gold through diplomatic channels from a foreign country, using forged authorizations and hawala networks. A central investigating agency invoked provisions of the UAPA, alleging a threat to economic security. The accused were in custody for over a year without trial.

The accused was alleged to have laundered Rs. 64 crores received from a corporate group after a bank sanctioned a Rs. 300 crore loan to that group. The loan was allegedly approved by the accused's spouse, who was then the chief executive of the bank. The funds were allegedly routed to a company owned by the accused through complex transactions. The enforcement agency arrested the accused the following year, though the accused had cooperated with the investigation since the preceding year.

The accused, a senior government engineer, was allegedly involved in laundering demonetized currency worth Rs. 6.12 crore through intermediaries. The accused had earlier been subjected to a raid by an anti-corruption authority for disproportionate assets. The Enforcement Directorate case is based on an FIR registered by a central investigating agency and is supported by incriminating statements recorded under Section 50 of the PMLA.

A large mob of about 1000–1500 persons gathered outside a police station on a particular day, allegedly incited by a social media status that depicted a flag on the dome of a place of worship. The mob attacked police personnel with stones and clubs, injuring personnel and damaging public and police property. Several persons were identified through CCTV footage, call detail records, and messaging groups. A central investigating agency took over the case and charged them under the IPC, the PDPP Act, and the UAPA.

On a date in August 2020, violent protests erupted near a police station in a city after a derogatory social media post about a religious figure. The accused, alleged to be a district-level office-bearer of a political organisation, was accused of conspiring with other members of that organisation and mobilising a mob to attack police stations and public property. The mob caused widespread damage despite prohibitory orders. The accused was arrested and charge-sheeted under multiple sections of the IPC and the UAPA.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was accused along with other family members of setting the victim ablaze over dowry demands. The incident occurred six years after the marriage. The deceased gave a dying declaration implicating the spouse and in-laws before succumbing to burn injuries. The applicant had been in jail for a period of time since the arrest, and the trial had not progressed.

The accused was arrested in connection with the alleged dowry-related death of their spouse. An independent witness confirmed that a quarrel had occurred between the couple before the deceased committed suicide. The FIR was filed under Sections 498A and 304B IPC, and the prosecution submitted statements of the complainant and the parent of the deceased alleging dowry demands and harassment.

The accused was found in possession of a countrymade revolver and live cartridges during a police search conducted while pursuing suspects in a murder case. The area had been declared 'notified' under TADA, and possession of arms without authorization led to registration of a case under Section 5 of the Act. The accused had prior criminal cases for assault and robbery and had been absconding for many years.

The accused, a coal transporter and director of a company, was alleged to have regularly paid levies to a banned terrorist organization in certain coalfields. The National Investigation Agency alleged that the accused was involved in terror funding, through bank transfers and cash payments, in order to secure protection for the business. The accused was earlier treated as a witness and was later named as an accused on the basis of supplementary chargesheets.

The accused was alleged to have acted as a conduit for transferring funds from terrorist sources, including a foreign intelligence agency and a designated terrorist, to separatist leaders in order to finance anti-national activities in a region. The investigating agency alleged that the accused received these funds through hawala channels and suspicious business transactions. A High Court had granted the accused bail, and the investigating agency challenged that order.

The accused was arrested for allegedly recruiting young people of a particular community to join an organisation that aimed to establish a religion-based system of rule in the country by a specified year. The accused was alleged to have organised training camps, raised inflammatory slogans, and received funds from that organisation and another foundation, both of which were later banned. The prosecution alleged that the camps involved indoctrination and preparation for subversive activities.

The accused, a Head Constable in a border security force, was accused of pilfering ammunition from the force's stores and supplying it to a banned extremist organisation through a co-accused. The investigating agency alleged that the accused received cash for the transactions and tried to mask shortages through inter-company adjustments. The case was based on witness statements, recovery of unaccounted arms, and entries in official logs.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was accused of dowry harassment and abetment of suicide. The prosecution alleged a demand for a four-wheeler and cruelty, leading to the deceased's suicide within 7 years of marriage. The FIR was lodged more than two months after the incident. The defence claimed delay in the complaint, depression of the deceased related to a miscarriage, and that the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused and others were charged with conspiracy to promote terrorist activities inspired by a proscribed terrorist organisation, through a trust that was allegedly a front organisation. They allegedly held martial arts and weapons training, raised funds, harboured co-conspirators, and transported individuals to target areas. The accused was found in possession of a pistol and ammunition and was accused of aiding in organising secret camps and procuring materials for improvised explosive devices.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was alleged to have burned the deceased to death due to dowry demands. The FIR alleged ongoing harassment since the marriage. The first informant later turned hostile during trial. The accused had been in custody for several years, with the trial pending and only 4 of 18 prosecution witnesses examined.

The victim alleged that the accused drugged and sexually assaulted the victim under the false pretense of employment and marriage. The accused threatened to upload the victim's nude photos, caused two forced abortions, and abused the victim using caste slurs. The accused used influence over the police to get the victim arrested in a false case. The accused also had a history of exploiting women, with 12 previous cases, including preventive detention under the GOONDA Act.

The accused, a member of the armed forces, was alleged to have shared sensitive information with a foreign handler via social media. The accused allegedly shared details about ships and installations, deleted incriminating chats, and used covert language to evade detection. The accused was charged under multiple sections, including the UAPA and the Official Secrets Act.

The accused has been in custody since May 2021 in connection with the death of their spouse, allegedly due to dowry harassment. The marriage took place in 2020. The FIR alleges that the accused and the accused's family harassed the deceased, who died from injuries inflicted on a date in May 2021. Despite court directions to expedite the trial, no prosecution witness had been examined by May 2024.

The accused's spouse suffered 90% burns and later died in hospital. In a dying declaration, the deceased accused the accused and the in-laws of dowry harassment and of setting the deceased on fire over an additional dowry demand of ₹5 lakhs. The FIR and statements by witnesses supported the allegations. A charge sheet was filed against the accused, the two in-laws, and one other relative; another co-accused was exonerated.

The accused was alleged to have harboured members of a banned extremist organisation and stored arms and explosives at their residence. Though not named in the FIR, the accused was arrested several years ago and charge-sheeted for aiding a banned terrorist organisation. A significant cache of weapons and propaganda material of the organisation was recovered from the accused's house. The accused was listed as an absconder and a reward was declared for their arrest.

The petitioner, co-accused 1, was arrested for allegedly kidnapping a child along with co-accused 2 and taking the child to the house of co-accused 3. The child was later rescued. The FIR was initially lodged against unknown persons. Co-accused 3 was granted bail, but the court found distinct roles for the petitioner and co-accused 2 in the kidnapping.

The accused was implicated in a case related to illegal mining and coal transactions, registered at a police station. The FIR alleged involvement in handling or dealing in stolen property. The Court, upon hearing both sides, found it appropriate to grant bail.

The accused, alleged to be involved in terrorist activities, was charged under several sections of the IPC, the Arms Act, and the UAPA. The accused had been in custody for several years, and 11 of the 12 charge-sheet witnesses had already been examined. The court rejected the accused's fifth bail application, citing the seriousness of the charges and the potential flight risk.

The accused allegedly kidnapped the complainant in 2018 and committed rape on the pretext of marriage, keeping the complainant at different places, and the complainant later delivered a child. The complainant later discovered that the accused was already married. The complainant was confined and threatened for dowry before escaping and filing a case in 2020.

The applicant was accused of defrauding the informant by not paying over Rs. 1 crore for 64 truckloads of onions purchased. The applicant had initially gained the informant's confidence by making a partial payment, and then defaulted. Multiple similar FIRs were registered against the applicant in different states.

The petitioner was accused of involvement in the kidnapping and murder of a minor child. It was alleged that the petitioner had promised to recover the child within 24 hours during a village-level community meeting, but the child's dead body was found the next day. The petitioner claimed to have been falsely implicated, pointing to the lack of eyewitnesses and procedural lapses in the investigation.

Some time earlier, there had been an incident in which the complainant's family was beaten. Later, the complainant and relatives went to the accused's house to reach a compromise regarding that earlier incident. The accused and the co-accused allegedly assaulted them with iron rods and swords because of election-related grievances. The complainant's sibling was fatally injured in the assault. An FIR was lodged from the hospital.

The accused was arrested for allegedly kidnapping a child along with the child's parent from a city. The prosecution claimed CCTV footage showed the accused's involvement. The defence argued false implication and pointed out that the child's parent had already been granted interim protection.

The accused was arrested in a case for allegedly kidnapping a child along with a co-accused and taking the child to the house of a third accused. The child was later rescued. The FIR was initially registered against unknown persons, but the accused was identified during the investigation.

The accused, who is an in-law of the victim, was accused in a case involving dowry demands and physical assault. It was alleged that the victim was harassed and assaulted by in-laws. No specific role of assault was attributed to the accused. The accused had cooperated with the investigation, and the charge sheet was already filed.

The applicant was accused of torturing their spouse for dowry (a buffalo and a motorcycle). The spouse allegedly consumed poison and died within seven years of marriage. The postmortem revealed that the deceased was pregnant. The FIR was lodged by the deceased's parent, alleging harassment and dowry demand.

The complainant lodged an FIR against their spouse, the accused, alleging harassment and torture for dowry. The complainant left the matrimonial home and now lives with their parents. The applicant claimed innocence and expressed willingness to take their spouse back.

The accused was arrested in connection with the death of their spouse within seven years of marriage. The FIR alleged dowry harassment. Out of three accused, two were exonerated and the charge-sheet was filed only against the accused who is the applicant. Some prosecution witnesses turned hostile, but key ones supported the case.

The sibling of the complainant was allegedly harassed for dowry and later died due to alleged poisoning. Initially, only the deceased's spouse was charge-sheeted, but after re-investigation, the deceased's in-laws, referred to as co-accused 1 and co-accused 2, were also included in the charge-sheet. They were granted bail by the Sessions Court. The complainant sought cancellation of bail, alleging misrepresentation of facts about their residence.

The accused was charged in connection with the unnatural death of their spouse within a year of marriage. The prosecution claimed dowry harassment and alleged that the deceased was poisoned and strangled. However, medical and FSL reports showed death due to hanging and no traces of poison. Witnesses gave contradictory statements.

The accused and the accused's family members were alleged to have subjected the accused's spouse to cruelty and harassment for additional dowry. After registration of the FIR, the couple underwent mediation and reportedly resolved their issues, deciding to live together again.

The deceased and their in-law were found dead in a well near their home. The FIR, filed by the deceased's relative, alleged dowry harassment by the deceased's spouse and the spouse's family, including the applicants. No direct evidence of assault or harassment by the applicants was provided. Similar allegations against other family members had resulted in bail.

The accused was charged along with two others with kidnapping a 14-month-old child. The child was recovered from the possession of co-accused 1. Both co-accused 1 and co-accused 2 were granted bail earlier. The informant later turned hostile and did not support the prosecution's case.

A minor was kidnapped and was recovered the next day. The name of the applicant surfaced only in the statement of a co-accused. The applicant was not named in the FIR, nor was the child recovered from the applicant's custody. Co-accused who allegedly had more direct roles were granted bail previously.

The accused was arrested in connection with the kidnapping and murder of a minor child. The accused was not named in the FIR. The accused's name surfaced in the statement of a co-accused (co-accused 1), who claimed that the accused brought the child's clothes for a ritual due to childlessness. Another co-accused (co-accused 2) had already been granted bail.

The accused was charged in a case involving allegations of kidnapping and sexual assault of a minor under the IPC and the POCSO Act. The FIR alleged that the accused kidnapped the victim to compel them to marry. However, the accused claimed that the victim was a consenting adult and that they had married willingly. The accused previously obtained interim protection and later the charge sheet was submitted as directed by the court.

The accused, a parent of the minor victim, was accused of repeatedly raping the victim since the victim was in a school class at primary or middle level, and of forcing the victim into prostitution. The victim alleged involvement of over 25 individuals, including relatives. Despite the serious nature of the allegations, multiple co-accused had already been granted bail. The victim's version remained consistent, but the victim failed to specify dates or locations.

The accused was implicated in a case concerning an alleged attempt to kidnap a minor. The accused was not named in the FIR, and their name surfaced based on a confidential informant's information. No CCTV or photographic evidence was collected. A co-accused with a similar role had already been granted bail. The prosecution acknowledged one additional case against the accused, filed after this FIR.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped and sexually assaulted a minor. The complaint was filed by the minor's parent, who alleged that the minor had been kidnapped. The accused claimed that the minor was their legally wedded spouse and that they had a child together. The marriage was registered, and the accused was not arrested during the investigation phase.

The accused, an in-law of a co-accused, was implicated in the kidnapping of a minor child. The prosecution claimed that the co-accused played the main role, while the accused's involvement was indirect. Another co-accused had already been granted bail. The accused had one prior case, which was explained in the affidavit.

The accused was alleged to have attempted to kidnap a minor child along with two others. The FIR was filed by the child's grandparent. However, the victim did not make any statement against the accused under Section 161 CrPC. A co-accused with a similar role had already been granted bail.

The accused and co-accused allegedly abducted a minor and delivered the minor to accused No.1, who detained and repeatedly raped the minor. The minor later alleged that their eyes were tied and that multiple rapes occurred. Medical reports confirmed hymen rupture. Though the accused cited a prior accident as a ground for incapacity, the court found sufficient prima facie evidence of the accused's involvement.

The survivor, a minor, was acquainted with the accused and frequently communicated with them. On a certain date, the survivor went missing and was later found in another village. It was alleged that the accused sexually assaulted the survivor, resulting in pregnancy and the birth of a child. The accused sought bail and expressed willingness to marry the survivor.

The accused, a parent of the main accused, was charged with facilitating a child marriage and abetting the rape of a minor. The victim alleged being forcibly married at a place of worship and sexually assaulted. The accused had previously secured anticipatory bail but failed to attend the trial court, leading to their arrest after over four years.

The accused was arrested for allegedly attempting to buy a kidnapped child, after losing their own baby. The accused claimed to be unaware that the baby had been kidnapped and stated that the intention was only to adopt a child. The accused had already spent nearly three months in custody and the trial had not commenced.

The accused and co-accused were implicated in the kidnapping of a child from a street vendor and the sale of that child through a chain involving multiple accused. Although one of the co-accused received the money, it was allegedly shared among all. The FIR was initially registered against unknown persons, and the accused was identified during the investigation.

The accused was arrested along with others for allegedly kidnapping a one-day-old child. However, the child's parent later submitted an affidavit stating that they had voluntarily given away their seventh child due to poverty, intending the child to be given to a needy couple. The co-accused had already been granted bail earlier.

The petitioner alleged that their estranged spouse (respondent no. 2) and the spouse's relative (respondent no. 3) forcibly stopped a bus, assaulted the petitioner's parent, stole ₹15,000, and kidnapped the petitioner's child. The spouse had previously handed over custody of the child to the petitioner through an attested statement. The trial court had granted anticipatory bail to both accused.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a minor child and committed obscene acts with them. The child's parent allegedly witnessed the act and lodged an FIR. The accused was arrested on the same day. The medical examination showed no injuries, and the forensic science laboratory report found no spermatozoa. The trial was delayed even though 10 of the 17 witnesses had been examined.

The accused was arrested in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor. The complainant had received ransom calls allegedly from the accused and the co-accused. The child was recovered in a city along with the accused. The accused remained in judicial custody for several years and was granted bail after examination of material witnesses.

The accused, a juvenile at the time of the incident, was accused of smothering an elderly person to death and robbing valuables from the victim's house. The accused was arrested based on mobile phone surveillance and had previously been convicted under Section 364A IPC in another case. Although previously released on interim bail, the accused was denied further bail after spending over 5 years in custody.

The applicant, who is the spouse of the respondent, alleged dowry harassment and cruelty by the respondent, including financial cheating and attempted kidnapping of their child. The respondent had previously been granted anticipatory bail. The applicant filed for its cancellation, citing non-payment of maintenance and concealment of income details.

The accused was alleged to have assisted the co-accused in kidnapping a minor for ransom by providing false documents. The minor was later found murdered, and the body was dumped in a canal. The accused was arrested based on the statement of a witness, whose identity documents were allegedly misused.

The accused, listed as accused No.5, sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest in a dowry harassment case registered in a city. The complainant, the accused's child's spouse, alleged that a dowry of Rs.50 lakhs and other articles was paid at the time of marriage, and that the complainant was later harassed and thrown out of the house. The accused claimed false implication and requested transitory bail from a High Court in a different state, as the accused resided in a city within that state.

The accused, a sibling-in-law of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased for dowry along with other in-laws. The deceased died of poisoning less than two months after the marriage. The deceased allegedly named the in-laws as responsible before death. The complainant also alleged that the accused threatened the complainant to compromise the matter. The FIR named the accused explicitly, and the court noted visible injuries on the deceased.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, applied for anticipatory bail after being implicated in the suicide of the deceased, who was the accused's child's spouse. The prosecution alleged harassment and dowry demands. The death occurred in the matrimonial home. The accused claimed false implication and stated that they lived separately, but investigation and witness statements indicated otherwise.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased spouse of their child for dowry and to have forcibly administered pesticide, which led to the victim's death. The complainant alleged that the victim was denied communication with the victim's family and was mistreated for insufficient dowry. A written dying declaration by the victim alleged that the accused mixed poison in water and later locked the victim in a room. The death occurred within four months of marriage.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was accused of cruelty and dowry harassment after the deceased died by hanging within one year of marriage. The FIR was lodged two days after the incident. Witness statements indicated a dowry demand of Rs. 5,00,000, but lacked specificity regarding timing. The accused's parents had already been granted bail.

The accused, spouse of the deceased, was accused of dowry harassment and causing the death of the deceased spouse within five years of marriage. The FIR alleged a demand for a motorcycle, a gold chain, and Rs. 1 lakh. The viscera report confirmed the presence of a poisonous substance. There was also an averment that the deceased had made a video recording regarding the harassment, though no such video was recovered.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was arrested after the deceased allegedly committed suicide within a few months of marriage. The complainant, the deceased's parent, alleged dowry harassment by the accused and the accused's in-laws. The deceased had left the parental home with cash and a vehicle to marry the accused against the parents' wishes. The complaint alleged mental and physical harassment, including on the night before the death.

The petitioners, including the victim's spouse (the accused) and the spouse's parents, were accused by the complainant (the victim's parent) of subjecting the victim to dowry-related harassment and threats, leading to the victim's suicide after nearly eight years of marriage. The FIR was filed following the victim's unnatural death at the matrimonial home. The complaint alleged consistent mental and physical abuse, dowry demands, and threats of remarriage. The victim had returned to the parental home just before the incident and died shortly after returning.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased for dowry from the date of marriage. The deceased died by hanging within two years of the marriage. The allegations included threats, abuse, and denial of communication. The complainant stated that the accused's family failed to inform them promptly after the death. A charge sheet was filed showing the accused as absconding.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was accused of dowry harassment leading to the deceased's suicide within seven years of marriage. The FIR alleged cruelty, demands for Rs. 5 lakh and a four-wheeler, and sexual harassment by another in-law of the deceased. The defence argued that the FIR was an afterthought and provided mobile evidence suggesting post-marital depression. Neighbours reported cordial family relations.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was accused in a case involving dowry death. The FIR was filed by the deceased's parent, alleging harassment and a demand of Rs. 5 lakhs that culminated in the alleged strangulation and cremation of the deceased without a postmortem. The deceased's sibling and both parents, all key prosecution witnesses, were examined but did not support the prosecution and were declared hostile.

The accused persons, who are the in-laws of the complainant, sought anticipatory bail after being named in an FIR alleging dowry harassment under Sections 406 and 498A IPC. The complainant alleged that they were left in the country at the mercy of the accused persons after their spouse moved abroad. Although the accused persons initially expressed willingness to mediate, they later disowned the settlement offers, and were accused of mental and physical harassment of the complainant.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was accused of harassing the deceased for dowry, leading to the deceased's suicide within four years of marriage. The FIR alleged demands of Rs. 3 lakhs, and mental and physical torture. The accused was evading arrest, failed to join the investigation despite notice, and did not cooperate during interrogation after being granted interim protection.

The deceased, the accused's spouse, died by suicide within seven years of marriage. An FIR filed by the deceased's parent alleged ongoing dowry harassment by the accused and the accused's in-laws, including a demand of Rs. 2 lakhs a day before the death. The postmortem confirmed death due to hanging. While two of the accused's in-laws (co-accused 1 and co-accused 2) received bail on medical or interim grounds, the accused remained in judicial custody. Material witnesses were yet to be examined.

The accused, along with their sibling and parent, were accused under IPC Sections 354C and 354D and IT Act Sections 66, 66C, 66E, and 67A, based on a private complaint filed by the accused's spouse. The complaint followed an earlier FIR under IPC Section 498A and Dowry Prohibition Act Sections 3 and 4. The complainant alleged harassment and invasion of privacy. The petitioners had already received anticipatory bail in the previous dowry case. They sought anticipatory bail again after the complaint was forwarded to the police for investigation.

The accused was charged in a case involving the unnatural death of their spouse, with charges under Sections 304B, 302, and related IPC provisions. The prosecution relied on statements from the deceased's parent and sibling alleging dowry harassment. However, neighbours gave statements that the deceased was not harassed. The co-accused, who is the accused's parent, was earlier granted bail on similar grounds.

The deceased, who had been married to the accused's child a little over a year earlier, died by suspected suicide (hanging). The deceased's sibling alleged dowry harassment and lodged an FIR under Section 304B IPC. The accused persons, namely the deceased's spouse and the spouse's parent (the accused seeking bail), were chargesheeted. Medical evidence suggested death by asphyxia due to throttling, contradicting suicide. Witnesses stated that the deceased was harassed and sent back to the parental home multiple times. The accused, the in-law of the deceased, sought bail after 1 year and 4 months in custody, citing absence of injuries and delay in trial.

The accused was arrested in connection with the kidnapping and murder of a child, whose decapitated body was found in an agricultural field. This was the accused's second bail application under Section 439 CrPC, the first having been withdrawn without merits. The incident was registered under Sections 363 and 302 IPC, and the accused had been in custody since 2015.

The accused was alleged to have purchased a child, aged under three years, who had been kidnapped by a co-accused at the accused's behest. However, the charge-sheet did not indicate the accused's direct involvement in the act of kidnapping. The accused had no criminal history and had been in custody since a date several years earlier. The child was returned to their biological parent, and the trial was not expected to start soon.

The accused, convicted in a prior POCSO case involving the complainant (the accused's now-spouse), was granted anticipatory bail in a subsequent FIR for domestic violence and threats. The complainant sought cancellation of this bail, citing suppression of the prior conviction and continued harassment. The couple had married after the conviction and were entangled in ongoing disputes with multiple cross-complaints.

A juvenile was accused of conspiring with co-accused to kidnap and murder a minor for a ransom of Rs. 14 lakhs. The Juvenile Justice Board and the Sessions Court rejected the juvenile's bail application under Section 12 of the JJ Act. The revision petition challenged these orders.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased for dowry, resulting in the deceased's suicide within 5 years of marriage. A complaint was lodged by the deceased's parent, alleging physical and mental abuse. Initially, the charges included Section 302 IPC, which was later dropped. The co-accused in-laws were granted bail. The accused and the deceased had two children, and the accused was in judicial custody.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was arrested in connection with the deceased's unnatural death by hanging within 2 years and 2 months of marriage. The FIR alleged dowry harassment. While there were consistent allegations, the co-accused, an in-law of the deceased, had already received bail. The accused had been in jail for a period of time since an earlier date in 2022, and only two out of 25 witnesses had been examined by the time of the bail hearing.

The accused, a head constable in a state police force, was accused by their spouse of dowry harassment and attempt to murder. The FIR alleged that the accused demeaned the complainant's appearance, demanded ₹5 lakh in dowry, and eloped with another person. It also stated that the accused's parent and sibling attempted to strangle the complainant. While the co-accused were already granted bail, the accused sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest.

The de-facto complainant accused their spouse and the spouse's relatives of dowry harassment and intimidation. Anticipatory bail was earlier granted to the accused. The complainant later sought its cancellation, citing non-return of jewellery and threats. The accused had partially complied with court directions to return belongings. The court noted that the remaining disputes related to matrimonial property and refused to cancel bail.

The accused married the deceased against the wishes of both families. They lived together peacefully for six months. Later, the deceased allegedly faced dowry-related harassment from the accused and the accused's family. The deceased died by suicide, allegedly due to continuous abuse and threats from the accused. The prosecution claimed a prior quarrel took place the day before the death, but no injuries were found during the postmortem. The accused and the co-accused have been in custody since the day after the death.

The accused, spouse of the deceased, was arrested for allegedly harassing the deceased mentally and physically, leading to the deceased's suicide by consuming poison. The couple had been married for 11 years and had two children. The deceased's parent alleged that the accused and the accused's family harassed the deceased and suspected the deceased's character. The co-accused (the accused's parents and sibling) had already been granted anticipatory bail.

The petitioner, the accused, was alleged to have harassed their spouse for dowry and to have maintained an illicit relationship with their sibling-in-law. The spouse died by suicide within three years of marriage. The complaint by the deceased's parent alleged dowry demands and harassment, including a payment of Rs. 1.5 lakhs and gold. Though initially booked under Section 302 IPC, the charge sheet was filed under Sections 304B and 306 IPC.

The deceased was married to the accused's child on a certain date. The deceased died by hanging within a few months of the marriage. The deceased's parent filed an FIR alleging harassment by the in-laws, including a demand for ₹20 lakhs and a car. The accused, who is the deceased's in-law (the parent of the deceased's spouse), was arrested. The postmortem showed death due to asphyxia from hanging, with no injuries besides a ligature mark.

The petitioners challenged the bail granted to the accused and the co-accused in two cases involving damage to property, criminal intimidation, and attempt to murder. The accused had allegedly attacked a hotel and an apartment building, causing severe property damage and injuries. After being released on bail, they were further accused of instigating attacks and distributing defamatory material.

The deceased died under suspicious circumstances within 1 year and 8 months of marriage. The deceased's sibling alleged that the deceased's spouse and in-laws, including the applicant who is an in-law of the deceased, were dissatisfied with the dowry and murdered the deceased by poisoning. However, the postmortem and inquest found no external injuries, and the cause of death was reserved for viscera analysis. The co-accused, another in-law of the deceased, was already granted bail, and the applicant claimed to live separately from the deceased.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was arrested after the deceased died by hanging within two years of marriage. The FIR alleged dowry harassment and a demand of Rs. 5,00,000 by the in-laws, along with threats of remarriage of the deceased's spouse. No external injuries were found except a ligature mark. The deceased had earlier complained to the police about harassment. The accused was arrested the day after the death.

The complainant alleged dowry harassment by their spouse and in-laws shortly after marriage, including physical abuse and a demand for ₹50 lakhs and a luxury car. The complainant also alleged that their spouse forced them into unnatural sex. When the complainant informed the in-laws, they supported the spouse. The complainant was eventually expelled from the matrimonial home and the complainant's belongings were retained by the in-laws. The complainant filed an FIR and sought cancellation of anticipatory bail earlier granted to the in-laws.

The deceased was married to the applicant's child (the deceased's spouse) about a year before the death. The FIR filed by the deceased's sibling alleged frequent dowry harassment and alleged that the applicant and other family members beat and strangled the pregnant deceased with lathis and sticks. The postmortem indicated asphyxia due to ante-mortem strangulation. The applicant, who is the in-law of the deceased, was arrested about a month later. The allegations against the applicant were general, and no specific role was assigned to them.

The complainant alleged that the accused introduced a co-accused who posed as the owner of 2 acres of land and duped the complainant into paying Rs. 2 crores. The accused allegedly fabricated documents and cheated several persons. Despite earlier withdrawal of anticipatory bail applications from the High Court, the accused secured bail from the Vacation Sessions Court without disclosing the prior applications. The complainant sought cancellation of the bail order.

The deceased was married to the co-accused, who is the child of the applicant, about three years before the deceased's death by hanging. The deceased's sibling lodged an FIR alleging a demand for dowry (a bike and ₹10,000) and that the deceased was murdered by the in-laws. The postmortem revealed no injuries other than a ligature mark. The applicant, who is the deceased's in-law, was arrested soon after. The applicant's spouse, also a co-accused, had already been granted bail.

The accused, the in-law of the deceased, was arrested following allegations of dowry harassment after the deceased, the accused's child's spouse, died from internal injuries. The FIR alleged a dowry demand of a motorcycle and cash by the accused and the accused's children. The deceased suffered internal bleeding due to liver and spleen rupture, with no external injuries. A co-accused, a relative of the deceased by marriage, had already received bail. The applicant had been in custody since a date in 2019.

At an earlier time, the complainant's relative was allegedly assaulted while questioning a person from the village about their missing child. Co-accused 1 allegedly slapped that person, while co-accused 2 and co-accused 3 allegedly threw bombs, causing injuries. The FIR also alleged kidnapping of the child. The petitioners were initially denied bail, but sought relief again after the charge sheet was filed several months later.

The accused, the spouse of the deceased, was charged under Sections 498A and 304B IPC and the Dowry Prohibition Act after the deceased died by suicide within two and a half years of the marriage. The FIR alleged general dowry harassment by the accused and the accused's family. The accused claimed that a quarrel preceded the incident and that the deceased locked themselves in a room and was later found dead. The postmortem confirmed death by hanging. No specific dowry complaint had been made before the death, and the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The petitioner filed a criminal complaint against their spouse and the spouse's relatives under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the TNPHW Act. Earlier, the accused sought anticipatory bail from the High Court, which was withdrawn after failed mediation. They then obtained bail from the Sessions Court without disclosing prior bail attempts. The petitioner sought cancellation of the bail granted to accused 1 to 6 and 8.

The accused, spouse of the complainant, was accused of dowry harassment, physical abuse, and threats, with the FIR also including attempted rape allegations against the accused's siblings. The accused had previously been convicted in a murder case from an earlier year, which was later reduced to Section 304(II). The complainant alleged loss of vision due to assault. After arrest and denial of first bail, the accused sought bail citing completed investigation, long custody, and that the complainant refused medical examination and had a pre-existing eye condition.

The deceased died by suicide in their matrimonial home within months of marriage. The deceased's sibling filed a complaint alleging dowry harassment by the deceased's spouse and in-laws. The deceased had allegedly called a relative shortly before the death, saying they were being pressured to commit suicide. The accused, the deceased's spouse, was arrested the day after the incident and sought bail, citing recovery after surgery and the fact that, on similar allegations, anticipatory bail had already been granted to the co-accused in-laws.

The deceased was married to the accused's relative (the deceased's spouse) in a year, and the deceased's parent alleged that the deceased was harassed by the spouse and in-laws for additional dowry. When the deceased visited the parental home for a festival, the deceased was allegedly asked not to return to the matrimonial home unless more dowry was brought. The deceased died by suicide at the parental home about a year after the marriage. The deceased's spouse was arrested and had been granted bail earlier. The petitioners, who are relatives of the deceased's spouse, sought anticipatory bail, claiming there were no specific allegations against them.

The accused, the spouse of the informant, was alleged to have subjected the informant to dowry harassment and physical abuse during their marriage, in more than one country. Despite earlier settlements and assurances not to harass, the accused allegedly continued the abuse, including withholding the child's documents. The FIR was filed after a physical assault in a city, where police intervention was sought. The Sessions Court had earlier denied bail to the accused while granting it to the accused's parents.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was charged after the deceased, who was the accused's child's spouse, died from ligature strangulation within 7 years of marriage. The FIR was filed by the deceased's parent, who alleged dowry harassment including demands for 51 sarees, gold ornaments, and ₹50,000. The deceased's child was also found dead by strangulation. Witnesses corroborated the harassment claims. The accused had been in custody for several years, since 2012, and sought bail citing the duration of custody and parity with their spouse, who was granted bail.

The deceased allegedly died by consuming poison within three years of marriage. The deceased's parent alleged dowry harassment by the deceased's spouse and in-laws, including the spouse's sibling, who demanded additional dowry and gold. The FIR included accusations of physical assault and murder. The postmortem showed no external injuries, and a co-accused had already been granted bail. The petitioners claimed false implication and lack of direct involvement.

The deceased died by suicide a few months after marriage, allegedly due to dowry harassment by the deceased's spouse and the spouse's parent. The FIR was filed by the deceased's parent, citing physical assault and dowry demands. The petitioner, the in-law of the deceased, sought bail after it was denied by the Sessions Court. The court observed that there were no specific allegations or materials against the petitioner and noted that the investigation was already complete.

The accused, spouse of the complainant, was accused of dowry harassment, misappropriation of stridhan, and an alleged attempt to administer phenyl. The FIR was filed after the complainant left the matrimonial home several years earlier. Co-accused family members had already received anticipatory bail. The accused claimed the allegations were false, and that articles belonging to the complainant were secured in the home locker, which required the complainant's thumb impression.

The complainant alleged that, after two months of marriage, the complainant was subjected to dowry harassment, including demands for additional cash and property transfer. The accused persons allegedly harassed and assaulted the complainant. Among the multiple accused, some were family members while others were unrelated third parties. The complaint included allegations of sexual harassment by a co-accused. Anticipatory bail was sought by accused 5, 6, 7, and 8. Accused 7 and 8 were third parties alleged to have supported the harassment.

The accused was arrested in a month of 2023 in connection with an FIR registered under Sections 363 and 376 IPC and Section 6 of the POCSO Act, based on allegations made by the victim's family. The accused was later granted bail by the Sessions Court. The victim, who is now the accused's spouse, stated before the Magistrate that the victim left home willingly and denied any sexual assault. A Settlement Deed followed, and the couple resumed cohabitation.

The accused impersonated an Anti-Corruption Bureau officer and demanded Rs. 3,00,000 from the complainant, an auditor, for allegedly closing a fake complaint. The accused received Rs. 4,40,000 through staged transfers and further demanded Rs. 20,000 before the complainant grew suspicious. An investigation revealed that no such complaint or officer existed. The accused was arrested, and Rs. 2,38,000 along with a car and a bike were recovered.

The accused persons sought anticipatory bail in a case involving allegations by the complainant, who is the daughter-in-law of the accused persons, of dowry harassment, assault leading to a miscarriage, and attempted rape by another child of the in-laws. An FIR was registered under multiple IPC sections. The accused persons allegedly interfered with the investigation and tampered with evidence.

The deceased was allegedly harassed and assaulted by their in-laws for additional dowry of ₹2,00,000. The deceased's spouse reportedly remarried without the deceased's knowledge. After sustained ill-treatment, the deceased set themselves on fire. The complaint was filed by the deceased's parent, and statements from independent witnesses supported the prosecution's case.

The case arose out of a marriage between two persons from different communities, which was opposed by the family of one of the spouses. The accused and others were alleged to have kidnapped two minors at gunpoint. However, an affidavit from one of the spouses stated that no kidnapping or injuries occurred. Protection orders had previously been issued for the couple.

The accused is the in-law of the deceased, who allegedly died by suicide after being harassed for dowry. The deceased had been living separately at their parental home, preparing for competitive exams. A suicide note alleged dowry demands by the deceased's spouse and the accused. The accused sought anticipatory bail citing their age, medical history, and a weak role in the incident.

The deceased died after allegedly consuming poison. The deceased had been married in one month of a year and died about five months later. Allegations of dowry harassment and assault were made against the deceased's spouse, the spouse's parent, and the spouse's sibling, who is the accused in this application. The dying declaration primarily named the deceased's spouse and the spouse's parent as the persons responsible, with only a general mention of the accused.

The accused was alleged to have tortured their spouse for dowry along with another co-accused. The spouse died from burn injuries in their house. The deceased's parent alleged repeated dowry demands and harassment. Statements from the deceased's parent and the landlord suggested that the deceased had made oral dying declarations about the ill-treatment.

The petitioner was arrested for allegedly kidnapping and marrying a minor, who later gave birth to the petitioner's child. The FIR was lodged by the victim's parent. The school record indicated the victim was a minor at the time of marriage and childbirth.

The victim, a minor, alleged that the accused embraced the victim and took a selfie against the victim's will, threatening the victim not to disclose the incident. The co-accused allegedly shared the photo with the victim's relatives. An FIR was filed under IPC sections and the POCSO Act. The court found prima facie material for sexual assault under POCSO.

The petitioners sought cancellation of interim bail granted to the co-accused (respondent no. 3), who was accused of abducting and forcibly marrying a minor and subjecting the minor to sexual violence. The FIR was lodged under Section 363/34 IPC, though the petitioners argued it should include Section 366 IPC and Section 4 of POCSO. The police filed the charge sheet under Section 363 IPC.

The petitioner, who is the parent of the victim, challenged the bail orders granted to the accused and others, who allegedly kidnapped and raped the petitioner's child, a minor. The victim later testified in court that they had married the accused willingly, had a child with the accused, and denied the earlier allegations, stating that those allegations were made under police pressure.

The complainant alleged that they were kidnapped and forcibly married to co-accused 1, who later sexually assaulted them. The petitioners, who are co-accused 5, 6, 7 and 8, were alleged to have assisted in events after the marriage. They sought anticipatory bail on the ground that their role was minor and vague, and that the main accused had already been granted bail.

The petitioner alleged that the respondent and the respondent's child took Rs. 7,00,000 on the promise of a job at a university and issued a forged appointment letter. Anticipatory bail was granted to the respondent by the Sessions Court, which the petitioner challenged. The High Court found that the Sessions Court had ignored the gravity of the offences and relevant precedents.

The accused, an in-law of the deceased, was accused along with their child and other relatives of harassing the deceased for dowry, leading to the deceased's suicide within seven years of marriage. The FIR was filed by the deceased's parent. The accused had been on interim bail and cooperated with the investigation; a charge sheet and a supplementary charge sheet were filed.

The complainant alleged that the complainant's sibling, the victim, was harassed by the victim's spouse (the accused) and the accused's family for dowry, including a demand of Rs. 50,000 and gold ornaments. The accused reportedly suspected the victim's chastity and made such demands. The victim returned to the parental home and committed suicide the same night, three and a half months after the marriage.

The petitioner, a foreign national, was arrested at an airport carrying 50 foreign-origin gold biscuits hidden in their suitcase. After the arrest and remand, the petitioner's bail application was rejected. While in custody, a detention order was passed under COFEPOSA. The petitioner challenged the detention, citing lack of compelling necessity.

The accused was arrested for smuggling 40 mobile phones hidden in a microwave oven. The accused was alleged to have travelled multiple times to a foreign country under instructions from their employer. After several bail rejections, the accused was eventually granted bail, but in the meantime a preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was issued and challenged.

The case involves a large arms smuggling operation originating from another country and centred around one principal accused, who named several recipients of illegal arms. Multiple FIRs were filed. Several accused filed writ petitions challenging their prosecution under TADA, arguing procedural lapses and misuse of the Act. Many of them were granted interim bail or parole during pendency.

The accused was arrested for involvement in the smuggling of ball bearings worth over Rs. 1.42 crore, based on statements recorded under Section 108 of the Customs Act. The accused was granted bail by the Sessions Court after 40 days in custody. A government investigating agency challenged this order, alleging preferential treatment and unjustified haste.

The accused, a foreign national, was arrested at an airport in a city for smuggling 70 tolas of foreign gold concealed in their shoes. Though granted bail by a High Court, the accused remained in custody due to a COFEPOSA detention order. The accused challenged the detention, claiming they did not understand the grounds of detention, which were in English, and that their representation was ignored.

The accused was arrested while attempting to travel abroad with foreign currency worth over Rs. 5.45 lakhs. Though already in judicial custody and with bail rejected twice, a COFEPOSA detention order was issued against the accused. The accused submitted multiple representations against the detention, citing delay and non-consideration.

The accused was arrested at an airport in a city with mobile phones and accessories valued at Rs. 13.9 lakhs, allegedly brought from a foreign country. The accused claimed that the untagged luggage did not belong to them and that they had no connection to the smuggled items. Though bail was denied, a preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was later passed against the accused.

The victim, a minor, was allegedly kidnapped and raped by a juvenile and a co-accused. The FIR named the applicant based on suspicion held by the victim's parent. However, the victim did not name the applicant in their statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC.

The accused and others allegedly kidnapped the complainant's younger sibling and assaulted that person with a sharp weapon after a demand for money was refused. Injuries were reported as simple, with one grievous injury. A compromise was reached between the parties, and the accused is reported to suffer from epilepsy.

On a certain date, the accused and co-accused were apprehended at an airport with large amounts of foreign currency while attempting to board a flight to a foreign destination. The currency had been passed to them after customs clearance by an employee of an airline. Detention orders were issued under COFEPOSA, and bail was sought by the accused.

The accused, a senior government official, was arrested in a money laundering case linked to gold smuggling through diplomatic baggage and alleged kickbacks from a government housing project in a state. The accused was alleged to have facilitated financial transactions and access to a bank locker allegedly used to store proceeds of crime.

The accused was detained under COFEPOSA for allegedly smuggling hashish through exported machinery. Large quantities of hashish were seized from trucks and a farmhouse linked to the accused. The accused was already in judicial custody for the same offence when the preventive detention order was passed.

The accused, a foreign national, was found at an airport carrying 26 gold tablets weighing 3742.4 grams without legal documents. Initially the accused denied it, but later admitted to intending to carry the gold to a foreign city. The accused was arrested, granted bail by a High Court, and later detained under COFEPOSA. The detention was challenged on several legal grounds.

The accused was implicated in a gold smuggling operation involving 14.7 kg of gold hidden in a refrigerator imported via unaccompanied baggage. The accused was arrested along with others, and a detention order under COFEPOSA was issued. The case involved earlier bail, alleged retracted statements, and WhatsApp chats used as evidence by the detaining authority.

The accused was arrested while attempting to travel abroad with foreign currency worth over Rs. 5.45 lakhs. Although the accused was already in judicial custody and their bail applications had been rejected twice, a detention order under COFEPOSA was issued. The accused submitted multiple representations against the detention, citing delay and non-consideration.

The accused was detained under the MPDA Act based on a case involving robbery and physical assault. The accused allegedly snatched money from the complainant using a knife and caused injuries. The detention was challenged by the accused's sibling on grounds of illegal preventive detention while the accused was already in custody, incorrect translation of documents, and delay in deciding the representation.

The accused was detained under COFEPOSA for allegedly smuggling large quantities of foreign-origin gold through consignments from one city to another city using employees and aliases. The accused was arrested following seizure of 9.9 kg of gold and was implicated in prior smuggling cases. The accused's spouse challenged the detention order.

The accused, a director of a company, was alleged to have imported duty-free polyester and silk yarn under the DEEC scheme and diverted the goods to the domestic market instead of exporting the resultant products, thereby violating the Customs Act and the EXIM policy. After an investigation by a revenue intelligence agency, a preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was issued against the accused. The accused's spouse filed a writ of habeas corpus challenging the detention.

The accused was implicated in a gold smuggling syndicate that used unaccompanied baggage from a foreign country to conceal and transport gold into India. Over 14 kg of gold was found hidden in a refrigerator at a container yard in a city. The detainee was arrested, later granted bail due to COVID-19 circumstances, and then subjected to a preventive detention order under COFEPOSA, which was challenged on multiple procedural grounds including non-supply of electronic evidence such as WhatsApp voice messages.

The accused was arrested at an airport for smuggling 42 mobile phones worth approximately Rs. 4.5 lakhs. Although the accused's bail applications were initially rejected, the accused was eventually granted bail by the High Court. Before release, a preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was issued. The accused challenged the detention on grounds of non-supply of documents, suppression of exculpatory materials, and delay in disposal of the representation.

The accused was arrested in connection with the kidnapping of a child. While a co-accused was alleged to have abducted the child, the accused was said to have merely kept the child at their house. The accused had been in custody since an earlier date in 2022. The co-accused had already been granted bail, and the child's statement was on record.

The accused was apprehended upon arrival from a foreign city with fake Indian currency notes (FICN) concealed in an LCD television. The accused was arrested under the Customs Act and later charged under IPC sections related to counterfeiting. A preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was issued seven months after the arrest, which the accused challenged as delayed and unjustified.

280 silver bricks worth over Rs. 7.37 crores were smuggled using fishing trawlers and vehicles. The accused was the owner of the house where the contraband was temporarily stored. The accused was present throughout the night of the loading operation and was involved in arranging boats and labour. The accused was already in custody under the Customs Act when the COFEPOSA detention order was passed. The accused's parent filed a habeas corpus petition challenging the preventive detention.

The accused was charged along with others in a case involving allegations of rape, abduction, and confinement. The victim alleged that they were forcibly confined and raped by a co-accused while their child was taken away. The accused sought anticipatory bail, arguing lack of direct involvement and raising credibility issues with the victim, who had filed a similar earlier case and later turned hostile in court.

The accused was arrested in connection with an organised cattle smuggling racket across an international border, allegedly involving corrupt border security and customs officials. The accused allegedly paid large bribes and used fraudulent business fronts to legitimize illicit income. A central investigating agency registered the case under sections of the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act. The petitioner claimed parity with co-accused who were granted bail, and denied any likelihood of witness tampering.

The petitioners, including tanker drivers, helpers, owners, and transport company staff, were accused of being part of a conspiracy to siphon off crude oil during transportation and storing it at unauthorized premises. The oil theft was detected through discrepancies in delivery and storage, supported by call detail records and physical samples taken during a raid.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a minor. The minor later testified in statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC that they had left willingly, married the accused, and had a child. The minor denied having been kidnapped. The petitioner had been in custody since several years earlier, and the charge sheet had already been filed. The co-accused had been granted bail earlier.

The accused was detained under COFEPOSA based on alleged involvement in a smuggling racket involving video cassette recorders and other goods brought in via air consignments from a foreign territory. The detention was challenged as being based on vague and insufficient grounds and an unexplained delay of 16 months between the incident and the detention order.

The accused, along with others including the main courier (co-accused), was implicated in smuggling fake Indian currency from a foreign country to a state in India. The co-accused was apprehended with ₹72.5 lakhs in fake notes at an airport. The detaining authority passed preventive detention orders under COFEPOSA. The petitioners challenged the orders citing failure to consider retracted confessions and non-application of mind.

The accused was apprehended at an airport carrying two foreign-marked gold bars concealed in a briefcase. The accused initially confessed under Section 108 of the Customs Act but later retracted the statement. A preventive detention order under COFEPOSA was issued while the accused was in custody. The accused's residential premises in a city were searched, resulting in nil recovery, but this fact was not placed before the detaining authority.

The accused, a truck owner, was arrested for transporting smuggled synthetic hosiery clothes from a neighbouring country into India. While in judicial custody following the seizure of 190 bales of smuggled goods from their truck, a COFEPOSA detention order was served on the accused. The accused challenged the order, claiming that they did not know the languages in which the documents were served on them, which prevented them from making an effective representation.

The accused, an in-law of co-accused 1, was accused in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor child. The accused was not named in the FIR, and their involvement was based solely on the alleged confessional statement of another accused (co-accused 2), who had already been granted bail. Other co-accused, including co-accused 3, co-accused 4 and co-accused 5, had also been granted bail. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2022.

The applicants were implicated in a case involving the kidnapping and murder of a minor, whose body was found in the house of a co-accused. The applicants are family members of the accused and were not directly linked to the act of kidnapping or murder. The case against them relied primarily on circumstantial evidence and association with a co-accused who had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested in a kidnapping-for-ransom case involving a minor child. Although not named in the FIR, the accused was implicated based on a co-accused's disclosure. The accused allegedly made a ransom call to the victim's parent. The petitioner had been in custody for several years, and the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was alleged to be an active member of an international smuggling racket that illicitly exported 54.7 metric tonnes of red sanders from India to a foreign country under forged documents, disguising the cargo as bath accessories. The red sanders were transported from one region of the country to a city and stored there before being exported through a port in that city. The accused was alleged to have been involved in multiple aspects of the operation, including procurement, packing, transport, and concealment.

The accused was arrested in a case under Section 19/54 of the Rajasthan Excise Act involving alleged liquor smuggling. The main accused, from whom the recovery was made, had already been granted bail. The accused was implicated solely on the basis of the co-accused's interrogation notes. The accused had only one unrelated prior case under minor IPC sections. The trial court had rejected the accused's bail application mechanically, without considering the High Court's prior bail orders for the co-accused.

The accused was arrested for coordinating the smuggling of 30 kg of gold through diplomatic cargo at an airport, allegedly linked to terrorism financing. The accused was already in custody under cases brought by the customs authorities and a national investigating agency, and was later arrested under the PMLA. The accused's first bail application under the PMLA was rejected, but a subsequent application was allowed by the Sessions Court. The enforcement agency challenged this order in the High Court, citing the rigour of Section 45 of the PMLA and recent Supreme Court decisions. The High Court, however, upheld the grant of bail, citing parity with co-accused, completed investigation, and compliance with bail conditions.

The accused was arrested in an NDPS case involving the seizure of methamphetamine and morphine. The accused was charged under Sections 21(c), 22(c), and 29 of the NDPS Act. The accused initially sought default bail on the ground that the charge-sheet was filed late, but this was refuted with official records showing that it was filed within the statutory 180 days. The accused renewed the bail request citing a family member's illness and health concerns, but the court declined relief as charges had just been framed and the trial was scheduled to begin.

The accused was arrested along with co-accused in connection with a train-based NDPS case involving alleged recovery of 10 kg of ganja from the accused's possession. The petitioners were apprehended while attempting to flee during a police inspection on a train. Despite charges being framed and 14 official witnesses cited, no prosecution witness had been examined for over a year.

The accused was implicated in a wildlife smuggling case involving the illegal sale of tiger and leopard skins. Based on a sting operation by police and a wildlife expert, a deal was struck with the accused for the sale of ten tiger and ten leopard skins. A payment of ₹80,000 was made in advance. During a raid, the co-accused were arrested and animal skins were recovered. The accused and another accused fled the scene. The accused sought anticipatory bail, claiming false implication and procedural lapses under the Wildlife Protection Act.

The accused was arrested along with two co-accused in a train-based NDPS case involving the recovery of 10 kg of ganja from the accused's possession on a particular date. The accused was apprehended during a railway inspection at a railway station while trying to flee. Charges were framed in April of the same year, and 14 witnesses (mostly official) were named, yet no witness had been examined for over a year.

The accused was the 5th accused in a high-profile case involving the abduction and gang rape of a popular actor in a state. The crime was planned by a group and executed in multiple stages involving several vehicles. The accused was alleged to have briefly confined the victim and assisted the main conspirators. The accused was not alleged to have committed direct sexual assault. The accused had been in custody for nearly two years, and several other co-accused with lesser or similar roles had been granted bail.

The accused was arrested in 2020 for alleged involvement in the murder of the deceased. The case was based on circumstantial evidence and the confessional statement of a co-accused, which implicated the accused. There was no eyewitness and no direct recovery from the accused. The bail plea cited the Supreme Court's COVID-19 guidelines on decongestion of prisons.

The accused was alleged to have collaborated with a foreign national to operate a fraudulent investment app scheme under a company, which collected money from the public through gaming apps and redirected the funds abroad via cryptocurrency. The company lured victims through online platforms and impersonated celebrities to gain trust. The accused, who is the petitioner, was arrested and has been in custody since a date in 2023.

The accused was detained under COFEPOSA for alleged involvement in serious gold smuggling. The accused sought temporary bail on medical grounds, citing advanced age and an ailment. The Single Judge denied bail citing the seriousness of the offence. An appeal was filed against this denial. During the pendency of the appeal, the main writ petition challenging the detention was heard and judgment was reserved, prompting the Court to dispose of the appeal without deciding it on merits.

The accused sought anticipatory bail after their child was caught red-handed trying to abduct a newborn from a hospital. The police suspected the accused's involvement in this and in a prior unsolved newborn kidnapping case. The accused claimed to have merely sheltered the parent of the kidnapped child and invoked Section 439-A of the state CrPC Amendment, seeking leniency on the ground of being a woman.

The complainant filed a case under Section 31 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act against their spouse, the accused. The complainant alleged that, despite a prohibitory order restraining the accused from interfering with the complainant's enjoyment of their shared household and an order for interim maintenance, the accused violated the order by leasing part of the property and threatening the complainant. The accused initially obtained bail and denied the charges.

The accused, an adult, was detained under COFEPOSA for alleged involvement in large-scale gold smuggling. The accused filed for temporary bail on medical grounds. The Single Judge denied the plea citing the seriousness of the offence. The accused appealed to the Division Bench, arguing that the rejection was inconsistent with the Supreme Court's view in a prior decision regarding temporary parole under Article 226 in preventive detention cases.

The accused was arrested in a case involving serious allegations of kidnapping and gang rape of a minor, along with offences under the POCSO Act and the Prevention of Child Marriage Act. The accused was not named in the FIR, and the victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC did not allege any overt act against the accused. Similarly placed co-accused had already been granted bail, and the accused had been in custody since a date in 2021.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a child along with the main accused (the co-accused) and later handed over the child to another person for a payment of ₹1,50,000. While the FIR identified unknown kidnappers, a witness testified that the accused and the co-accused brought the child to them for adoption. The accused had been in custody for over 2 years and was on interim bail due to health issues.

The accused was accused by a sibling-in-law of poisoning the accused's in-law, leading to that in-law's death in a particular year. An FIR was lodged more than two years later, after the discovery of a diary allegedly written by the accused. The accused denied the diary's contents and claimed coercion by in-laws. The accused had also initiated multiple legal proceedings against their spouse and in-laws under domestic violence and dowry laws, suggesting ongoing matrimonial disputes.

The accused was alleged to have committed gang rape and criminal conspiracy in an incident that took place in a year several years before the FIR, together with the victim's spouse and others. The FIR was filed three years after the incident, alleging rape, video recording of the act, and trafficking. The accused sought bail on the ground of parity with the co-accused, the victim's spouse, whose bail had been upheld by the Supreme Court. The defence presented social media photographs of the victim, taken during and after the alleged incident, to question the victim's credibility.

The petitioner was accused under Sections 498A, 406, and 323 IPC by their spouse, who had earlier filed a case under the Domestic Violence Act. The petitioner alleged that the FIR was a repetition of the earlier complaint and stated that a divorce petition had been filed before the FIR. The petitioner also sent a notice for return of articles and joined the investigation.

The accused was alleged to have told the informant that the informant would receive money for giving birth to a child and allegedly introduced the informant to a co-accused, who was a nurse. That co-accused and another co-accused allegedly kidnapped the minor child. The accused denied giving any number or participating in the kidnapping. The accused had no prior criminal record and had been in custody since a date in 2022. A co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was charged in a case involving the suicide of their spouse, who allegedly took poison due to domestic violence after 12 years of marriage. A prior bail application was rejected with liberty to renew the plea after framing of charges. Following the framing of charges in a Sessions Trial, the accused moved for bail again.

The accused was alleged by their spouse, the complainant, to have committed gang rape on the complainant together with the co-accused in an earlier year, to have recorded the act, and to have threatened to release the recording. The FIR was filed several years later, and the complainant cited fear and threats as the reason for the delay. The accused, who is the applicant, allegedly ran a human trafficking and blackmail racket under cover of a security firm. The complainant had filed multiple FIRs earlier, and the accused had been granted bail in various other cases. However, the latest FIR disclosed allegations of serious and organized criminal conduct.

The accused was provisionally granted bail by the trial court in a cyber crime case registered several years earlier. The accused then filed an interlocutory application before the High Court seeking confirmation of this bail. The case involved alleged offences under cybercrime laws, though specific IPC sections were not mentioned in the order.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case involving allegations of cheating through mobile phones. The main accused, referred to here as co-accused 1, was apprehended with mobile phones and ATM cards, and named several others. The accused's name did not appear in co-accused 1's confession but emerged in the police supervision note. The petitioner claimed clean antecedents and readiness to cooperate with the investigation.

The complainant lodged an FIR under Section 377 IPC against their spouse, alleging unnatural sexual assault within marriage. The spouse was initially arrested and granted bail by the Sessions Court. The complainant filed for cancellation of the bail, citing a history of domestic violence and multiple prior complaints.

The accused, a senior police officer, was the investigating officer in a case under the NDPS Act involving digital evidence. The accused was alleged to have tampered with seized electronic gadgets (laptops, hard drives, etc.) after their seizure, while they were supposed to be sealed. Forensic reports from a forensic science laboratory and a government digital forensics centre showed unauthorized file creations. Witnesses alleged that the accused directed them to create mirror images, failed to follow seizure procedures, and offered inducements to manipulate data.

The accused sought anticipatory bail in a cybercrime case involving cheating via mobile phones. Another accused was caught with incriminating items and disclosed the names of some co-accused, though the accused's name did not appear in that person's confessional statement. The accused's name later surfaced in the supervision note during investigation. The accused claimed innocence and agreed to cooperate with the investigation.
