The informant accused their spouse, the accused, of torturing them for dowry of Rs. 5 lakhs, including threats and physical assault. The FIR cited multiple IPC sections. The petitioner referred to a prior Domestic Violence case in which the magistrate found that no violence was proven, and also cited an agreement with the informant's parent. The accused had no criminal antecedent.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case involving fraudulent activities using mobile phones. The main accused (referred to here as the co-accused) was apprehended with incriminating materials, but did not name the accused in their confession. The accused's name later emerged during the investigation. The petitioner maintained clean antecedents and promised full cooperation with the investigation.

The accused was alleged by their spouse to have subjected them to dowry harassment and physical assault following their marriage, which took place several years before the complaint. The complaint was filed several years after the marriage, and cognizance was taken the following year. The accused filed a first anticipatory bail plea several years after cognizance was taken, which was rejected. A second application was made, claiming delayed awareness of the summons and asserting cooperation in related cases, but the Court found no merit in reconsidering bail.

The accused was alleged to have violated a court protection order under the Domestic Violence Act by denying their spouse entry to the marital house, threatening the spouse with a gun, and firing the weapon at one of the spouse's relatives. The attack allegedly also involved physical assault by the accused's parent and sibling. Injuries were confirmed by a medical report. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2021.

The accused was named in an FIR related to a cybercrime and cheating case involving 20–25 individuals. During a raid, 7 people were arrested with mobile phones and ATM cards. The accused was not apprehended at the scene but was named based on disclosures made by the co-accused. No material was recovered from the accused's possession. The accused claimed clean antecedents and cited parity with others already granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have violated an interim protection order issued under the Domestic Violence Act by failing to pay maintenance to their spouse and children as ordered by the court in an earlier year. The case was converted into a miscellaneous case under Section 31 of the Act. The accused claimed that the order had been challenged in revision and sought anticipatory bail after the trial court denied it.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case involving alleged cheating of innocent persons, along with 20–25 other co-accused. Seven of the co-accused were arrested with mobile phones and ATM cards. The accused's name surfaced only in a co-accused's disclosure. No material was recovered from the accused's possession. The accused had clean antecedents and sought parity with other co-accused who had been granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was arrested for cyber fraud involving impersonation as an employee of a bank, leading to the illegal transfer of ₹23 lakhs from the complainant's account using fake wallets and SIM cards. Though the accused was not named in the FIR, the accused's name appeared in a supplementary statement, and investigation revealed use of 28 fake wallets and possession of 19 mobile phones and hundreds of SIMs. The accused had multiple similar cases pending in various states.

The accused was arrested for defrauding a person of ₹23 lakhs via phishing. The accused was not named in the FIR but was added after a supplementary statement based on hearsay. The accused allegedly purchased 18 fake bank accounts and was part of a cyber fraud gang. The accused had been in custody since 2019, and charges were framed a few months later in the same year. Three other similar cases were pending against the accused in different states.

The accused was arrested in connection with a cyber fraud involving a fake call center impersonating a life insurance company. The accused was not named in the FIR but was later arrested after disclosure statements linked them to bank accounts used in the fraud. No direct recoveries were made from the accused, and the accused was said to have been employed just a month before the FIR.

The accused was arrested in connection with the suicide of their spouse, with whom they had two children. The prosecution alleged abetment of suicide and cruelty under Sections 306 and 498A IPC. The defence claimed the deceased had a difficult temperament, that the relationship was strained but under reconciliation, and that the suicide stemmed from depression unrelated to any instigation by the applicant. The chargesheet had already been filed.

The accused, a journalist, was accused by their spouse in multiple complaints alleging various offences under the IPC, Information Technology Act, Official Secrets Act, and Emblems and Names Act. These arose from a matrimonial dispute and included allegations of dowry harassment and digital fraud. The High Court had rejected the accused's anticipatory bail plea. The Supreme Court found the complaints vengeful and lacking prima facie substance.

The accused, a foreign national, allegedly impersonated a person on social media and deceived the complainant into transferring over ₹10 lakhs under the pretext of sending a gift. Although the accused was not named in the FIR, they were linked to the offence through call detail records and the recovery of the mobile phone used in the offence. The accused's visa had expired several years earlier, and they were residing in the country illegally.

The accused was alleged by the complainant, a relative by marriage, to have visited the complainant's home while the complainant was alone and attempted to force physical relations, including forcibly kissing the complainant and tearing the complainant's clothes. The complainant alleged repeated harassment and threats. The accused claimed the FIR was false, citing a prior vacation taken together and past false cases filed by the complainant. The accused sought anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC.

The accused was charged, along with the accused's sibling-in-law and that sibling-in-law's spouse, with abetting the suicide of the accused's spouse. The deceased drowned and left a suicide note blaming the applicants. The accused had previously filed a Domestic Violence complaint and a maintenance application against the deceased. The Court considered the strained relationship between the accused and the deceased, and the suicide note.

The accused was charged by their spouse under sections of the IPC and the Dowry Prohibition Act, alleging harassment and dowry demands during the marriage and after the couple returned from a foreign country. The spouse claimed to have been assaulted and thrown out of the house after refusing to bring ₹50 lakhs. The Sessions Court had rejected anticipatory bail, citing the accused's divorce petition as indicative of cruelty.

The applicants, who were relatives of the deceased's spouse, were accused of abetting the suicide of the deceased, who died allegedly due to prolonged dowry-related harassment. The deceased had filed a domestic violence case several years earlier, which ended in a compromise, after which the deceased resumed cohabitation. The FIR alleged continuous dowry demands and ill-treatment. The applicants had been in custody since a date in an earlier year.

The case involves allegations that a person befriended the informant via a social media platform, developed a relationship, and later married the informant before demanding ₹50 lakhs and extorting ₹10 lakhs through threats and blackmail using intimate photographs. The informant alleged a pattern of similar conduct with multiple persons. While the bail of the main accused was denied, anticipatory bail was granted to two relatives of the main accused, as no specific role was attributed to them.

The accused was arrested in connection with a cyber fraud case registered under multiple IPC and IT Act sections. The accused had previously been denied bail due to evidence including recovery of 100 pre-activated SIM cards and tracing of the crime proceeds to the account of the accused's parent. In this second application, the accused cited prolonged custody and offered to deposit Rs. 50,000. The accused had also been granted bail in a related case in another state.

The complainant filed an FIR against their spouse (Appellant No.1) and in-laws under provisions of the IPC and the SC/ST Act, alleging abuse based on caste, dowry harassment, and physical and mental torture following their marriage several years earlier. The FIR followed earlier proceedings under the domestic violence law and a non-cognizable complaint. The Sessions Court had rejected anticipatory bail, citing the bar under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act.

The informant alleged that the accused, who is an in-law of the informant's spouse, along with others, committed rape and dowry-related abuse. The incidents were alleged to have occurred in a particular month, but the FIR was filed over a year later. The accused contended that earlier domestic violence and maintenance proceedings had been withdrawn by the informant without any mention of these allegations. The informant claimed fear of a video being leaked as the reason for the delay in making the complaint.

The applicant was accused of rape under Sections 376 and 376(2)(n) IPC by a person who had a prior consensual relationship with the applicant. The complainant later married another person and filed domestic violence proceedings against that spouse. In the FIR, the complainant blamed the applicant for the breakdown of the marriage, while in the domestic violence proceedings, the complainant cited the spouse's affair. The FIR was challenged on the ground of these contradictions and consensual intimacy.

The complainant alleged rape by the two accused on different occasions in a particular year, facilitated by the complainant's spouse and the spouse's parent, who also recorded a video of the incident. The FIR was filed over a year later. The accused argued that earlier domestic violence proceedings, proceedings under Section 125 CrPC, and proceedings under Section 498A had been withdrawn by the complainant without any mention of these allegations. The prosecution claimed that the delay was due to blackmail using the video.

The accused was arrested after being found near a forest with three others during a police raid based on information about cybercrime. Two individuals fled, while the accused and one other person were apprehended. The accused claims innocence and states that no cyber-related items were recovered from them. The accused has no prior criminal history and seeks bail on grounds of parity with a co-accused who has already been granted bail.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case after a raid in a town where five people were arrested and several mobile phones and SIM cards used in cyber fraud were recovered. Though the accused was not arrested at the scene, a phone and SIM belonging to the accused were recovered and linked to a fraudulent digital payment account used to defraud victims. The accused denied involvement, claiming that nothing was recovered from their possession.

The accused was initially granted bail in a case under IPC Sections 419, 420 and Section 66-C of the IT Act. After further investigation, additional serious charges under IPC Sections 467, 468, 471, 120B and Sections 66/66D of the IT Act were added, leading to a new bail application after the lower court rejected it. The accused had also secured bail in another case and had been in custody since a date in 2020.

The accused was implicated in a cyber fraud case involving deceitful extraction of money from victims under false pretenses. The accused's name appeared in the confessional statements of co-accused who were arrested on the spot. The accused was not apprehended during the raid and no recovery was made from the accused's possession. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2019 and had also been granted bail in a similar earlier case.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case under multiple IPC sections. They had been in custody since a date several years earlier. The main accused, the accused's child, had already been granted anticipatory bail, and charges had been framed several months after the accused's arrest. The trial had not progressed significantly, prompting this second bail application.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case following a raid by the cyber police at the residence of a person, where several persons were apprehended with mobile phones and digital devices linked to fraudulent activity. The accused was not arrested during the raid but was later named in a co-accused's confession. The accused sought bail on grounds of parity with others already granted bail.

The accused was arrested during a cyber police raid on the house of a co-accused, conducted on the basis of confidential information. Mobile phones and electronic gadgets were recovered from multiple accused persons, including the petitioner. No victim directly named the accused in relation to the cyber fraud. Co-accused persons in similar circumstances had already been granted bail.

The accused was charged in a cybercrime case and was named on the basis of the confession of a co-accused who had been apprehended during a raid. Rs. 1,25,000/- was recovered from the accused, which the accused claimed was meant for their medical treatment. No victim directly implicated the accused. The accused sought bail on the ground of parity with co-accused who had already been granted bail.

The accused was previously granted bail under the initial IPC sections in a cybercrime case. After further investigation, additional sections, including forgery and IT Act offences, were added. The prosecution did not present new facts beyond those considered in the original bail order. The co-accused persons had already been granted bail under the added sections.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case registered at a cyber police station under several provisions of the IPC and the IT Act. The accused had been in custody since a date in early 2022. Out of the six accused in the case, four had already been granted bail by coordinate benches of the High Court.

The accused was arrested by a cyber police station in a case related to cybercrime under several sections of the IPC and the IT Act. A mobile phone was recovered from the accused. However, there was no specific evidence on record directly connecting the accused to the cybercrime. The High Court considered that a similarly situated co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a cybercrime case registered at a cyber police station. The case involved six accused persons in total. Four of the co-accused had already been granted bail. The accused had been in custody since an earlier date, and the custody had continued for a considerable period.

The accused was arrested after a raid at their parent's house led to the recovery of ATM cards, bank passbooks, and Rs. 3,14,100/- from a co-accused. The State alleged the accused was a member of a cybercrime gang. The defence argued that a similarly placed co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was alleged to be involved in the kidnapping of a newborn baby from a hospital in a city. The baby had been placed in the ICU after delivery and was later found missing. It was discovered that the co-accused had taken the child from the accused. The accused was arrested and the charge sheet was filed.

The accused was preventively detained under the COFEPOSA Act for smuggling a large quantity of gold. While challenging the detention, the accused applied for temporary bail on health grounds, citing their age as an adult and various ailments. The Single Judge denied temporary bail, citing the seriousness of the offence. The accused appealed, but the Division Bench refrained from ruling because the main detention case had already been heard and reserved for judgment.

The petitioner was not named in the FIR initially but was implicated during investigation for their role in facilitating the kidnapping of two children for their in-law, who wanted to adopt a child. One of the children, a minor, was murdered to prevent exposure of the conspiracy. The younger child was recovered from the in-law's house based on the petitioner's confessional statement.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case under several IPC sections. The accused was alleged to have been involved in cyber fraud along with others by using mobile phones. Police seized the accused's phone but failed to gather admissible evidence linking the accused directly to the crime. The accused had been in custody since the date of arrest, and the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was apprehending arrest in a cybercrime case registered under multiple sections of the IPC and the IT Act. The allegations in the FIR were general in nature and did not specifically name the accused. The accused argued that they had clean antecedents and expressed readiness to cooperate with the investigation. The co-accused in the same case had already been granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was named in a cybercrime case involving forgery and cheating, but the FIR contained general allegations without specific accusations against them. The accused maintained clean antecedents and assured the court of full cooperation with the investigation. Multiple co-accused in the same case had already received anticipatory bail.

The accused was arrested by a central revenue intelligence agency for allegedly smuggling 14 foreign-origin gold bars and 10 kg of rough diamonds across an international border, with a total value exceeding Rs. 2.6 crores. The bail application was the third successive attempt. The Court noted that the accused was not merely a carrier but a prime accused, and that the delay in trial was partly attributable to the defence's conduct.

The accused was charged in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor child, allegedly involving serious charges such as criminal conspiracy and attempted murder. The FIR claimed the child was abducted, but the child was found at home shortly after the alleged incident. The child's parent submitted an affidavit stating no objection to the applicant's bail.

The accused was alleged to have impersonated a police officer and induced the complainant to pay Rs. 5 lakhs under the pretext of helping the complainant register an FIR for sexual assault. The complainant also alleged that the accused facilitated the termination of a pregnancy. However, the FIR was filed years after the alleged incidents, and statements showed inconsistencies regarding dates and events. The court found no immediate need for custodial interrogation.

The accused apprehended arrest in a cybercrime case registered under several sections of the IPC and the IT Act. The FIR made only vague and general allegations without attributing a specific role to the accused. The accused had clean antecedents and assured the court of full cooperation with the investigation. A co-accused in the same case had already been granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case under several sections of the IPC and the IT Act. The allegations against the accused were general in nature, with no specific role attributed. The petitioner had clean antecedents and expressed readiness to cooperate with the investigation. The co-accused in the same case had already been granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was alleged to have sexually assaulted the complainant and to have been involved in extorting money through impersonation. The FIR was lodged several years after the alleged incidents, which were said to have occurred as early as six years before the FIR was registered. The complainant's statement under Section 164 CrPC contradicted the FIR, and there were inconsistencies regarding the complainant's residence and the timeline. The accused claimed to have assisted the complainant in a domestic violence case earlier and to have been falsely implicated later.

The accused and their relative (an uncle, referred to here as a sibling of the accused's parent) were accused in a cybercrime case involving forgery and impersonation. The FIR did not specify their role in detail and the allegations were general. The petitioners submitted that they had clean antecedents, were willing to cooperate with the investigation, and cited that the co-accused had already been granted anticipatory bail in the same matter.

The accused, a foreign national, was granted regular bail in 2021 in a cybercrime case involving allegations of cheating (Section 420 IPC) and an offence under Section 66(D) of the IT Act, based on a complaint from a company. A condition of bail restricted the accused from leaving the jurisdiction of the court. The accused later sought to relax this condition in order to travel abroad, but the request was rejected by the Sessions Court and the rejection was upheld by the High Court.

The accused was implicated in a cyber fraud case involving impersonation of services through an online business listing app. Five persons were arrested based on an informer tip during a police check, and various financial documents were recovered. The accused was not arrested at the scene but was named in confessional statements of the co-accused. The prosecution alleged that the accused was part of an organized cybercrime network.

The accused, a director of a company, was accused of cheating a customer who paid over Rs. 4.3 lakhs for an overseas tour that was not conducted. The customer alleged non-refund despite repeated requests. The petitioners claimed they were unable to secure a visa in time and refunded the amount. They sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest in an FIR registered at a police station.

The accused was booked under Sections 406 and 420 IPC in a cyber fraud case registered at a cyber crime police station in a district. The accused was initially granted interim anticipatory bail and directed to join the investigation. Upon compliance, the State confirmed that custodial interrogation was not necessary.

Two accused persons were arrested in a cybercrime case involving possession of incriminating articles linked to cyber offences. They had been in custody since an earlier date, about several years before the present application. A co-accused had already been granted bail by the lower court.

The accused was arrested in connection with a cybercrime case in which the police, acting on information, raided certain premises and recovered mobile phones and documents. Some of the persons involved fled, while others were apprehended, and the accused's house was searched. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2024, and the charge sheet had already been submitted.

The accused was arrested in a cyber police station case involving multiple sections of the BNS and the IT Act. Following information about cyber crime activity, police conducted a raid and recovered mobile phones and documents from the petitioner's premises. The accused had been in custody since an earlier date in 2024, and the charge sheet had been submitted.

The petitioner had already been granted bail in an FIR registered at a cyber crime police station in a city. A second FIR was subsequently filed for the same offence at a police station in another city. The petitioner sought anticipatory bail, fearing arrest again for the same act.

The accused was arrested in a cyber police station case registered under several provisions of the BNS and the IT Act. The accused was implicated following a raid on their premises, which was conducted on information about ongoing cybercrime. Although some of the other accused escaped, the accused was apprehended, and items including mobile phones and documents were recovered. The accused had been in custody since the date of arrest, and a co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was charged in a cybercrime case involving fraudulent transfers through e-wallets. Multiple victims provided statements under Section 161 CrPC, alleging they were defrauded for amounts ranging from Rs. 16,000 to Rs. 34,000. The accused's previous bail application had been rejected, and this application was filed on the basis of parity with co-accused who were later granted bail.

The accused was implicated in the theft of Rs. 14.60 lakh from an ATM without any physical damage to the machine. The FIR was initially lodged against unknown persons, but the accused's name surfaced six months later based on the confession of a co-accused. Authorities recovered ATM-related materials from the accused. The co-accused claimed the theft was conducted using computer technology and that similar crimes were committed in other districts.

The petitioner had previously been convicted for rape and deception under IPC Sections 376 and 417 in a case filed by the complainant, whom the petitioner later married. Following the marriage, the complainant filed another FIR alleging physical and mental cruelty, forced abortion using a harmful substance, and pressure to give divorce. The prosecution opposed anticipatory bail citing the petitioner's past conviction and ongoing harassment.

The petitioner was accused of kidnapping an infant of a few months of age from a roadside location in a town at night, while the child's parent was feeding the baby. Eyewitnesses chased the kidnappers' car but failed to stop it. Initially, the case was registered against eight persons, but only six were charge-sheeted. The petitioner contended that they were falsely implicated and that the prosecution lacked clear identification.

The accused was granted conditional bail in a cybercrime case. The prosecution later sought cancellation of bail on the ground of the accused's non-cooperation. A non-bailable warrant was issued against the accused, but the application for cancellation of bail was never decided. Over the next eleven years, the warrant was not executed, and the petitioner did not appear. The accused eventually filed a petition seeking quashing of the non-bailable warrant order.

The accused was alleged to have fraudulently transferred money from a person's account in a state. The accused was previously arrested in a cyber crime case in a city. While being arrested in that case, a related case was registered in another state. The accused had been in custody since a date several years earlier and was granted bail in the earlier case in the city.

A minor child went missing and was later found to have been kidnapped and murdered by the accused after the accused failed to obtain ransom. The accused was arrested and confessed. Bail was granted by a High Court, but the deceased's parent (the appellant) challenged it in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found that the High Court had made premature conclusions and remanded the matter for reconsideration.

After the deceased, who was the in-law of one of the petitioners, allegedly died by suicide in police custody following the suicide of their spouse, the deceased's parent filed a complaint accusing several members of two families. The petitioners allegedly assaulted the deceased in a hospital, destroyed the deceased's property, and kidnapped the deceased's child. The petitioners sought anticipatory bail citing health issues and parity with other accused persons who had received bail.

The accused and multiple co-accused were arrested in a cyber crime case involving impersonation as bank officials. Items such as mobile phones, SIM cards, passbooks, and ATM cards were recovered from the petitioners. They had been in custody since a date in December 2023. Some petitioners had past cyber crime cases; others did not. The court considered the custodial period and the absence of strong antecedents before granting bail with strict conditions.

The accused and others were arrested by a cyber crime police station in a city in connection with a cybercrime case and were later granted bail with a condition requiring daily reporting. While in custody, they were also arrested on a PT warrant in another cybercrime case registered in a different city and were granted bail in that case with another reporting condition. Because of the conflicting appearance requirements at the two locations, they petitioned the High Court to modify the earlier reporting condition.

The accused and a co-accused were granted provisional bail by the Sessions Court in a cyber crime case registered at a police station. They later filed a timely appeal in the High Court for confirmation of the provisional bail, which was allowed.

The petitioner, a juvenile, was implicated in a cyber crime case based on the confessional statement of a co-accused. The petitioner had been in custody since a date in 2016. Bail was initially denied by the Juvenile Justice Board and affirmed by the Sessions Court. The High Court granted bail, noting that the co-accused had already been granted bail and the parent's assurance to keep the petitioner away from antisocial elements.

The accused was granted provisional bail by an Additional Sessions Judge in a cybercrime case registered against them, arising out of a police station case. The accused filed an interlocutory application before the High Court seeking confirmation of that bail. Both parties were heard and the High Court confirmed the provisional bail.

The accused filed an anticipatory bail application under Section 438 CrPC in connection with a crime registered at a police station. During the hearing, the accused's counsel withdrew the application with liberty to surrender before the trial court and file a regular bail application.

The accused was implicated in a cybercrime case in which large amounts were fraudulently transferred from a company's bank account through net banking. A total of ₹1.91 crore was distributed among various accounts. The accused allegedly received ₹25,000 in their account, and the Court noted there was no further direct evidence implicating them. The accused had been in custody for several years.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case involving fabricated documents and electronic evidence. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2021. The accused had already been granted bail in another cybercrime case involving similar sections. The prosecution cited recovery of false certificates and a laptop containing fraudulent data, which were disputed by the accused.

The accused was arrested in connection with a cyber crime case in which a police raid on the accused's house resulted in the recovery of ATM cards and passbooks. The accused was suspected of involvement in cyber crime and had a prior case in another state, but was not sent up for trial in that case. Co-accused in similar cases had already been granted bail. The accused had been in custody for a period of time since the arrest and was an adult of advanced age.

The accused was named in a cyber police station case and suspected of involvement in cyber crime. The accused was granted anticipatory bail but was apprehended before surrendering. Four additional FIRs were filed against the accused after the instant case. Co-accused in similar cases had already been granted bail. The accused had been in custody since a date in November 2020.

The accused was convicted for kidnapping a minor for ransom. The minor was abducted and later released after a ransom of ₹81 lakhs was paid. The accused was allegedly involved in dropping the minor at a hotel but was not part of the original conspiracy meeting. The prosecution relied on a co-accused's confession and identification by chance witnesses. The Court observed discrepancies and inconsistencies in the prosecution's evidence.

The accused and their spouse, a journalist, allegedly visited the complainant's hospital to extort money by threatening to release a private video of the complainant on social media. When the complainant refused and said they would approach the Cyber Crime Police, the accused allegedly slapped the complainant. The video was later made public, tarnishing the complainant's reputation. The FIR was filed under sections of the BNS and the IT Act.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a cyber extortion scam in which victims were lured through fraudulent loan apps. Upon installation, the app accessed users' personal data and contacts. Victims were blackmailed with morphed images that were shared with their contacts. The accused allegedly received Rs. 2.11 lakh in their bank accounts and had absconded after vacating rented premises and disconnecting the associated mobile numbers. The accused was arrested after technical surveillance.

The accused and others were accused of cybercrime involving fraudulent withdrawals of ₹4.8 crore using cloned or unauthorized ATM/PTM cards. The accused mostly belonged to the same city and were allegedly part of a well-planned conspiracy. The case involved multiple FIRs across districts. CCTV footage and recovery of ATM cards, cash, and digital devices connected the accused to the offences.

The accused, a businessperson, discovered unauthorized transactions in their business bank account and reported it to the bank. Subsequently, the accused received a notice from the police of another state regarding a cybercrime case registered in a different state under Section 420 of the IPC and Section 66(D) of the I.T. Act. Apprehending arrest, the accused approached a High Court for transit anticipatory bail to appear before the court in the state where the case was registered.

The accused was arrested in connection with a violent altercation allegedly stemming from political rivalry, in which the complainant was attacked by a group that included the petitioner. The accused was alleged to have hit the complainant with a baseball bat. The accused had been in custody since a date in an earlier year. Allegations were made regarding threats from jail, but no phone was recovered and no call records confirmed it.

The accused, a foreign national, was accused in a cyber fraud case involving ₹10 lakhs deposited in multiple accounts allegedly connected to a fake gift scheme. The accused's initial bail application was denied because of an expired passport and visa. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2022. The court found that no funds were transferred to accounts in the accused's name and that the accused had been incarcerated for a long time with the trial proceeding slowly.

The complainant, a government employee, was induced into foreign exchange trading by known persons through fake social media profiles. The complainant deposited ₹11.4 lakhs into various accounts believing it to be legitimate trading. Investigations revealed that fraudulent bank accounts had been opened using forged documents, and that the accused were part of a network forwarding account kits for commission. The petitioners were arrested based on the disclosure statements of a co-accused.

The accused was booked under various sections of the IPC and Section 66-D of the Information Technology Act in a cyber crime case. The FIR alleged financial wrongdoing. The accused filed multiple bail applications; the fourth was granted based on parity with a co-accused who had already secured bail following a compromise with the complainant. The complainant submitted no objection to the bail grant.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a cyber fraud in which the complainant was induced into foreign exchange trading through fake social media profiles. Over ₹11 lakhs were fraudulently collected. The investigation linked the accused to the offence through disclosure statements and the forged opening of bank accounts. The accused had been in custody since early 2023. A compromise was reached with the complainant, and a co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused and others were charged in a cybercrime case involving fraud. They were allegedly caught during a raid, and mobile phones with SIM cards were recovered. The defence claimed that the accused had been falsely implicated and that there was no incriminating recovery. A co-accused had already been granted bail.

The applicants were accused in a cybercrime case involving forgery and fraud. A co-accused had already been granted bail. The applicants had been in custody since a date in the previous year and sought bail on grounds of parity.

The petitioner, the spouse of the opposite party, alleged that the opposite party left the petitioner and their two children after an extramarital affair. Following the petitioner's divorce petition, the opposite party filed an FIR under IPC Sections 323 and 498A. The opposite party also initiated proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act and was granted interim custody of the children, which the petitioner challenged.

The petitioner was arrested during a police raid at a call center in a city, which was allegedly involved in cyber fraud. The petitioner was found operating a laptop and admitted to running the center with associates. Several electronic devices were seized. The defense argued that there was no direct complaint and no victim identified, and that the co-accused had received bail.

The petitioner was accused in a cybercrime-related FIR. The petitioner denied involvement and claimed false implication. Only a mobile phone was recovered. Co-accused persons facing similar charges had already been granted bail.

The applicant was accused in a cybercrime case involving forgery and cheating. The applicant had been in custody for a period of time since an earlier month in the previous year or the same year as the application. The co-accused had already been granted bail, and the applicant's case was argued to be on identical footing.

The petitioner was accused in a cybercrime case and had been in custody since a month in late 2023. The petitioner claimed false implication and invoked parity with two co-accused persons, who had been granted bail.

The juvenile petitioner was arrested along with six others in a cybercrime case involving the use of mobile phones and SIM cards. All the co-accused had already been granted bail. Despite an allegation from one victim, the court found the petitioner's case similar to that of the co-accused.

The applicant was accused in a cybercrime case registered under multiple IPC and IT Act sections. The applicant had been in custody for a period of time, since a month in the middle of the previous year. Bail was sought on the ground of parity with a co-accused, who had already been granted bail.

The applicant was arrested in a cybercrime case involving cheating and forgery. The applicant had been in custody since a date in the previous year. The applicant sought bail on the ground of parity with the co-accused, who had already been granted bail in the same case.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case involving forgery and online fraud. The accused had been in custody since a date in the previous year. Bail was sought on the ground of parity with the co-accused, who had been granted bail earlier.

The accused was arrested in a cybercrime case involving forgery and fraud under multiple IPC and IT Act sections. The accused was in custody since a date in 2024, and had been in custody for several months. Bail was sought on the ground of parity with a co-accused, who had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested during a raid on a rented flat in a locality of a town, along with six others. Several mobile phones and SIMs were found in the accused's possession. However, no specific victim or transaction was attributed to the accused. Co-accused in identical circumstances had already been granted bail.

The applicant was accused in a cybercrime case involving extortion, cheating, and forgery. The applicant had been in custody since a month in the previous year. The applicant sought bail on the ground of parity with a co-accused, who had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested for alleged involvement in cyber fraud, with five mobile phones recovered from their possession. The accused claimed innocence and sought bail on the ground of parity with two co-accused, who had already been granted bail.

The accused was charged in a cybercrime case in which the main accused was apprehended with mobile phones and ATM cards. The accused's name did not appear in the main accused's confessional statement but surfaced in the supervision note during the investigation. The accused claimed false implication and agreed to cooperate with the investigation.

The accused, a student in a state, was accused of aiding cyber fraud by getting four bank accounts opened under false pretenses. The accused allegedly received ₹8,000 per account from the main accused for linking these accounts to fraudulent transactions. The complainant realized the misuse after checking the account for an educational loan.

The case involves large-scale organized cyber fraud carried out through mobile apps, which promised doubled returns on investments. The accused, a professional accountant, was alleged to have helped restructure a shell company that was later used to route the fraud proceeds. The accused received ₹50,000 for facilitating changes in the company's directors.

The accused was named in a cybercrime case in which a co-accused was caught with mobile phones and ATM cards. That co-accused named several other persons as co-accused, though the accused's name surfaced only in a supervision note made during the investigation. The accused claims to have been falsely implicated and promises to cooperate with the investigation.

The accused was arrested with 8 mobile phones, 44 ATM cards, cash, SIM cards, and an ATM cloning machine. The accused was alleged to be involved in multiple cyber fraud cases, including prior involvement in similar offences, and victims gave statements alleging monetary loss through e-wallet transfers.

The accused was arrested under cyber crime-related sections of the IPC and the IT Act in a case registered at a cyber police station. A mobile phone was recovered from the accused, but no financial transactions or prior criminal record were established. The investigation did not link the accused to the financial fraud.

The accused was arrested in a cyber crime case registered under the IPC and the IT Act. The accused had no previous criminal history and had been in custody for a period of time since arrest. The case involved group-based cyber fraud, but the petitioner's specific role was not detailed. The court considered the accused's custody duration and clean record in granting bail.

The accused was named in a crime registered at a cyber crime police station in a district, with allegations of online fraud under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66D of the IT Act. The accused feared arrest during the ongoing investigation.

The accused was arrested for allegedly purchasing a child sexual abuse video through a UPI payment from a messaging group run by co-accused 1. The arrest took place on a date in December 2023. The accused's mobile phone was seized, and the accused was interrogated. No prior criminal history is recorded.

The accused was alleged to have created forged documents to sell land fraudulently and was suspected in the kidnapping of the complainant's nephew, who remains missing. Despite serious allegations, charges under Section 302 or 364A IPC were not framed. The accused had spent five years in custody, and the trial was delayed due to a court-imposed stay.

The accused, named in a crime registered at a police station, is alleged to have committed online fraud. The accused was booked under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act. The offence is punishable with imprisonment of less than seven years. The accused approached the High Court seeking anticipatory bail, fearing arrest.

The accused, an adult, is alleged to have committed online fraud, in connection with a crime registered at a police station in a district of a state. The accused approached the High Court fearing arrest during the ongoing investigation. The alleged offences are under Section 318(4) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Section 66D of the IT Act.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a kidnapping-for-ransom case under Section 364A IPC, registered several years earlier. The accused was not named in the FIR, and both the informant and the victim later stated that the accused was not present or involved. Despite a previous rejection of bail and a court direction for a speedy trial, only 8 out of 31 witnesses had been examined by the time of the present application, with trial delays persisting.

The accused, an investigative journalist, was arrested under provisions of the IPC, the Arms Act and the Explosive Substances Act for allegedly harbouring and assisting a gang led by a notorious outlaw. The accused was alleged to have revealed hidden weapons and explosives in a forest and to have published photographs of torture carried out by the gang. The prosecution cited the accused's involvement in several crimes and the recovery of arms linked to an earlier dacoity case.

The accused was charged with aiding in the kidnapping of a minor and abetting sexual assault on the minor, under provisions of the IPC and the POCSO Act. Bail was granted to the accused on a certain date. Later, citing fresh FIRs and alleged threats to witnesses, the bail was cancelled. The High Court found that the cancellation was based on incorrect assumptions, including the accused's absence during judicial custody.

The accused was arrested for allegedly being part of a conspiracy to kidnap the complainant and extort money. The complainant was shot at during the attempted kidnapping. The accused was not named in the FIR but was later implicated based on co-accused statements and call detail records. No recoveries were made at the accused's instance.

The accused was convicted in a prior year for raping two minors, both young children, and sentenced to life imprisonment under Section 376(2)(i) IPC and the corresponding POCSO sections. The appeal was filed with a delay of over five years, and bail was sought during its pendency. The accused had developed a relationship of trust with the victims' family, lured the children away, and committed rape.

A juvenile and a co-accused kidnapped a minor for a ransom of ₹20 lakh. When the ransom was not paid, the minor was murdered and the body was hidden. The juvenile had a history of substance abuse and was found to be in bad company. Bail was denied by both the Juvenile Justice Board and the appellate court.

The accused was arrested in a case involving kidnapping, assault, and ransom under multiple IPC sections and the Arms Act. The accused had no prior criminal history and sought bail, citing extended incarceration and a low risk of absconding or influencing witnesses.

The accused was initially arrested under Sections 366 and 109 IPC for allegedly abducting a person with whom the accused claimed to have a consensual marriage. The accused was later re-arrested when Section 376 IPC (rape) was added based on the victim's delayed statement. The victim's affidavit and a registered marriage document indicated a consensual relationship. The prosecution failed to apply for cancellation of the earlier bail before re-arresting the accused.

The accused and others were implicated in a case arising from a protest against the kidnapping of a person. The protest allegedly turned violent, with stone pelting and injuries to officials. The petitioners claimed they were villagers merely present at the protest and were falsely implicated. The FIR contained general allegations without specific roles.

The accused was arrested for allegedly conspiring to kidnap a child together with the co-accused, who is the child's parent. The FIR included multiple IPC sections. The accused had a prior criminal history and had been in custody since a date in an earlier year, which amounts to an extended period of pre-trial incarceration. The accused sought bail on the ground of extended pre-trial incarceration and challenged the prosecution's reliance on antecedents alone.

The accused was arrested for allegedly kidnapping and assaulting the complainant along with co-accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2022 and claimed to have no prior criminal record. The allegations included physical assault and illegal confinement. The State opposed bail, citing the seriousness of the charges.

The accused and others were named in a case arising from a protest over the kidnapping of a minor. The protest allegedly led to road blockage, stone pelting, and assault on police officials. The petitioners claimed they were only present as villagers and were falsely implicated, with no specific overt act attributed to them.

The accused and a co-accused were charged in a criminal case arising from a public protest against the kidnapping of a minor. The protest allegedly escalated to road blockage and violence against authorities. The accused and the co-accused claimed they were falsely implicated on account of their mere presence at the protest site, and no specific acts were attributed to them.

The accused was implicated in an FIR arising from a protest against the kidnapping of a minor. The protest escalated into stone-pelting and violence against law enforcement. The accused claimed to have been merely present as a villager and to have had no specific role in the violence. The allegations were general in nature.

The accused was implicated in a case involving a protest over the kidnapping of a minor. The protest allegedly turned violent, with stone pelting and injuries to police personnel. The petitioner claimed to be a villager who was present at the protest without any specific role in the violence. The allegations against the accused were general in nature.

The case relates to a gang rape incident. The complainant alleged that other co-accused committed the rape, but no specific role was attributed to the accused. The prosecution did not allege direct participation of the accused in the sexual assault.

The accused, a minor at the time of the offence (just under 18), was accused of entering the home of an elderly person, smothering and strangulating the victim, and robbing valuables including jewellery and electronics. The accused was apprehended using surveillance data from the victim's phone. The accused had a prior criminal case involving charges under Sections 302 and 364A IPC. Though tried as an adult, the accused sought bail citing long incarceration and compliance during previous interim bail.

The accused was arrested for kidnapping and gang-raping an adult. The FIR alleged that the accused and the co-accused abducted the victim at knifepoint, kept the victim undressed in a car overnight, and raped the victim. Forensic evidence supported the rape allegation. The victim's statement under Section 164 CrPC reiterated the charges. However, questions were raised about the victim's phone use, injury details, and credibility, which the court considered while granting bail.

The complainant alleged that their spouse was kidnapped due to a financial dispute related to agricultural work and detained at a factory. The accused, who is the appellant, was not directly involved in the kidnapping but was the registered owner of the vehicle used. The accused approached the court after being denied anticipatory bail by the Sessions Court.

The accused was convicted under Section 364A and other IPC provisions for kidnapping a minor student for a ransom of ₹2 crores. The minor was rescued in a police encounter in which police personnel sustained firearm injuries. The accused and the co-accused were arrested from the spot. This was the third bail application after conviction, and the earlier ones had been rejected. The defence cited long incarceration and humanitarian concerns.

The accused and the co-accused were alleged to have been involved in a case of kidnapping, assault, and forced video recording of the complainant. The complaints filed in earlier years were found inconsistent during the police investigation, and key witnesses denied knowledge of the incident. The accused and the co-accused had joined the investigation, and no strong evidence supported custodial interrogation.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped and raped a married person, the victim, who was allegedly taken to a city and a state under false pretenses. The FIR was lodged by the victim's spouse, and the victim later alleged rape, confinement, and threats in their statement to the magistrate. The accused claimed the victim left voluntarily, but the prosecution maintained that the abduction and sexual assault were non-consensual and coercive.

The accused was alleged to have participated in the kidnapping and attempted murder of an adult who was allegedly abducted, assaulted, and nearly strangled. The victim later named the accused in a statement, claiming prior sexual exploitation and threats related to video recordings. The court found the allegations serious and supported by the victim's testimony, though no direct evidence linked the petitioner to all prior events.

The accused was alleged to have aided in the kidnapping of a minor, who was later raped by the co-accused. The accused allegedly transported the victim and the co-accused to another location on a motorcycle but was not alleged to have been directly involved in the rape. The victim's statement identified the accused as an accomplice in the kidnapping. The prosecution opposed bail citing the severity of the offence, while the defence argued prolonged custody and the accused's limited role.

The accused was arrested for allegedly helping conceal a vehicle used in a kidnapping for ransom that resulted in the victim's murder. The main accused had killed the victim and disposed of the body and the vehicle in a canal. The accused was contacted afterward and allegedly assisted in hiding the vehicle. The investigation did not show that the accused was part of the original conspiracy. The accused had been in custody for more than three years at the time of the bail hearing.

The accused was alleged to have received Rs.4.35 lakhs in a case involving extortion threats and criminal conspiracy under the KCOC Act. Although the accused was initially charged under lesser IPC sections, later charge sheets invoked Sections 364A and 397. The victim was allegedly abducted and forced to transfer funds. The accused was not directly involved in the abduction but allegedly received part of the extorted money, which was used by the accused's sibling to buy vehicles. The accused had been in judicial custody since 2019 and was previously denied bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a kidnapping case in which they were accused of abducting the victim and threatening the complainant not to testify. Though the accused had seven other criminal cases pending, they argued for bail citing parity with co-accused who had been released following a compromise. The accused had been in custody for several years.

The accused was alleged to have conspired in the murder of their parent, allegedly because of a property dispute with their step-parent. The FIR was filed by the step-parent, who claimed that the accused had repeatedly threatened them and conspired with others to kill the accused's parent. The accused had also allegedly abducted the complainant's sibling previously. The only evidence linking the accused to the offence was tower location (CDR) data and the accused's confessional statement, with no direct eyewitness and no forensic recovery. The accused had been in custody for several years, since 2020.

The accused (A1) and co-accused 1 (A2) were convicted for kidnapping a minor (P.W.2) and demanding a ransom of ₹12,00,000. The minor was abducted while going to school and later escaped. The accused had taken the minor from home at the instance of co-accused 2 (A3), while co-accused 1 joined later during transport. They were convicted under Section 364A read with Section 34 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment. Their applications for bail were filed on grounds of prolonged incarceration and lack of legal evidence.

The accused was alleged to have burned their spouse alive in the presence of the spouse's parents following dowry-related disputes. An FIR was registered after the victim's parent approached higher authorities. Initially, a charge was filed under Sections 306 and 498A IPC, and the accused obtained anticipatory bail. Later, the charge was amended to Section 302 IPC, but the accused continued to enjoy bail and obtained regular bail from the Magistrate. The High Court dismissed a revision petition seeking cancellation of bail by a single-sentence order.

The accused was charged with murdering the appellant's spouse, as part of a criminal conspiracy. The accused had a history of over fifteen serious criminal cases, including murder and attempt to murder. Despite this, the High Court granted bail under liberal terms. The appellant argued that the accused's conduct during trial included non-cooperation and witness intimidation, prompting the Sessions Court to require police security.

The accused, a member of a gang, allegedly extorted money from the deceased to fund legal expenses for the accused's sibling's bail. The deceased was harassed and forced to pay Rs. 25,000, had gold ornaments snatched from them, and faced repeated threats. Unable to bear the pressure, the deceased committed suicide. A suicide note and witness statements specifically named the accused.

The accused and others were alleged to have orchestrated a large extortion scheme against two businesspersons, extracting over Rs. 1.85 crores through threats and coercion. The accused was arrested and made multiple confessional statements detailing the conspiracy, the money trail, and the investments. The co-accused were granted anticipatory bail by a Sessions Court, but the complainant sought cancellation. The High Court considered banking transactions, property purchases, and the roles of the various accused in rejecting and cancelling bail.

The accused, the alleged spouse of an absconding leader of a banned extremist organisation, was accused of channeling extorted money collected by the organisation's operatives through various bank accounts and companies owned by the accused. The investigating agency alleged that the accused knowingly participated in laundering proceeds of terrorism and in a conspiracy for terrorist financing. The accused's bail plea was rejected by the special court, and the present appeal was dismissed on grounds of prima facie involvement and an ongoing trial nearing conclusion.

The case arises from the murder of the deceased, a youth leader, allegedly by members of a gang due to enmity connected with a previous murder case. The attack was allegedly premeditated and involved multiple accused armed with weapons, who assaulted the victim while using slurs directed at the victim's community. The accused, who is arraigned as accused No.16, was charged with harbouring co-accused and with involvement in the gang's operations. The prosecution submitted that the accused were involved in organised crimes including extortion, murder, and intimidation in a particular area.

The accused was co-accused 16 in a major conspiracy involving the murder of a youth leader in a town. The attack was allegedly orchestrated by members of a gang in connection with previous enmity of a social and political nature. The accused was charged with harbouring gang members, being part of the gang for several years, and facilitating concealment of evidence and extortion. The case includes multiple charges under the IPC, the SC/ST Act, the Arms Act, and the state organised crime control law.

A police constable was accused of extorting money, on behalf of the then Superintendent of Police, from a businessman, who later died by suicide after making public complaints and videos. The deceased had alleged continued harassment and extortion threats, and had named police officers in suicide notes and videos. The accused was initially charged under Section 302 IPC, but the case was later converted to Section 306 IPC based on forensic findings. The accused allegedly acted as a collection agent and threatened the deceased.

The accused was alleged to have cheated complainants who purchased a flat from the accused for ₹80 lakhs. Despite payment having been made and a sale deed having been executed, the accused allegedly delayed mutation, disconnected electricity, and demanded ₹6.5 lakhs extra. Multiple FIRs under Section 420 IPC were filed against the accused. The accused argued that the matter was civil in nature and involved contractual obligations. The accused was granted interim anticipatory bail and sought confirmation of it.

The accused was alleged to be an active member of an organized crime syndicate led by a gang leader. The accused was allegedly involved in extortion activities, collecting money on behalf of the gang, and facilitating the gang leader's escape from custody. The accused's role was allegedly confirmed through confessional statements of co-accused under MCOCA and the accused's own disclosure statement. The gang was allegedly involved in extortion, murder, and terrorizing local businesses in two states.

The petitioners were accused in a case registered at a police station for the offence of robbery under Section 392 IPC. The court, after hearing both sides, found it appropriate to grant bail on the basis of the case facts.

The accused, spouse of the co-accused, was alleged to have participated in a massive extortion and money laundering operation. The co-accused allegedly impersonated a senior law official and extorted ₹214 crores from the complainant under the guise of arranging legal relief. The accused allegedly helped launder the money through bank accounts, hawala channels, and purchases of luxury goods and vehicles. The accused remained in constant communication with their spouse, who operated the syndicate from jail using illegal mobile phones.

The accused, who had been extradited from a foreign country, was convicted under TADA for conspiracy to murder a person and sentenced to life imprisonment. The accused had served over 21 years in custody and sought bail pending a remission application. However, the accused was also implicated, while in custody, in a later kidnapping-for-ransom case, for which the accused was under active investigation.

The accused, a sub-contractor for a road construction project, was alleged to have paid extortion money to and supplied goods to members of a banned extremist group so that the work could be executed smoothly. The accused was charged under the UAPA, a state special public security Act, and the IPC. The allegations were primarily based on the confessional statements of co-accused persons, with no direct recovery from the accused. The accused had been in custody for several years, since 2020, and only 13 of 100 witnesses had been examined.

The accused police officials allegedly detained unknown individuals illegally, threatened them with false implication in criminal cases, and extorted large sums of money with the help of an accomplice. An internal inquiry confirmed the admissions made by the accused police officials and documented the extortion and the distribution of the money among themselves.

The accused, involved in a local political rivalry, was accused of demanding ₹2 crore from a village head under threats. Though the FIR included Section 386 IPC, the court found no actual delivery of money and stated that at most an offence under Section 385 IPC could be made out. The accused had a history of 10 criminal cases, but had been granted bail in all of them. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2023 and argued that political enmity motivated the charges.

The accused was alleged to be an active member of a banned extremist group and of collecting levies from coal transporters and traders in a coal area of a state. A raid based on secret information led to the recovery of a huge amount of cash and weapons from associates of the accused, and the accused was found to have acquired trucks and equipment with suspected terror proceeds. The charge-sheet filed by a central investigating agency listed the accused as the fifth accused and detailed the accused's role in collecting money on the instructions of senior leaders of the group.

The complainant alleged that the accused, a public representative, along with others, fabricated a false N.A. order and demanded Rs. 70 lakhs under threat of lodging FIRs and creating trouble regarding a land transaction. A part-payment of Rs. 10 lakhs was made, and one co-accused was caught red-handed accepting Rs. 20 lakhs in a police trap.

The accused was alleged to be an active member of a syndicate that collected an illegal coal levy of Rs. 25 per tonne in a district, working under a co-accused and in coordination with another co-accused. The accused allegedly collected extortion money at a shop and sent confirmation messages to facilitate the issue of NOCs. Investigations revealed weekly delivery of large sums to the heads of the syndicate in a city and digital tracking of the funds.

The accused, already serving life imprisonment in a separate murder case, was charged under POTA for allegedly coordinating a terrorist conspiracy from jail. The accused allegedly directed the extortion of Rs. 25 lakhs from petrol pump owners, of which Rs. 20 lakhs was allegedly routed to another country through hawala to fund terror activities. The accused was also alleged to have connections with absconding co-accused, including the accused's sibling, a known terrorist linked to a criminal gang. Despite the POTA Review Committee's exoneration, the High Court cancelled the accused's bail based on confessional statements and corroborating witness evidence.

The accused was alleged to be a key manager in a large coal extortion syndicate operating in a state, allegedly led by a co-accused. The accused was allegedly responsible for collecting coal levy payments from coal traders and preparing financial records, including maintaining spreadsheets and coordinating the issuance of NOCs through bribery. Diaries, instant messaging chats, and witness statements allegedly linked the accused to illegal coal and iron pellet levy collections.

The accused, posted as a Mining Officer in a district, was alleged to have collected Rs. 1 per tonne as a personal illegal levy and to have facilitated the extortion of Rs. 25 per tonne by a coal syndicate headed by a private individual. The accused allegedly coordinated with co-accused 1 and co-accused 2 to ensure that transporters paid the levy before receiving NOCs. Messaging application chats and transporter testimonies corroborated the accused's role in the conspiracy.

The accused, a sibling of the co-accused, was part of a coal levy extortion syndicate led by another person. The accused allegedly used messaging application messages to coordinate with coal traders, instructing them to pay Rs. 25 per tonne for clearance of delivery orders (DOs). Witness statements and electronic evidence suggested the accused's direct role in pressuring traders and facilitating extortion operations.

The accused, during their tenure as a Deputy Director in a mining department in a district, was allegedly involved in collecting Rs. 2 per tonne from coal traders for issuing NOCs, while facilitating the illegal coal levy of Rs. 25 per tonne run by a syndicate led by another person. Witness statements, including from the accused's operator, and seized documents from Income Tax raids linked the accused with the illegal operations. Coal traders confirmed they were asked to pay before NOCs were issued.

The accused, a relative of a co-accused, was allegedly involved in collecting an illegal coal levy of Rs. 25 per tonne from traders in a district, as part of a syndicate led by another person. The accused allegedly worked with other syndicate members, including a co-accused and a mining officer, and delivered the proceeds to another person. Witnesses confirmed the accused's role in exerting pressure and coordinating levy collection with mining officials.

The accused, along with other co-accused, was implicated in a case involving the extortion of nearly Rs. 50 lakhs from traders by a gang. The money was intercepted in a vehicle, and confessional statements by co-accused named the accused as a recipient of the extorted funds. The case was initially registered under IPC Sections 385/386/34, with later cognizance taken under UAPA Sections 16/17/20/21 after requisite sanction.

The accused was alleged by an enforcement agency to have assisted in collecting extortion amounts from rice millers in order to facilitate the passing of custom milling and incentive bills, thereby engaging in money laundering activities. The trial court initially took cognizance, but that order was later set aside due to lack of prosecution sanction. A fresh cognizance order was issued after sanction was obtained. The accused remained in custody for over a year, during which the trial had not begun.

The applicant was accused, along with other co-accused, of conspiring to extort Rs. 62 lakhs from a businessman under threats linked to a gangster. The extortion allegedly included a luxury car and money transfers. The prosecution invoked MCOCA based on alleged membership of a crime syndicate and the prior criminal history of the main accused, co-accused 1 and co-accused 2. However, the applicant had no direct role in the threats or extortion, and had no prior criminal record.

The accused was implicated in a case under MCOCA involving extortion allegedly planned during a birthday party attended by over 200 guests. The FIR originally named only two other persons, co-accused 1 and co-accused 2, and the accused was added later based on supplementary witness statements alleging a conspiracy. Witnesses claimed the accused was present during conversations hinting at extortion, but no direct evidence linked the accused to receipt of money or threats.

The accused, then the station house officer of a police station, was alleged to have aided a senior police officer in running an extortion racket targeting a businessman in the stone crushing trade. The businessman later died of a gunshot wound in an alleged suicide. Witnesses and the deceased's own complaints indicated harassment and extortion threats from the police. The accused was arrested and remained in custody until bail was granted.

The accused, then a police officer in charge of a police station, was accused of threatening and extorting money from a businessperson, allegedly on behalf of a senior police officer. The deceased refused to pay Rs. 6 lakhs per month and later died from a gunshot. The deceased had made social media posts accusing police officers of coercion. The court found evidence of sustained threats and extortion attempts involving the accused.

The accused allegedly entered a hotel, handed over a threatening note and fired a pistol round to extort money, as part of an organized crime conspiracy linked to a criminal gang. The accused fled with an accomplice on a motorcycle. The incident led to invocation of MCOCA. Despite this, the trial had not commenced after nearly 7 years of custody.

The accused was charged under MCOCA along with others of conspiring to extort Rs. 62 lakhs from a businessman using threats associated with the syndicate of a gangster. The informant was allegedly coerced into transferring money and a luxury vehicle. The accused was said to have attended a party where the conspiracy was allegedly hatched, but there was no direct evidence linking the accused to the extortion. Witnesses did not confirm delivery of extorted funds to the accused.

The accused sought anticipatory bail in a theft case involving iron grills worth ₹60,000 allegedly stolen by co-accused 1, co-accused 2, and co-accused 3. The stolen material was transported in a van owned by the accused, but CCTV and other evidence did not show the accused's involvement in the theft. The accused deposited ₹40,000 voluntarily during investigation. The trial court rejected bail citing past criminal history, but the High Court found no sufficient material for arrest.

The accused, a former General Manager of a company, was alleged to have conspired with members of a banned extremist outfit to facilitate the collection of levy from coal transporters in a state. The accused allegedly supported the formation of village committees for the distribution of the levy and attended meetings with operatives of the outfit. However, no money was recovered from the accused, and the accused's role appeared administrative, meant to ensure peaceful coal operations.

The accused was arrested for an alleged role in converting extorted levy money, collected by an extremist organisation, into white money. The accused was alleged to have received Rs. 2 lakhs directly and to have been involved in the transfer of Rs. 48 lakhs through a hawala operator. Although initially treated as a witness, the accused was later arrested and has remained in custody since 2019, a period of several years. A national investigating agency filed multiple charge sheets, and over 100 witnesses were examined. The prosecution argued that the accused played a key role in facilitating the surrender of the organisation's leader through illegal financial routes.

The accused was arrested in February of a later year in connection with an incident the previous year at a hotel in a city, where shots were fired and extortion threats were issued in the name of a gangster. The accused was alleged to be a co-conspirator who provided funds generated by an organised crime syndicate. The case was registered under MCOCA due to alleged syndicate involvement.

The accused was alleged to be a co-conspirator in an extortion case involving threats at a hotel in a city, allegedly carried out on behalf of a gangster. The accused was said to have procured funds from other co-accused and hired two individuals to commit the threatening act. Though the case was registered under MCOCA, the accused had been in custody since 2017 with no material progress in the trial.

The accused was alleged to have participated in an extortion attempt at a hotel in a city, several years earlier, involving threats and firing allegedly linked to an organised crime syndicate led by a gangster. The accused allegedly accompanied the shooter and fled on a motorcycle. Charges were framed under MCOCA and various provisions of the IPC and the Arms Act. The accused had remained in custody for over seven years without any progress in the trial.

The accused, an elected public representative, was alleged to have led a criminal gang involved in extortion and threats, with charges under the Gangsters Act. The accused had previously been in custody for related offences, including threatening witnesses from jail using phones accessed through their spouse. The gang chart included four other members, and the accused was already facing 10 other criminal cases, including under the PMLA. The FIR alleged that the accused and their associates instilled fear in the local area and extorted people for financial gain.

The accused, alleged to be a zonal commander of a banned extremist outfit, was accused of involvement in a coal levy extortion racket across a state. The accused was implicated in a supplementary charge sheet filed by a central investigating agency, which vaguely alleged the accused's participation in raising extortion funds. The evidence included recovery of cash from associates and confessional statements, though no direct or specific act of extortion was attributed to the accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in an earlier year.

The accused was charged under POTA and the IPC for an alleged role in a terrorist conspiracy, including extortion of Rs. 25 lakhs from a petrol pump operator. The accused was alleged to have channeled funds to another country via Hawala for militant activities, while serving a life sentence for an earlier murder conviction. The POTA court granted the accused bail, citing parity with co-accused and lack of strong evidence, but the High Court reversed this decision.

The petitioner and others were accused of assaulting the informant and extorting Rs. 5 lakh from them due to an ongoing land dispute. It was noted that the FIR was lodged 11 days after the incident and that the spouse of one of the petitioners had previously filed a complaint against the informant. The court found the delay and counter-allegations relevant to the decision on bail.

The informant, a businessman, was allegedly honey-trapped by an accused person and later blackmailed with a compromising video by co-accused. The case involved a demand for Rs. 10 crores. The applicant was implicated for suggesting a meeting with their sibling (co-accused 6) for settlement but was not directly involved in threats or extortion. Call transcripts revealed no demand or coercion from the applicant.

The complainant, a former political worker, alleged that a sitting public representative raped them while they were under the influence of a stupefying substance, and subsequently extorted them using obscene videos. The accused had earlier filed an FIR against the complainant alleging extortion. The complainant's FIR was lodged several months later, and the accused was granted anticipatory bail. The complainant later sought cancellation of the anticipatory bail, alleging continued threats and delay in the trial.

The accused, along with co-accused, allegedly created and served fake notices purporting to be from a central enforcement agency on executives of a company, and demanded Rs. 2–20 crores in exchange for settling a fictitious investigation. The accused was arrested during a raid at a hotel in a city, where a meeting with the complainant and a person impersonating an officer of the enforcement agency took place. CCTV footage, call records, and hotel bookings were cited as evidence of the accused's central role in the conspiracy.

The accused was alleged to have facilitated online betting through platforms such as a betting website, allegedly misleading users, including the complainant, who lost large sums. Manipulation of the app was alleged but was not substantiated in the charge-sheet. The accused had been in custody for over four months, and the trial was expected to take significant time.

A constable was accused, along with others, of posing as Crime Branch officers and extorting Rs. 23 lakhs from individuals running an online gaming site in a city. The complaint alleged that the accused took mobile phones and transferred money from the victims' accounts. The accused sought anticipatory bail, claiming they were falsely implicated and were cooperating with the investigation.

The accused was arrested in a case registered under MCOCA for allegedly running an organized crime syndicate in a city and other states, involving heinous crimes including extortion, murder, and obstruction of government officers.
