The accused had previously been declared a proclaimed offender in a separate case under the Arms Act.

The accused, a person engaged in activism under a transparency law and also an advocate, was alleged to have advised the co-accused to carry a licensed firearm and "teach a lesson" to a government officer who had obstructed their alleged extortion activities. The officer was subsequently shot dead by the co-accused. The prosecution claimed that the accused conspired to extort officials by using pressure tactics under the transparency law. However, there was no independent corroboration beyond the statements of the co-accused.

The accused, along with several co-accused, allegedly conspired to extort Rs. 2–3 crores from senior executives of a company by impersonating officials of a central investigating agency. Fake summons were sent, meetings were arranged under false pretenses, and threats were issued to force payment. The accused was present at a hotel in a city during the sting operation and was apprehended there. The accused's location and communication were corroborated by CCTV and call records.

The accused, a public servant in a government department, was alleged to have conspired with others to extort Rs. 2 crore from a senior engineer by impersonating officials of an anti-corruption body. The complaint involved impersonation, threats, and a handover of Rs. 5 lakhs through a private driver. Statements and technical evidence supported the allegations. The case was alleged to have brought disrepute to the anti-corruption institution and was under investigation by a high-level special investigation team.

The case relates to the alleged fake encounters of three persons, one of whom was killed along with their spouse, and another who was killed separately. The accused, then holding a senior ministerial office in a state government, was alleged to have orchestrated the murders with the help of police officers and to have run an extortion racket using fake encounters as threats. The investigating agency alleged that the accused used their influence to suppress the investigation and tamper with evidence. The High Court granted the accused bail, which the investigating agency sought to cancel.

The accused was charged under Sections 384, 323, 504, and 506 IPC for allegedly extorting and threatening the informant. The accused argued that the essential ingredients of extortion under Section 383 IPC were missing and that there was a history of litigation between the parties. A co-accused had already been granted bail, and the trial had not commenced despite the accused's long custody of many years.

The accused, arrayed as accused No.4, was arrested for allegedly posing as a member of a human rights committee and conducting an unauthorized raid at child care centres along with others. They allegedly demanded Rs. 2 lakhs from the workers at the centres and attempted to seize their phones. The co-accused were already granted bail.

The case arose from a large-scale illegal sand mining operation in a district of a state. Police raided the site based on secret information and seized multiple vehicles, machinery, and sand. The petitioners, including the accused, were implicated as drivers or owners of the vehicles. The petitioners sought anticipatory bail after being named in the FIR registered under IPC Section 379 and MMDR Act provisions.

The accused, arrayed as accused No. 9, was alleged to be part of an organized crime syndicate led by two other persons, involved in extortion and murder. The accused allegedly facilitated payments from a builder to contract killers who murdered the deceased. The High Court had granted the accused bail, which the State challenged in the Supreme Court.

The accused, the spouse of the main accused, was implicated under MCOCA for allegedly facilitating an organized narcotics syndicate. The accused was found in possession of large unaccounted wealth and was suspected of assisting the gang during the main accused's incarceration. The case involves over 75 past cases against the main accused, confessions of co-accused, and financial transactions linked to narcotics proceeds.

Two trucks owned by the petitioners were found transporting illegally extracted sand without valid documents or permits. The drivers were arrested on the spot, and the petitioners claimed the trucks were operated without their consent. The vehicles carried 300 CFT of sand each and were intercepted by a mining officer. The petitioners sought anticipatory bail, denying direct involvement.

The accused and a co-accused were allegedly members of a banned organisation and plotted to join a militant training camp in a foreign country. They were arrested at a railway station in a city and booked under the UAPA. The State failed to file a valid extension for investigation as required under Section 43D(2)(b) of the UAPA. Despite the accused being entitled to statutory bail due to delay in filing the charge-sheet, the Sessions Court cancelled the bail. This was challenged in revision.

The accused was alleged to have forged an affidavit in order to falsely implicate a complainant in a fabricated FIR, allegedly as part of a conspiracy to extort money and pressure the complainant to sell land. The accused's first anticipatory bail application was withdrawn with an undertaking to surrender, which the accused failed to honour. The accused later filed a second anticipatory bail petition without justification.

The applicant was accused by their in-law of misappropriating gold ornaments from a joint locker. The FIR was filed after the applicant had initiated domestic violence and Section 498A proceedings against their spouse. The applicant sought anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC, claiming the FIR was retaliatory and that they had cooperated with the investigation.

The accused was alleged to have assisted in the kidnapping of a child for the purpose of illegal adoption. The accused and a co-accused allegedly took the child from the child's parent and handed the child over to another co-accused who wished to adopt. The incident stemmed from a personal dispute involving the informant and the informant's former and current partners. The child was recovered the same day and handed back to the child's other parent.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a minor child. The child was later recovered from the accused's possession along with the co-accused. The case was initially registered against unknown persons, and the accused's name surfaced during the investigation. The accused's first bail application was rejected, and the accused had been in jail for several years at the time of the present application.

The accused and their sibling, the co-accused, were charged with violating an interim protection order passed under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act by allegedly assaulting the complainant. The court found the order too vague to attract criminal liability under Section 31(1) of the Act, as it lacked specificity about the prohibited conduct.

The accused was alleged to have committed an offence in a domestic violence case involving assault on the informant and the informant's children during a family dispute. The FIR invoked several IPC sections and Domestic Violence Act provisions. The accused claimed that it was a family feud exaggerated into serious charges and that no injury report was submitted.

The accused was alleged by their spouse to have committed an offence under Section 498A IPC in a complaint case filed in 2015. The accused was already on bail in two other related cases: a complaint case under Section 498A IPC and a domestic violence case, both instituted in 2017. The accused claimed to have been unaware of the 2015 complaint at the time it was filed.

The petitioner sought cancellation of anticipatory bail granted to their spouse, the accused, in a domestic violence and cruelty case. The petitioner alleged that after the bail was granted, they were subjected to harassment and eviction from the matrimonial home. A Domestic Incident Report supported the petitioner's claim. The accused argued that the dispute was the fallout of a divorce case and that the bail conditions were not violated.

The accused was granted anticipatory bail on a date in 2022, based on an undertaking to pay Rs. 30,000 per month as maintenance to their spouse and child. However, the accused failed to make any payments. The spouse, the complainant, filed for cancellation of bail citing non-compliance. The accused also sought modification of the bail order citing financial hardship, which was rejected. The court found that the accused had used the offer of maintenance deceitfully to secure bail.

The complainant alleged cruelty and dowry harassment by their spouse's family, including physical and mental abuse for not fulfilling dowry demands and for not bearing a male child. An FIR was registered and a complaint was filed under the Domestic Violence Act. Two of the persons named were absolved due to the absence of a domestic relationship. Bail granted to four family members was challenged but upheld.

The accused was charged with offences under the IPC based on allegations by the complainant that the accused had sexually assaulted the complainant under a false promise of marriage. The accused was granted interim bail on an undertaking to marry the complainant, which the accused did. Later, disputes arose between them and the complainant filed a domestic violence case. The accused sought to quash the domestic violence and IPC proceedings, and the complainant sought cancellation of bail, alleging harassment after the marriage.

The complainant accused the accused of cheating them with a false promise of marriage and of sexually assaulting them. The accused was granted interim bail on agreeing to marry the complainant, and the accused did so. After the marriage, the complainant alleged that the accused harassed them, evicted them from the matrimonial home, and obstructed their access to it. The complainant filed for cancellation of the accused's bail and for reliefs under the DV Act. The accused sought quashing of the DV Act and IPC proceedings.

The accused filed for anticipatory bail in connection with a domestic violence case under IPC Sections 498A, 325, 384, 307, and 34. The accused had earlier been granted interim bail and had complied with the conditions, including appearing before the investigating officer and giving a statement. The Court found no need for custodial interrogation.

The accused, an in-law of the complainant, was accused of administering acid in a case involving domestic violence and dowry harassment. The FIR was lodged nearly a year after the alleged incident. The medical report showed no external injuries. The accused's role was first mentioned only in the statement recorded under Section 164 CrPC. A mutual divorce and a settlement under the DV Act were reached between the victim and the co-accused, who is the victim's spouse.

The accused was accused under Sections 406 and 498A IPC by their spouse, the complainant. The accused joined the investigation, returned a PAN card, and 14 out of 18 tolas of gold along with other dowry articles were recovered. The complainant alleged that the accused was evading service in proceedings under the DV Act and maintenance proceedings. The court confirmed interim bail with directions to appear before the trial court.

The accused, the spouse of the informant, was accused of domestic violence and dowry harassment. The accused was granted provisional anticipatory bail with conditions based on reconciliation attempts. The bail lapsed the following year, and the accused later sought modification, citing advanced age and inability to surrender due to a communication gap.

The petitioners were accused of assaulting and outraging the modesty of the complainant in a shared household. The complainant had previously alleged rape and filed a petition under the DV Act. The Magistrate found the complainant's petition to be an abuse of the DV Act and directed the complainant's eviction. Soon after, the complainant filed the current FIR alleging assault. The petitioners claimed the FIR was retaliatory. The Court found no serious injuries and granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was charged under IPC Section 498A and other provisions, as well as provisions of the Domestic Violence Act and the Dowry Prohibition Act. The accused was earlier granted bail several years before, subject to the condition of paying a certain amount to the informant. Bail was cancelled due to non-payment, and the accused was taken into custody later. After depositing the dues, the accused applied for fresh bail.

The applicant was accused by their in-law of misappropriating gold ornaments from a joint locker during a matrimonial dispute. The FIR alleged that the applicant took the ornaments in a particular month of 2019. The applicant had earlier filed proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act and Section 498A of the IPC. A B Summary was filed but was not accepted by the Magistrate. The Sessions Court denied anticipatory bail, and the applicant then filed a petition before the High Court.

The accused's anticipatory bail application was rejected by a High Court in a case under IPC Section 406 filed by the accused's spouse, despite a prior compromise and the return of dowry articles. The complainant had also earlier initiated domestic violence proceedings, which were settled. The accused had filed a petition for restitution of conjugal rights but failed to follow it up. The Supreme Court was informed that no recovery remained and that the complainant still wanted to resume marital life.

The accused was alleged by their child's spouse (the complainant) to have misappropriated gold ornaments from a jointly held bank locker. The complainant had previously filed complaints under the Domestic Violence Act and Section 498A of the IPC, and the FIR was seen as retaliatory. A B Summary was submitted but not accepted. The court found the accused cooperative and held that custodial interrogation was unnecessary.

The accused was accused by their spouse, the complainant, of harassment, assault, and unnatural sex under multiple IPC sections and the Dowry Prohibition Act. The complainant had also filed proceedings under the DV Act, but allegations under Section 377 IPC were not raised there. The FIR was allegedly filed in retaliation to a civil suit by the applicant's grandparent. The trial court had denied bail but the High Court found custodial interrogation unnecessary and granted bail.

Two accused persons (accused 1 and accused 2) were alleged to have assisted the co-accused, a cousin of accused 1, in drugging and robbing the co-accused's spouse, the complainant. The co-accused then allegedly left the complainant and married accused 1. The co-accused had earlier been the subject of a case under the DV Act brought by the complainant. The FIR was filed nearly 10 months after the alleged events. The complainant alleged the loss of gold and the assault of children. The accused sought anticipatory bail on the ground of parity with the co-accused, who had already been granted bail.

The accused, the spouse of the complainant, was charged under Section 498A of the IPC and Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act for allegedly assaulting and attempting to kill their spouse. The accused claimed the allegations were false and stated a willingness to keep their spouse with dignity and care. The prosecution opposed the plea, citing that the accused failed to fulfil their commitment after a compromise.

The accused was alleged to have orally pronounced 'triple talaq' and threatened their spouse, leading to charges under Section 4 of the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act and Section 506 of the IPC. The complaint was lodged several months after the incident allegedly took place, with a gap of about four months between the two. The complainant had previously filed a case under the DV Act and maintenance proceedings, both of which were dismissed. The applicant argued that they had been falsely implicated because of strained relations between the parties.

The applicants, including the complainant's in-laws and the complainant's spouse's siblings, were accused of offences under IPC Sections 498A, 406, and others in connection with a matrimonial dispute. The FIR was filed following the withdrawal of proceedings under the DV Act. The applicants had failed to attend the police station when initially noticed, leading to rejection of their bail plea by the Sessions Court. However, they committed to cooperating with the investigation.

The accused and the accused's parents were accused under IPC Section 498A and related provisions, along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The complainant, the accused's spouse, alleged dowry harassment and physical and mental abuse after their marriage, which took place several years earlier. A complaint under the Domestic Violence Act was filed a couple of years after the marriage. Following unsuccessful mediation, an FIR was registered, and the accused sought anticipatory bail fearing arrest.

The accused and the accused's family members were alleged to have subjected the complainant, the accused's spouse, to dowry harassment and assault after a short-lived marriage. There had been prior complaints, an attempt at reconciliation, and ongoing civil proceedings and proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act. The complainant also allegedly assaulted the petitioners in a cross-case. The injuries were simple in nature.

The accused and the accused's second spouse were accused by the accused's first spouse of domestic violence and assault, with an FIR lodged under multiple IPC sections and provisions of the DV Act. The marriage was said to have occurred 40–45 years ago, and the complaint was filed several years ago. Though a mediation process failed, the court noted that the allegations were vague and other co-accused had been granted bail.

The accused and their spouse, who are the complainant's in-laws, were accused under IPC Sections 498A, 406, 323, and 341, along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The FIR was lodged after a six-month delay. They were granted interim protection earlier, and the complainant had also filed a petition under the DV Act and a petition under Section 9 of the HMA.

The accused was charged under IPC sections and the POCSO Act for alleged physical assault and molestation. The accused had a prior FIR under Section 498A IPC and the Domestic Violence Act, lodged by the victim's parent. The victim later married someone else, and no medical evidence was presented. The charge sheet had already been filed and cognizance taken. The lower court had earlier rejected anticipatory bail.

The complainant's parent committed suicide and left a note blaming the complainant's spouse (the deceased's in-law) and the in-law's parents. The in-law had filed domestic violence and other legal complaints against their in-laws. The court noted that although the deceased was under mental stress due to these complaints, there was no direct evidence of instigation to commit suicide by the accused.

The complainant filed a private complaint against their spouse and the spouse's family under Sections 498A and 506 read with 34 of the IPC, and Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act. The complainant alleged harassment and dowry demands, including coercion to obtain ₹50 lakhs by selling the complainant's parent's property. The accused did not respond to the court's summons, which led to the issuance of a non-bailable warrant.

The accused was alleged by the accused's estranged spouse (the complainant) to have committed physical and mental cruelty, threats, and child abuse during an ongoing matrimonial conflict. The FIR was filed years after the separation. Interim inquiries into the child abuse allegations found them unsubstantiated and possibly motivated by custody disputes. The complainant had also filed cases under the Domestic Violence Act.

The accused was arrested in connection with charges under IPC Sections 306, 498A and 114, along with provisions of the Dowry Prohibition Act and the Domestic Violence Act. The allegations stemmed from the suicide of the accused's spouse after 12 years of marriage. The defense argued that Section 306 IPC was not applicable and sought bail citing absence of direct evidence.

The accused allegedly befriended the informant through a social media platform, developed a relationship, and later blackmailed the informant using obscene photographs. The accused and their relatives allegedly demanded ₹50 lakh and received ₹10 lakh. The accused had previously lodged a domestic violence and sexual assault complaint against the informant. The court noted a pattern of the accused marrying multiple persons, blackmailing them, and extorting money through false cases.

The accused was arrested in a kidnapping case but was not named in the FIR. The accused's name appeared only in the confessional statement of a co-accused, who claimed responsibility for kidnapping a child and returning the child the same day. The prosecution alleges conspiracy on the part of the accused. The accused has one prior case, which is explained in the bail affidavit. A similarly placed co-accused was already granted bail.

The accused was arrested along with co-accused after a kidnapped child, aged under two years and therefore a minor, was recovered from a co-accused's house. The FIR was registered against unknown persons. The accused's name emerged after the arrest of a co-accused, on the basis of CCTV footage. The accused was not named in the FIR, and nothing incriminating was recovered from the accused. The accused was arrested during the raid.

The complainant married the accused in an earlier year and alleged dowry demands, threats, and misappropriation of streedhan by the accused and the accused's family. An FIR was filed several years later, nearly four years after the parties separated. The complainant had previously filed a Domestic Violence case. The accused claimed that most of the items had already been returned and offered to return the remaining items voluntarily.

The accused, the spouse of the complainant, sought anticipatory bail in a case filed under Section 498A IPC. The court referred the matter to mediation, which failed as the accused insisted on an accounting of Rs. 15 lakhs allegedly paid to the complainant earlier. The complainant opposed the bail, calling the demand unreasonable. A domestic violence case was also pending. The court rejected anticipatory bail but allowed the accused to seek regular bail.

The accused was charged under IPC Sections 361 and 364 in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a child by a person who referred to the accused as their spouse. Though not legally married, the complainant and the accused had three children, and a prior case had established the accused's parentage of the children through DNA. The accused had been acquitted in that matter. The complainant expressed no objection to bail. The accused had been in custody for a period of time since early in the previous year.

The complainant, the spouse of the applicant, alleged that on a certain date in late December 2019, the complainant was assaulted by the applicant, who banged the complainant's head on the wall and caused multiple injuries including a leg fracture. The FIR was lodged a few days later. The applicant claimed the injuries were sustained during a trip to a city and that custodial interrogation was unnecessary.

The accused was alleged to have robbed a gold chain along with a co-accused and sold it to a third person. The accused was initially granted bail but later failed to appear in court. The trial court issued a non-bailable warrant. The accused claimed that the absence was due to an accident involving their spouse and a domestic violence complaint the spouse had filed against them, but no evidence was provided to support this claim.

The accused was alleged by their spouse to have assaulted the spouse with a knife and attempted to strangle them. The couple's relationship was strained due to the accused's inability to conceive. The accused had previously filed domestic violence proceedings. The FIR alleged injuries, including one from a sharp object. However, the medical evidence did not confirm any neck injury and suggested that a blunt object had caused the other injuries.

The accused was alleged by their spouse to have subjected them to continued physical and mental cruelty after their marriage, which took place several years earlier. An earlier case under Section 498A IPC, registered about a year after the marriage, had resulted in anticipatory bail for the accused, but a new complaint was filed after repeated acts of abuse. In court, the spouse expressed willingness to reconcile, but the accused refused.

The accused sought anticipatory bail in a case filed by their in-law, involving allegations of fraud and domestic violence. The case stemmed from claims that the accused's spouse falsely represented themselves as the informant's child in order to access the informant's bank accounts. The accused was alleged to have participated in the fraudulent acts and to have committed domestic violence.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case registered at a police station under Section 103 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, for the alleged death of a person. The petitioner submitted a dying declaration recorded by a doctor, claiming it negated murder or dowry death charges. However, the prosecution argued that the dying declaration was not part of the case diary, and statements under Section 161 CrPC showed evidence of domestic violence. The court found incriminating material in the case diary.

The deceased committed suicide allegedly due to mental torture and monetary pressure (Rs. 90,000) from their spouse, the spouse's parent, and the spouse's sibling. A suicide note recovered at the scene mentioned the applicants. The marriage was a love marriage solemnized several years before the death. The applicants claimed innocence and sought anticipatory bail, which was opposed by the State citing serious allegations supported by a suicide note.

The petitioner filed a petition seeking cancellation of anticipatory bail granted to the petitioner's spouse and in-laws, citing violation of bail conditions and assault. The petitioner alleged that after the bail was granted, the respondents threatened the petitioner to withdraw the case and assaulted the petitioner and the petitioner's sibling, leading to registration of a fresh FIR. The respondents disputed the location and occurrence of the incident and claimed that a counter FIR had been filed against the petitioner.

The accused was initially granted bail based on a compromise agreement between the accused's family and the accused's spouse, which included a mutual consent divorce and payment of Rs. 16.5 lakhs. The accused was released after paying Rs. 5 lakhs. However, the accused later refused to comply with the divorce agreement. The accused's spouse filed for cancellation of bail. The trial court initially rejected the application but later accepted a second petition after observing the accused's non-compliance and abuse of the judicial process.

The accused, a director of two companies, was arrested along with their spouse (the co-accused) in a case alleging cheating of Rs. 2.7 crores from investors in a commercial real estate project. The complainants alleged that shops were allotted to multiple buyers, and that the project land was fraudulently mortgaged and auctioned by a financial institution. The accused claimed to be only a nominal director with no role in the daily operations.

The accused, the Managing Director of a company, allegedly availed a loan of Rs.5 crores from a lender using forged bank statements. The accused is alleged to have embezzled over Rs.109 crores from various lenders and diverted funds to related entities. Investigation revealed fabricated documents, misuse of employee accounts, and attempts to evade arrest, leading to the accused's apprehension near the border between two states.

The accused and their family members were accused of subjecting the informant to cruelty for dowry and because the informant's spouse allegedly intended to marry another person. The FIR was filed a year after the last incident. The informant had also filed a domestic violence case at a different location. The court noted the delay, the over-implication of family members, and the lack of custodial need.

A company awarded a contract to another company, which was led by the accused, and advanced a large payment. The first company alleged that the second company diverted the funds and failed to mobilize resources, prompting it to cancel the contract and file a criminal complaint. Amid parallel civil recovery proceedings, a criminal FIR and investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC were initiated. The second company and the accused sought quashing of these proceedings.

The accused, a director of two companies, was arrested for allegedly cheating investors of Rs. 2.7 crores by fraudulently allotting the same shops in a commercial project to multiple buyers. The project land was mortgaged and later auctioned by a financial institution. The accused had been declared a proclaimed offender due to failed service of summons. The accused later became the sole successful resolution applicant in CIRP proceedings and sought bail, citing efforts to resolve the disputes.

The accused allegedly defrauded friends by claiming to be an employee of a company who could get cabs hired by that company. On this pretext, the accused took over ₹1 crore from multiple individuals over a period of about two years. Investigation revealed that the accused never worked at the company and did not run a cab business. Bail was sought on the ground of absence of intent to cheat, but the Court found prima facie evidence of fraud.

The accused, a partner in a firm with their spouse, allegedly orchestrated a ₹10.70 crore fraud involving 22 fraudulent loan accounts using forged warehouse receipts. The funds were embezzled into personal and business accounts. The accused sought anticipatory bail, arguing cooperation and lack of custodial necessity, which was opposed by the investigating agency based on the accused's active role in the forgery and deception.

The accused, an Executive Engineer (a public servant), was alleged to be a key figure in a major corruption scandal in a river channelization project. The accused allegedly manipulated the tendering process to award contracts to ineligible firms, relaxed norms without authority, forged documents, and caused a loss of public funds amounting to hundreds of crores. Investigations by a committee led by a retired judge and by a central investigating agency revealed serious irregularities under the accused's charge.

The petitioners were originally granted bail on the basis of records showing that 7 kg of ganja had been seized. A subsequent inquiry revealed that 277 kg had actually been seized, and that false documents, including forged court orders and misstatements, had been used to mislead the court. A larger conspiracy involving advocates, clerks, and manipulated filings was uncovered.

The accused, a former director of a company, was alleged to have siphoned off over ₹500 crores from investors in real estate projects by promising assured returns. Following multiple FIRs and an investigation by a central agency dealing with serious fraud, the accused remained in custody for over two years. The accused submitted revival schemes to complete pending projects through co-developers and sought bail to expedite implementation.

The accused, a former managing director and chief executive of a bank, allegedly conspired with the promoters of a company to invest ₹3,700 crores of public funds in that company's debentures in exchange for kickbacks of ₹600 crores, which were laundered through companies owned by the accused's family. The accused is alleged to have misused their official position for personal gain, involving large-scale economic offences and the layering of proceeds of crime across international jurisdictions.

The accused was apprehended while fleeing after allegedly committing a robbery against a truck driver. A case under the Arms Act was registered separately for recovery of arms from the accused. The accused's bail plea was rejected considering the seriousness of the charges and the circumstances of arrest.

The accused was charged in a robbery case involving theft of ₹40,000, 15 new mobile phones, and personal documents. Seven of the looted phones were recovered from the accused's house, and the accused was also identified in CCTV footage. The accused had prior criminal cases involving robbery and the Arms Act.

The accused was charged in a robbery case involving a jewellery shop heist. The accused was arrested along with co-accused and was identified in a Test Identification Parade. Some of the looted items were recovered based on the accused's confession. The accused's previous bail application had been rejected several months after the incident.

The accused, as proprietor of a firm, allegedly conspired with a bank manager and others to fraudulently obtain a cash credit loan of ₹4 crore using forged financial documents. The funds were misused and not repaid. Despite being summoned repeatedly after the charge-sheet was filed, the accused failed to appear in court and remained absconding.

The accused was charged under Sections 420 and 406 IPC. After the High Court denied the accused's bail, the accused obtained bail from the Chief Judicial Magistrate in a city without disclosing the earlier rejection. On learning of this concealment, the Chief Judicial Magistrate cancelled the bail, and the order was upheld by the Sessions Court. The petitioner challenged these orders under Article 227, which was dismissed.

The accused, as a founder director of a company, allegedly failed to remit Rs. 3.19 crore that the company received as part of a settlement agreement with another company. This amount was to be paid to the complainant's company. The complaint accused the accused of misappropriating funds and of not providing any accounting for over ₹1.12 crore originally invested by the complainant.

The accused was alleged to have been involved in a robbery during which they allegedly shot the informant in the chest when identified. The accused had been in custody since late December of a particular year, and their bail had previously been denied twice by the High Court. Despite the long custody period, the Court considered the direct and serious nature of the accusation to deny bail again.

The deceased had given Rs. 71,500 to a person for a promised job for the deceased's sibling, but the cheque received in return was dishonoured. The deceased's spouse and the spouse's parents (the accused) allegedly pressured the deceased to separate from the deceased's family and threatened to file a false dowry case. The deceased later committed suicide. The FIR named the accused under Sections 306 and 420 IPC. The Sessions Court granted anticipatory bail, which was cancelled by the High Court but restored by the Supreme Court.

The accused, a senior officer of a public sector oil company, was arrested in an investigation led by a central investigating agency. The accused allegedly facilitated the fraudulent diversion of High-Speed Diesel (HSD) to ineligible firms using forged eligibility certificates and misrepresentations. The accused allegedly signed delivery orders without the required technical evaluations, contributing to revenue losses of ₹400-500 crores. The investigation was court-monitored due to systemic non-cooperation from the agencies involved.

The accused and a co-accused were convicted of murdering an auto-rickshaw driver in furtherance of a robbery, which took place on a date in 2004. The victim was last seen with the accused, and the victim's blood-stained vehicle and belongings were later recovered from the accused. Post-mortem and circumstantial evidence matched the timeline. The accused filed for suspension of sentence and release on bail pending appeal.

The accused, a political figure and the head of a state fisheries development corporation, was alleged to have orchestrated a brutal assault on an advocate, the victim, to prevent the victim from appearing before the Supreme Court in a case challenging a state's reservation policy. The investigation by the central investigating agency revealed that the accused financed and directed a group of hired attackers. The accused was also shown as an absconder in a prior robbery case.

The accused, the spouse of one of the co-accused in a major bank robbery case involving the loot of ₹98 lakh and the DVR of CCTV footage, sought anticipatory bail. While no female was seen at the time of the robbery, it was alleged that ₹48 lakh of the looted money was traced to the accused through a land purchase. A copy of the sale deed was recovered from the accused's possession.

The petitioner was arrested in a case involving a fatal stabbing incident. The FIR was based on the statement of the complainant, who alleged that the petitioner instigated the co-accused to carry out the attack. The deceased died in the incident. Material witnesses did not identify the petitioner and stated that the petitioner was not present at the scene. The prosecution relied on the recovery of a knife, a black cap, and a motorcycle allegedly linked to the petitioner.

The accused was arrested in connection with a major bank robbery case involving the theft of ₹98 lakh and CCTV DVR equipment. Although initially unnamed in the FIR, the accused's involvement was revealed through investigation and the accused's confessional statement. Recovery of looted property and land bought using the stolen funds was linked to the accused and the accused's family members.

The accused was arrested in a ₹98 lakh bank robbery case in a town. Although initially unnamed, the accused was implicated through investigation and their own confession, which led to recovery of looted money and property. It was found that the accused's in-law purchased land using proceeds from the crime.

The accused was arrested in connection with a robbery of ₹98 lakh from a bank. The accused was not named in the FIR, and the only allegation came from a supplementary case diary in which a co-accused stated that the accused had supplied arms. No weapons or stolen property were recovered from the accused. The accused has clean antecedents and has been in custody since a date in late 2023.

The accused was alleged to have committed armed robbery at a jewellery shop in a town, along with others, stealing 12.5 sovereigns of gold. The accused was arrested and remained in judicial custody for over five years without the trial concluding. Bail was initially denied on the ground of the accused's status as a foreigner, but the accused later provided residence details and sureties.

The accused, an adult employed with the police, sought bail after being arrested in connection with a bank robbery case involving ₹98 lakh. Though not named in the FIR, the accused was later implicated through their own confessional statement, which led to the recovery of looted property and documents. The investigation also revealed that the accused's child was involved and that land was purchased in the name of the accused's child's spouse using stolen funds.

The accused was alleged, along with the co-accused, to have forcibly entered the victim's house, assaulted the victim with a stick, and robbed jewellery and cash worth ₹1–1.5 lakhs. CCTV footage placed the accused near the crime scene, but no recovery was made from the accused. The accused was arrested and had remained in custody for 1.5 years. The prosecution alleged conspiracy and grievous injury, while the defence contested the strength of the evidence and the reliability of witness statements.

The accused was alleged to be a conspirator in a dacoity case in which a group of 8-10 armed persons robbed a showroom in a city, resulting in gunfire injuries and one fatality. Though not named in the FIR, the accused's name appeared in a co-accused's disclosure statement. The accused was arrested later, and no direct role in entering the showroom was attributed to them. The accused had been in custody for over four years.

The accused was arrested in connection with an attempted robbery case involving recovery of a knife and an air gun. The accused had multiple prior FIRs, including for robbery and arms offences. The accused had been in custody since a date in early 2023 and sought bail under Section 439 CrPC.

The accused was implicated in an armed robbery case from 2019 in which a group of accused persons stormed a showroom in a city, firing shots and looting valuables. Although the accused was not named in the FIR, their name surfaced during a co-accused's disclosure. The accused was alleged to have conspired in the offence and to have transported the assailants, but was not present during the actual robbery. The accused was in custody for over a year.

The accused was arrested in a case of armed robbery involving the snatching of ₹1 lakh from a car at gunpoint. The FIR was initially registered under Section 392 IPC and the Arms Act, and was later converted to Sections 395, 397, and 427 IPC. The accused declared no prior criminal record and applied for bail citing long incarceration.

The accused was arrested in December of a particular year for allegedly robbing ₹1 lakh from a car at gunpoint. The FIR was initially registered under Section 392 IPC but was later enhanced to include Sections 395, 397 and 427 IPC and sections of the Arms Act. The accused claimed to have no prior criminal record and sought bail citing prolonged pre-trial detention.

The accused was arrested several months before the present application for alleged involvement in the murder and robbery of a borewell contractor. It is alleged that the accused and others conspired to murder the victim, disposed of the body in a septic tank, and looted the victim's gold and mobile phone, later selling the items. The first bail application had already been rejected; this second application was based on the filing of the final report.

The accused was arrested in connection with an attempted robbery at a bank branch in a town. The accused was alleged to have conducted a recce and provided logistical support to the co-accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in early 2022, with no previous criminal record. The accused's bail was considered on grounds of the accused's gender, role, and prolonged pre-trial detention.

The accused was alleged to have been part of a conspiracy in the brutal murder of the deceased, allegedly for reasons related to a marriage between persons of different communities. The deceased was allegedly tracked via GPS, kidnapped, and murdered. The prosecution claimed that the accused ordered the murder, but CCTV footage and witness inconsistencies cast doubt on this. The accused was arrested from another state after absconding for a period.

The accused was granted bail by the Sessions Court despite being the spouse of the deceased, who allegedly committed suicide within one year of marriage due to dowry harassment. The complainant alleged that the victim was subjected to cruelty and harassment for a car and ₹5 lakh. The prosecution submitted post-mortem and circumstantial evidence indicating ante-mortem injuries and consistent dowry demands. The High Court found the trial court failed to consider key evidence and exercised discretion improperly.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case where the complainant was allegedly abducted, beaten with a pistol butt, robbed of valuables, and a video was made. Although the complainant alleged multiple assailants including the accused, there was no recovery from the accused, and the firearm-related allegations were against a different co-accused. The medical report showed a simple injury, and the charge sheet had been filed with the trial yet to begin.

The case involved the murder of the deceased by seven accused persons who allegedly used axes and sticks. The prosecution relied on dying declarations. Bail was granted initially on grounds such as an incomplete charge-sheet and the health condition of one of the accused. However, the State applied for cancellation of bail, citing threats to witnesses and public tension in the village.

Four accused were charged with a double murder committed with deadly weapons and in furtherance of a common object. Two of the accused were initially absconding and were later granted bail without being taken into custody. The other two had earlier been denied bail but were granted bail later without any new grounds. The State sought cancellation of all four bails.

The petitioner was arrested several years earlier in connection with an attempt to murder case involving alleged use of firearms. The petitioner remained in custody for over two and a half years. No injuries were reported from the incident. The petitioner had been acquitted earlier in a different case of attempt to murder.

The accused was arrested for alleged involvement in a shooting incident in which a co-accused caused a firearm injury. The allegation against the accused was limited to exhortation, without any direct assault. The accused is an adult and had no prior criminal history. The charge sheet had not yet been filed at the time of the hearing.

The accused was arrested in a certain month of 2020 for an alleged attempt to murder involving assault with a lathi on the victim's head. The charge-sheet had been filed, and the injuries sustained were not grievous. The accused had no prior criminal record and had been in custody for over two months.

The accused, a head constable, was alleged to have accepted a bribe of ₹1,500 for facilitating anticipatory bail in a theft case. A trap was laid and currency notes were recovered from the accused's home. However, evidence showed that the actual demand was made by the station house officer, and the accused may have only received the money on that officer's behalf. The trial court convicted the accused, who then appealed the decision.

The accused was involved in multiple cases, including murder, attempt to murder, assault on police, and illegal arms. While detained, the accused secured bail under Section 167(2) CrPC due to delay in the filing of the charge-sheet, but did not avail of it until later. The accused was also granted bail in another case by allegedly misrepresenting facts. After the accused's release, fresh offences were committed allegedly under the accused's instigation, including murder and possession of bombs.

Juvenile petitioners sought anticipatory directions for Juvenile Justice Boards to accept their surrender and decide their bail applications on the same day, in connection with offences including attempt to murder, insulting a community, and posting derogatory content online. The petitioners feared being detained in observation homes before their bail applications were considered and argued that such detention caused psychological harm.

The accused was charged in a case involving alleged assault and wrongful restraint following the interception of a lorry transporting rice. The complainant and others were allegedly beaten by persons associated with the accused. The accused claimed the complaint was false and stemmed from political and business rivalry, and pointed out that the co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused, allegedly affiliated with a political party, conspired with others to murder a leader of an organisation. On a certain date in 2014, a country-made bomb was hurled at the deceased's vehicle, causing it to crash. Subsequently, the accused attacked the deceased with swords and choppers, killing them, and injured the deceased's associate. A central investigating agency took over the case and charged the accused under provisions of the IPC, UAPA, Arms Act, and Explosives Act.

The complainant was assaulted early in the morning by the accused, a co-accused, and an unidentified accomplice using iron pipes. The attack was motivated by previous enmity over a property dispute. The complainant suffered multiple fractures and head injuries. Despite the grant of anticipatory bail, the accused failed to cooperate with the police and allegedly threatened the complainant again.

The accused were granted bail by the Sessions Court in a case involving attempt to murder and other offences under the IPC. The complainant sought cancellation of bail, citing the serious injuries suffered by the victim and the accused's history of prior criminal cases. The Sessions Court had noted that the accused had no antecedents, but the High Court found this incorrect based on records that had been overlooked. Despite this, bail was not cancelled because of the age of the case and the stable condition of the victim.

The accused, a former public representative, was booked under the Gangster and Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act based on two FIRs involving a double murder and an assault on police. The accused allegedly led a gang involved in land grabbing, extortion, and other violent crimes. The accused had 37 prior cases, including murder and dacoity, and had been in custody for several years.

The detenu was involved in multiple criminal cases including murders, attempted murders, and extortion. The detenu was branded a 'Goonda' under the state's Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act. The detenu's parent filed a Habeas Corpus petition challenging the preventive detention order, arguing that no bail application had been filed in the current case and thus there was no real likelihood of the detenu's release.

The accused allegedly invited the complainant, a neighbour, to the accused's house under the pretext of letting the complainant speak to the accused's spouse in a foreign country. While the complainant was on the call, the accused allegedly tried to forcibly disrobe the complainant and sexually assault the complainant. The incident was reported 12 days later. The accused claimed the complaint was motivated by resentment after the accused failed to help the complainant get employment in that foreign country.

The accused was arrested in a case involving gang rivalry between two rival gangs. The accused was alleged to have conspired to assault a minor with deadly weapons as part of a criminal syndicate. The FIR was filed 40 days after the incident, and there was no injury or direct evidence tying the accused to the scene. The case was allegedly a counterblast to a previously filed FIR.

The accused was alleged to have carried out a contract killing of a businessman in a city. The murder involved a conspiracy led by a co-accused. The evidence included CCTV footage, sketches, a ballistic report linking the weapon recovered from the accused to the crime, and witness statements. The accused has a criminal history of at least 18 cases involving murder, dacoity, and arms offences across multiple states.

The accused was arrested in connection with a conspiracy to murder a person who had earlier been acquitted in a rape case, which was allegedly falsely lodged at the behest of the co-accused. The FIR did not name the accused initially; the accused was later implicated through witness statements. The accused had no direct role in the murder or in the use of weapons. Although charges had been framed, no witnesses were examined for over six months.

The accused was previously granted anticipatory bail in a related case. The accused was later implicated in a conspiracy for a subsequent murder, though not named in the FIR. The accusation is based on statements recorded under Section 161 CrPC. The accused has been in custody for over a year, with no progress in the trial.

The petitioner, a doctor and former head of a government hospital, was accused of falsifying medical records to cover up custodial torture of a former public representative. A Medical Board chaired by the petitioner reported no injuries, which contradicted later findings by another hospital showing foot fractures. The court noted manipulation of medical evidence and denied anticipatory bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a house theft that took place on a night in January involving cash and jewelry. The accused was not named in the FIR but was later linked to the offence through alleged recovery of stolen property. The accused has a criminal history of 63 similar cases and has been in custody since the following month, roughly the end of February.

The accused was charged along with others in a group assault that followed an incident involving sexual harassment of a minor. The altercation resulted in the death of a person and injuries to multiple people. The accused was allegedly armed and involved in the assault, but witness statements were inconsistent and contradictory regarding the accused's role.

The accused was alleged to have been involved in a violent group altercation that followed a report of sexual harassment involving a child. The altercation led to the death of the child's parent and injuries to several family members. The accused was alleged to have been armed but did not directly inflict the fatal injuries. Bail was granted due to inconsistencies in witness accounts and the applicant's marginal role.

The accused, along with seven others, was convicted for double murder and attempt to murder under multiple IPC sections. This was the accused's third bail application, after earlier rejections in two previous years. The accused sought bail on grounds of parity with co-accused who had been granted bail and long imprisonment. The court noted the accused's misconduct involving a forged bail order and declined relief.

A parent of the detenu filed a habeas corpus petition challenging the preventive detention of their child under a state preventive detention Act. The authorities cited the detenu's involvement in multiple violent crimes, including attempt to murder, extortion, and criminal intimidation. The detenu had been granted bail in all pending cases, but was considered a habitual offender and a threat to public order.

The accused and co-accused were charged with the murder of the victim, who had previously assaulted some of them. The accused allegedly tracked the victim using GPS, ambushed the victim, and killed the victim with weapons. The petitioner was accused of participating in the assault. Prior cases under attempt to murder and preparation for dacoity were also noted.

The accused, a school manager, was alleged to have taken ₹15 lakh as a bribe for appointing the informant as a teacher, but later demanded more money and denied the informant the post. The FIR was filed six years later, allegedly as retaliation for a kidnapping FIR that the accused had filed against the informant's relatives. The accused has 34 pending cases, mostly under the NI Act, but no convictions.

The accused was charged in a murder case arising from a violent land dispute in which two individuals were shot dead and others were injured. Though not named in the FIR, the accused was identified during investigation on the basis of witness statements and the recovery of a vehicle used in the crime. The accused had been in custody since a date in an earlier year and sought bail on grounds of delayed trial and personal circumstances.

The petitioner is accused in eight previous cases involving serious IPC offences and is being prosecuted under the PMLA for allegedly acquiring assets worth over ₹4 crore from criminal activities. Authorities claim the petitioner and their family engaged in systematic land fraud and created layers of ownership to conceal proceeds of crime. Despite claiming legitimate business income, the petitioner failed to provide valid documentary evidence during investigation.

The accused was alleged to have provided shelter at their farmhouse to the assailants involved in a premeditated murder executed by a crime syndicate. The murder was allegedly carried out in retaliation against a local public representative who resisted the syndicate's activities. The accused was not involved in the attack itself but allegedly facilitated it by hosting the assailants prior to the crime.

The accused was arrested in 2020 based on allegations of being part of a gang involved in armed robbery and conspiracy to commit terrorist acts with links to foreign entities. The accused was charged under various sections of the IPC, UAPA, Arms Act, and Prisons Act. The prosecution relied heavily on disclosure statements of the co-accused and did not present direct evidence connecting the accused to terrorist activities.

The accused was charged in a brutal murder case linked to an organized crime syndicate led by a co-accused. While the deceased was killed by a group of assailants, the accused was allegedly seen near the scene. The prosecution invoked the MCOC Act, alleging gang involvement, but the accused claimed no role in the conspiracy or the assault.

The accused was detained under the Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Act, 2006 of a state, as a habitual offender involved in 15 serious criminal cases, including murder, extortion, and dacoity. The detention was ordered by the District Magistrate and later approved by the Advisory Board. The accused challenged the order, citing procedural lapses and a reduction in the frequency of recent offences.

The accused, a repeat offender, was granted interim bail in 9 serious criminal cases to facilitate the accused's marriage. The State challenged this bail, arguing that the accused was involved in more than 20 cases including multiple murders, robberies, and extortion. The High Court found that the lower court had not adequately considered the gravity of the charges.

The accused was detained under the National Security Act, 1980, based on allegations spanning several years involving criminal intimidation, assault, arson, extortion, and other offences. The accused had earlier been arrested once and released on bail. The detaining authority cited multiple FIRs and general diary entries to justify the detention.

The accused was alleged to have orchestrated land grabbing and extortion by creating forged documents relating to disputed agricultural land. The accused and associates allegedly threatened and intimidated the complainant to relinquish ownership. The FIR stated several instances of coercion, including ransacking of property and physical intimidation.

The accused and their child were accused of sheltering a murder accused, who was involved in the death of an employee allegedly caused while the employee was held in confinement. The deceased was allegedly kidnapped, confined, and beaten to death on suspicion of financial fraud. The petitioners allegedly harboured the murder accused while that person was evading the police.

The accused, allegedly a key member of an organised gang, was charged with conspiring in the murder of a municipal councillor, who had opposed the gang's activities. The murder was executed by hired killers using firearms and scythes in a public hotel. The accused was implicated on the basis of confessional statements of co-accused and call detail record (CDR) evidence.

The accused, a typist in a civil court, was alleged to have acted as a middleman in a bribery case involving a demand of ₹2,50,000 to influence a witness in a judicial complaint. The accused allegedly coordinated meetings and communicated demands between the complainant and the co-accused. The demand and the accused's role were supported by call recordings.

The accused, an advocate, was alleged to have conspired to extort ₹4 crore from a businessman through a honey trap scheme involving a false rape case. The businessman later died by suicide. The accused allegedly advised the co-accused and participated in planning meetings. There was no direct communication or meeting between the accused and the deceased.

The accused and their children were accused of attempting to extort ₹12–20 lakh from the complainant, following the death of a relative with whom there was a property dispute. The complaint alleged threats and dishonoring of an earlier agreement. The FIR was filed over a year after the alleged extortion attempt, and five months after the accused filed a counter-FIR against the complainant.

The accused was alleged to have confined and sexually assaulted a minor, along with the accused's sibling, who is the co-accused, in 2019. The victim alleged repeated abuse and eventual coercion to marry into the accused's family. The complaint was lodged over three years later, despite the victim having lived in a relationship with the co-accused and having borne a child with the co-accused.

The accused was alleged to have channelized extorted money for a terror outfit. The accused was arrested along with others who were found with cash deposits, and was charged under the IPC, the UA(P) Act, and the CLA Act. The national investigating agency alleged that the accused collected extortion money from contractors and was involved in legitimizing terror funds.

The accused was detained preventively under a state law on the prevention of dangerous activities (enacted in 1986) on the basis of four FIRs filed within a span of about three weeks in the same month. The detaining authority alleged persistent involvement in criminal acts, but the offences were not of grave nature. The accused had already been granted bail in the relevant criminal cases.

The accused was preventively detained under a state law on the prevention of dangerous activities, based on four criminal cases registered within a period of about three weeks in a single month. The detention was challenged as excessive, on the grounds that the accused had already been granted bail in those cases and that the alleged acts did not disturb public order but involved only law and order issues.

The accused was alleged to have conspired with members of an organized crime syndicate to extort ₹62 lakhs from a businessman under threats connected to a criminal gang. The extortion allegedly occurred through coercion at a party attended by over 200 people. The accused was arrested under IPC and MCOCA provisions but claimed parity with co-accused who had been granted bail earlier.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a criminal conspiracy in which fake enforcement agency notices were sent to executives of a company in order to extort ₹2–3 crores. The accused, along with the co-accused, introduced a fake enforcement agency officer to the victims at a hotel in a city and threatened them with arrest in a fictitious case. CCTV footage and witness identification corroborated the accused's role.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a criminal conspiracy to extort ₹62 lakhs from a businessman. The conspiracy was allegedly coordinated by two co-accused, who were said to be linked to an organised criminal gang. The prosecution claimed that the extortion plot was discussed at a party attended by over 200 people and that the accused was one of the alleged beneficiaries.

The accused was arrested in a case involving an extortion racket operated by an organized crime syndicate. The complainant, a businessman, alleged that the complainant received threatening calls demanding money after selling land. During investigation, the accused was arrested and linked to the crime syndicate, which was led by a convicted gangster. The charge sheet included serious offences under the IPC and the state's Control of Organised Crimes Act.

The accused was detained under preventive detention laws on grounds of involvement in four criminal cases registered in the same year, involving attempt to murder, cheating, trespass, and extortion. The State claimed the accused's actions created public fear, but the accused remained in judicial custody when the detention order was issued. The accused's spouse challenged the legality of the detention.

The accused was preventively detained under a state law dealing with habitual offenders (the Goondas Act), based on allegations of multiple criminal activities including murder, extortion, and sale of ganja. The Advisory Board confirmed the detention, but the accused's representation, submitted some time earlier, was not considered by the State Government or the Advisory Board. The High Court found this to be a violation of constitutional safeguards.

The accused was alleged to have cheated a buyer by selling a flat that was already mortgaged to a bank, and by entering into a second sale agreement with another person after accepting earnest money. The accused allegedly failed to return ₹24 lakhs paid by the complainant. The anticipatory bail granted by the Sessions Court was challenged on the grounds of the accused's criminal antecedents and absconding behaviour.

The accused was alleged, along with others, to have made repeated threats and extortion attempts against the principal of a school, including a demand of Rs.5 lakhs. While the main allegations of assault and threats were made against the co-accused, the accused was only named in omnibus allegations. There was a delay of about a month in lodging the complaint, and no direct accusations of threats or assault were made against the accused.

The accused was alleged to have extorted ₹1,80,000 from the complainant by threatening the complainant and ransacking the complainant's shop. CCTV footage allegedly captured the incident. The prosecution claimed that the accused had a pattern of filing false FIRs, including five separate complaints under Section 376 IPC against various individuals. The accused's application for bail under Section 439 CrPC was rejected by the trial court and again on appeal.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a case concerning a false FIR and extortion, in which a person allegedly lodged a rape complaint against another person and later demanded ₹50 lakhs for that person's release. The accused's only alleged role was responding to a message from a co-accused. Co-accused individuals alleged to be involved in the extortion and false implication racket had already been granted bail.

The accused, a serving police constable, was alleged, along with others, to have attempted to extort money from a complainant in connection with a property transaction. The accused was initially granted bail but was re-arrested after Section 395 IPC was added. The prosecution alleged that the accused and others had coordinated entry into the complainant's house and then made an extortion attempt. The prosecution cited CCTV evidence and anonymous threats.

The accused was alleged to have conspired with their spouse to extort ₹32.5 lakhs from the family of a police officer, who had earlier been arrested in a rape case filed by the accused. The complainant alleged that the accused and their spouse promised to withdraw the FIR in exchange for the money. The prosecution claimed that ₹11 lakhs went to the accused and ₹19 lakhs were recovered from the accused's spouse. The case involved audio/video recordings, though the accused's specific role in those was unclear.

The accused was arrested along with a co-accused based on secret information while transporting 1.2 kg heroin and illegal arms. The accused was booked under Sections 21 and 29 of the NDPS Act and Section 25(6) of the Arms Act. Despite being in custody for a considerable period, since the arrest, and the trial commencing, none of the 25 prosecution witnesses had been examined as of the bail hearing.

The accused was arrested in a money laundering case under the PMLA based on allegations that included extortion, murder, forgery, and cheating. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2024. An enforcement agency had filed a complaint in 2014, and the charge sheet had already been submitted. The accused cited the Supreme Court's bail order for the co-accused, who was granted bail due to lack of prima facie evidence of proceeds of crime.

The accused was arrested for allegedly participating in a blackmail scheme in which a person falsely accused an individual of rape and then demanded money for withdrawal of the case. The complainant claimed that the accused and others were involved in extorting Rs. 50 lakhs. The FIR against the accused followed the discovery of this extortion attempt after the initial rape FIR was found to be false.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case in which the prosecutrix allegedly filed a false rape FIR and then, along with family members, tried to extort Rs. 50 lakhs from the complainant to withdraw the case. The accused was named as a co-accused in the follow-up extortion FIR. The prosecution alleged a pattern of blackmail by the prosecutrix, while the accused denied direct involvement.

The accused was implicated in a case arising from a false rape FIR allegedly lodged by the accused's spouse to extort money from the complainant. The complainant claimed that the spouse and others demanded Rs. 50 lakhs for withdrawing the FIR. The accused was arrested along with others but denied involvement in the extortion or receipt of any money. The charge sheet was filed and the accused had been in custody since a date in 2024.

The accused was arrested in an extortion case in which the prosecutrix allegedly lodged a false rape FIR to demand Rs. 50 lakhs in exchange for its withdrawal. The accused was part of a group that included the accused's spouse and other co-accused. The complainant alleged that the prosecutrix had a history of blackmailing through false cases and was referred to by a derogatory nickname. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2024.

The accused was arrested in an extortion case in which the prosecutrix allegedly filed a false FIR under Section 376 IPC in order to blackmail the complainant and demand Rs. 50 lakhs for withdrawing it. The accused was named as a co-accused along with several others. The prosecution claimed that the complainant was misled into meeting the prosecutrix and the prosecutrix's spouse at a public square in a city, where the extortion demand was made. The accused denied any direct involvement.

The accused was arrested in 2019 for allegedly being part of an organized crime syndicate, led by a person referred to as the syndicate leader, which operated illegal Matka gambling. During a police raid, violence ensued and attempts were made to snatch seized cash. The prosecution claimed the accused helped facilitate the organized crime. The accused was charge-sheeted in the same year and remained in custody for almost 5 years with no trial progress.

The accused was arrested for allegedly facilitating the activities of an organized crime syndicate, led by another person, that was engaged in Matka gambling. During a police raid, violence erupted, and the accused allegedly attempted to obstruct the police from seizing illegal proceeds. The charge sheet was filed several months after the arrest, and charges were framed a few years later, but no witnesses had been examined over 4 years and 10 months of custody.

The accused was alleged to be part of an organized crime syndicate, led by another person, involved in illegal gambling operations. During a police raid, the accused allegedly helped obstruct the investigation and attempted to snatch seized cash. The accused was arrested, charge-sheeted a few months later, and remained in custody for almost 5 years with no material progress in the trial.

The accused was alleged to have demanded ₹10 lakhs as extortion and to have abducted the informant, who was released after two days on a promise to pay ₹20 lakhs. No money was delivered. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2023. The accused had old, unrelated criminal antecedents.

The accused, an adult, was accused of intercepting a delivery person and attempting to extort ₹500. When the victim refused, the accused allegedly attacked the victim with a knife, causing a simple abdominal injury. The FIR was lodged the same day. The accused had four prior simple offences and had been in custody since a date in 2020.

The accused was alleged, along with others including the accused's parent and a co-accused, of extorting ₹1.07 crores from the complainant by threatening the complainant with false accusations of rape, robbery, and other serious charges. The threats allegedly began after a party in a certain month of 2022 and continued over time. The FIR was lodged only several months later, in the following year. The accused had been in custody since their arrest, which took place shortly after the FIR was lodged.

The accused, a medical doctor at a public institution, was accused of repeatedly sexually assaulting the prosecutrix under the false pretext of marriage, allegedly involving drugging, confinement, and physical abuse. The complainant initially delayed reporting and was in a live-in relationship with the accused for 15 days. Contradictions emerged in the medico-legal certificate, and the prosecutrix's history included similar FIRs against other individuals.

The accused, a history-sheeter, allegedly demanded ₹2 lakhs from a vegetable vendor, threatening to stop a demolition project and to harm the vendor. On a certain date in 2022, the vendor was assaulted, and the vendor's sibling was shot dead while intervening. Witnesses reported that the attackers fled in a car in which the accused was present. Prior threats and extortion attempts by the accused were corroborated by multiple witness statements.

The accused, along with co-accused, allegedly lured the complainant by pretending to offer financial investment services. The complainant was taken to a house, forced to disrobe, filmed, and blackmailed with the threat of public defamation unless the complainant paid Rs.10 lakhs. Though the extortion amount was not received, Rs.2.5 lakhs was agreed upon, and the plan was disrupted before the transaction occurred.

The accused was alleged to have raped the victim many years earlier, after luring the victim to a job interview under a false identity. The complaint was filed only many years later, despite earlier attempts to complain, the first of which was several years after the alleged incident and another about a decade and a half after it. The delay and discrepancies in the victim's complaints raised concerns about the veracity of the victim's claims.

The accused was alleged to have circulated a video showing a hospital compounder performing surgery that allegedly resulted in a patient's death. The video was used by others to demand ransom from the hospital's owner. The prosecution did not claim that the accused themselves demanded ransom.

The accused was charged in a murder case in which the deceased, a real estate businessperson, had previously received extortion threats. The accused was implicated several months after the FIR was registered, on the basis of suspicion. The accused has been in custody for over three and a half years while the trial has progressed slowly. Prosecution evidence has been completed, and the trial is pending for defence evidence. The co-accused had been granted bail earlier.

The accused was arrested after being found in possession of two .32 bore pistols and 10 cartridges. Based on secret information, the accused was identified as a habitual offender with 21 prior cases in a state, including extortion and dacoity. The present case was registered under the Arms Act. The accused had been in custody for almost a year and the investigation was complete, but no prosecution witnesses had been examined.

The accused was convicted of murdering the deceased, a soldier who was found hanging in military quarters. The allegation was that the accused, who had an affair with the deceased's spouse, conspired with the spouse to kill the deceased. However, the original FIR reported the death as suicide. Subsequent statements by the deceased's children and sibling were found to be inconsistent, and no evidence placed the accused at the scene. Medical evidence confirmed death by hanging with no signs of struggle or forced strangulation.

The accused and their family floated real estate investment schemes through their companies, promising assured returns for investing in IT park projects in two cities. Over 1500 people invested around ₹400–600 crores. The projects remained incomplete for years and the promised returns stopped. FIRs were filed for cheating and fraud. The accused allegedly siphoned off funds to personal accounts and failed to pay taxes.

The informant alleged that the petitioner purchased cattle feed worth over ₹75 lakhs over four to five years, but stopped making payments in the last two to three years. On a certain date in 2022, the petitioner allegedly threatened the informant with a pistol and demanded ₹1 crore as extortion. The petitioner denied the allegations, claiming the dispute was commercial in nature and arose from a breakdown in supply and payment during the COVID-19 lockdown period.

The accused was charged in a criminal case under IPC sections relating to cheating and forgery. A High Court had granted anticipatory bail, but it imposed a condition requiring the accused to deposit Rs. 1 crore as a fixed deposit in the complainant's name. The Supreme Court intervened, stating that such a financial condition was onerous and outside the permissible scope of Section 438 CrPC.

The petitioner was accused of defrauding members of an association of information technology businesses of around ₹15 crore by inducing them to sell computer equipment through the accused's companies and failing to return the sale proceeds. The cheques issued were dishonoured, and proceedings under Section 138 NI Act were initiated. The accused had been in judicial custody for several years.

The accused, a proprietor of a trading business, was accused of receiving large quantities of apples from multiple growers over a period of several years without making payments. An FIR was filed later, alleging a total unpaid amount exceeding ₹6.7 crores. Cheques issued by the accused were dishonoured, leading to proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The accused was arrested about a year after the FIR was filed and was granted interim bail to facilitate settlement with the victims.

The accused was alleged to have conspired with others to defraud job aspirants by collecting Rs 85 lakhs under false promises of employment. Two FIRs were filed under Sections 408, 420, 506, and 120B IPC. Bail was granted in both cases. Despite this, a preventive detention order was passed months later under a state Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act.

The plaintiffs, who were promoters of a hotel-owning company, alleged that their shares were forcibly taken from them under threat and coercion. They accused the defendants of using threats, physical violence, and political influence to make them transfer 100% of the shareholding without proper consideration. The plaintiffs claimed that they were stripped and tortured, and that their family was coerced into sending money. Multiple FIRs and litigations were filed involving both parties.

The accused was alleged to have sold the same flats to multiple parties, resulting in allegations under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 120B IPC.
