The complainant filed a criminal complaint after also initiating a civil suit for specific performance. The accused claimed that the criminal process was being misused due to ongoing civil litigation and personal rivalry. Multiple anticipatory bail applications were rejected before the matter reached the Supreme Court.

The petitioner was detained under a state preventive detention law based on involvement in three FIRs alleging extortion, assault, and intimidation. Despite being granted bail in two of the cases and remaining in custody for the third, authorities issued a preventive detention order citing habitual criminal conduct and public fear.

The complainant, an employee of a cattle shelter, alleged that they were lured to a hotel by a person under false pretenses and later abducted and assaulted by three persons, including the petitioner. The group demanded money by threatening to falsely implicate the complainant in a rape case. They took the complainant's money, phone, and identity documents. The incident was captured on CCTV, and the petitioner was identified as a main conspirator.

The petitioner was accused along with others of demanding extortion money from the informant's child, who was later shot dead by another co-accused. The petitioner had been in custody since a date in 2022, and the main allegation of firing was not against the petitioner. The petitioner claimed parity with other similarly placed co-accused who had already been granted bail.

The appellant was accused of being part of a criminal gang led by a gang leader that extorted money from coal traders and businesspersons through threats and HAWALA transactions. The appellant was found in possession of Rs. 32 lakhs, allegedly extorted money, and was a business partner in a firm run by a co-accused. Multiple co-accused were granted bail earlier.

The complainant was lured by two persons into a house where an obscene video of the complainant was recorded and used to extort Rs. 2.5 lakhs by threatening to defame the complainant publicly. The accused was part of a gang that used similar tactics on 14-15 persons. The accused followed the vehicle carrying the victim and participated in the extortion process.

The petitioner, accused of pressuring the complainant's child into a relationship and then blackmailing them with photographs and audio clips, allegedly demanded money. When the complainant's family tried to report the matter, they were allegedly attacked by the accused and the accused's associates. The accused was arrested and remained in custody for over a month.

The complainant alleged that between 2018 and 2019, they were drugged and blackmailed with nude photographs taken without their consent. The complainant claimed to have been extorted of Rs. 58 lakhs and forced to execute a property sale deed under coercion. The FIR was filed only several years later. The accused was allegedly involved in the conspiracy and received the benefit of the extortion.

The accused was alleged to be part of a gang led by another person, which extorted money from coal traders using fear and hawala channels. Although booked under UAPA Sections 20/21, the court noted that the accused was not charged under UAPA Sections 15, 16, or 17, which are prerequisites. The accused had been in custody since 2022, and some co-accused had already been granted bail.

In an earlier year, the petitioner and their parent allegedly attempted to extort Rs. 5 lakhs from the informant by threatening the informant with a firearm in a public location. The informant reported the incident after the accused fled upon noticing a police patrol. The petitioner was arrested later and had previously been involved in multiple cases, primarily during their juvenile years.

The accused was alleged to be part of a gang led by another person, which extorted money from contractors using HAWALA routes and threats. Though booked under Sections 20 and 21 of the UAPA, the accused was not charge-sheeted under Sections 15, 16, or 17. Several co-accused had already been granted bail, and there was no direct reference to the accused in witness statements. The accused had been in custody since a date in January 2022.

The accused was alleged to be part of a group that extorted illegal gratification from sand truck owners and drivers in exchange for allowing the transport of illegal sand. A mobile phone was seized from the accused during investigation. The accused had been in custody since a date in early 2022 and had no prior criminal record. Co-accused in similar positions had already been granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have fraudulently obtained money from a complainant by falsely representing themselves as a general manager of a battery company offering a franchise. The accused took lakhs of rupees as investment and shop setup costs but allegedly failed to deliver products or respond to queries. Upon confrontation, a dispute broke out, and counter-complaints were filed by both parties.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a fraudulent data-entry job scam in which the informant was induced to sign bogus agreements and was later extorted through legal threats and abusive messages. A total of Rs. 3.46 lakhs was extorted. Although the accused was not the main accused, small transactions were traced to the accused's account. The co-accused had already been granted anticipatory bail and had refunded the full extorted amount.

The complainant, while returning home, was intercepted near a hotel by the applicant and a co-accused, who allegedly snatched the complainant's gold chain and fled on a motorcycle. The applicant was arrested and confessed during interrogation. However, the chain was not recovered from the applicant's possession and the applicant was not identified in the test parade. The applicant had been in custody for several years.

The applicant allegedly tried to abduct and threaten the complainant's parent in order to recover a loan the applicant had given to that parent. The applicant was accused under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita of extortion-related offences. The applicant denied wrongdoing and submitted an affidavit agreeing not to claim the money again. The court noted that the applicant had no past criminal record and that nothing remained to be recovered from the applicant.

The applicant was arrested for housebreaking and theft of gold and silver ornaments from a private residence. Based on the applicant's confession, stolen items were recovered. The prosecution opposed bail citing 28 similar prior cases. The applicant had been in custody since early 2020 and sought release due to health risks during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The detenu was accused in three cases of robbery and extortion under IPC Sections 394 and 384. Despite being granted bail in each case, the authorities detained the detenu under a state preventive detention Act, labeling them a 'goonda' who threatened public order. The detenu's sibling challenged the detention via writ petition, arguing that the offences concerned individual victims and did not justify preventive detention.

The detenu was involved in three criminal cases related to robbery and extortion and had already been granted bail in each. Despite this, authorities invoked the state preventive detention law and detained the detenu on the grounds that the detenu was a habitual offender causing public panic. The detenu's sibling challenged the detention, arguing it was unjustified given existing criminal proceedings.

The accused and the co-accused were allegedly involved in a scam in which they induced the complainant to join a bogus data entry job. They later threatened the complainant with legal notices and extorted Rs.3,46,700/-. The co-accused had already deposited the full amount and was granted anticipatory bail. The complainant had also allegedly attempted to extort the co-accused in return and demanded settlement via hawala.

The complainant was abducted by a group under the pretext of purchasing medicines, taken to a deserted place and tortured. The complainant was threatened with false implication in cases involving firearms and black-market Remdesivir injections. Videos were made to blackmail the complainant and extort ₹5 lakhs. During the incident, the complainant transferred large sums through digital payment applications. The accused, who was known by an alias, joined the group later and directed the movements using a scooter.

The detenu was booked in two FIRs for threatening individuals with a knife, committing arson, and extortion. Although granted bail in both cases, the authorities detained the detenu under a state preventive detention Act, citing the detenu as a habitual offender causing public panic. The detenu's spouse challenged the detention order by way of a writ petition.

The complainant, who had earlier received investment funds from a co-accused, was later threatened by four individuals, including the accused. They demanded ₹50 lakhs, threatened the complainant with a revolver, and forcibly collected ₹5 lakhs. The accused allegedly accompanied the others in threatening the complainant and making the complainant sit in a vehicle, and had ties with a known criminal.

The complainant received threatening calls demanding ₹1 crore from individuals who claimed to be two named persons. The petitioner was named as accused No.2. It was later discovered that the number used for the threatening calls was registered to a third person. The prosecution alleged the petitioner's involvement in a conspiracy, while the petitioner claimed false implication and sought anticipatory bail, citing bail already granted to other co-accused.

The accused was alleged to have aided in extorting illegal gratification from sand vehicle drivers and owners in order to facilitate the transport of illegal sand. A mobile phone and ₹19,000 were recovered from the accused. The accused had no prior criminal record and had been in custody since a date in an earlier year. Co-accused persons alleged to have played similar roles had already been granted bail earlier.

The accused was alleged to have snatched a gold chain from the complainant near a hotel. The crime was initially registered against unknown persons. The accused was later arrested along with others based on a confession, and a motorcycle was recovered. However, the chain was not recovered from the accused, and the accused was not identified in a test identification parade. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2019.

The accused was alleged, along with others, to have extorted illegal gratification from drivers and owners of sand-loaded vehicles in order to facilitate illegal sand transport. The accused was arrested, and Rs. 99,300 and a mobile phone were recovered from them. The accused had been in custody since an earlier date and had no prior criminal record. Co-accused persons who were alleged to have played similar roles were granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have extorted ₹20 lakhs from the complainant by threatening to file a false rape case. The accused had previously been appointed Director of the complainant's college and allegedly took ₹17 lakhs earlier. The accused claimed the money was a loan, repaid from the accused's salary. The accused counter-alleged that the complainant had raped the accused over a period of several years and had used videos for blackmail. The FIRs by both parties were lodged around the same time.

The accused, an advocate, was alleged to have conspired with a client, the co-accused, to extort money from the complainant by threatening to falsely implicate the complainant in a rape case. The case was built on WhatsApp chats between the accused and the co-accused. The prosecution claimed the chats showed intent to extort Rs. 5 lakhs, but no money had changed hands. The applicant asserted a professional relationship with the co-accused and denied any wrongdoing.

The accused and co-accused were involved in a violent confrontation arising from a land dispute. The complainant party alleged that the accused group, armed with lathis, rods, and an axe, assaulted them after a prior report was lodged regarding a crop theft. Multiple victims sustained grievous injuries. The bail plea was made jointly with other co-accused, but the Court found no mitigating change from earlier rejected applications.

The accused was alleged to have abused and assaulted the complainant with caste-based insults. The prosecution stated that the offence occurred in a public place. The defence claimed that the complainant had entered the accused's house to commit theft and was assaulted inside the house, and that the SC/ST Act was therefore wrongly applied.

The accused, a media professional, allegedly posed as a power broker and extracted ₹16.4 crores from a real estate company under the false pretense of having influence in a government tax department. The accused entered into a sham consultancy agreement and laundered the funds. The enforcement agency alleged laundering of ₹52.5 crores overall. Some properties were bought with the laundered money. The central investigating agency filed the predicate offences, and bail had already been granted in them.

The accused was alleged to be part of an extortion racket that continued for 12–13 years and targeted an elderly complainant through morphed photographs and blackmail. The conspiracy allegedly included lawyers and reporters who threatened to release fake material in order to extort up to ₹10 crores. The accused was named by a co-accused and by witnesses, and allegedly created and destroyed fake media. The accused was absconding before surrendering in court.

The accused was implicated in a case where the child of the informant was allegedly surrounded and murdered due to non-payment of extortion money. One co-accused was the alleged extortionist, another co-accused ordered the shooting, and a third co-accused executed it. The accused was alleged to have snatched a gold chain from the deceased, but no recovery was made. The accused had been in custody for a substantial period, since 2021, and the charge sheet had already been filed. Bail was granted on parity with the co-accused.

The applicants, who are siblings, were accused of extorting money from the complainant under the pretext of halting illegal construction by repeatedly filing RTI applications and allegedly demanding a flat or ₹6,00,000. The complainant paid ₹3,00,000. The complaint was filed four months after the alleged incidents. The applicants claimed to have acted to uphold municipal law, and had no prior criminal history.

The complainant, a developer, received threats from a person allegedly linked to the underworld, demanding ₹3.5 lakhs. That person's in-law, the accused, allegedly visited the complainant's office with armed persons and sent abusive messages demanding money. CCTV and messaging application evidence did not conclusively prove intimidation or weapon use. The FIR was filed after a delay.

The accused was alleged to be part of a group that blackmailed a property developer, the complainant, into paying ₹1 lakh and demanding ₹5 lakh more under threat of leaking nude photographs taken without consent. The alleged blackmail involved a fake social media identity and a staged meeting where the complainant was secretly photographed. The accused was one of the people allegedly present during the extortion.

The accused, the second accused in the case, along with another person, attempted to steal cement bags from a construction site. They fled upon being caught by the complainant, abandoning the cement and an autorickshaw. The High Court had earlier denied anticipatory bail, which was later granted by the Sessions Court without disclosure of the earlier rejection.

The accused was arrested for allegedly allowing their bank account to be used in a sextortion racket, where victims were blackmailed using nude video calls and threatened with online exposure. The accused claimed that their roommate requested a one-time use of the account to receive money, and that they handed it over the same day without knowledge of the crime. No money was retained by the accused, and the accused had no past record.

The deceased committed suicide, leaving behind a note accusing the accused and the accused's spouse (the co-accused) of repeated extortion and threats to implicate the deceased in a false rape case. A prior FIR under IPC Sections 376 and 506 had been filed by the co-accused against the deceased. The accused was arrested along with the co-accused. The suicide note was verified and supported the allegations. Police reports indicated a pattern of extortion behaviour involving the co-accused initiating false sexual allegations to extract money.

The accused was alleged to have attempted to murder the de facto complainant by attacking them with a knife at a bus stop, resulting in a lacerated injury to the forehead. The accused argued that the accused was intercepted and attacked by the complainant's group, and that the injury occurred from a fall. The accused had a prior extortion case involving the complainant's sibling.

The case involved a large-scale extortion racket targeting an elderly adult over a period of 12–13 years, in which morphed images were used to blackmail the complainant. The accused was alleged to be part of the conspiracy and to have fabricated the morphed materials. The accused initially absconded and was later remanded. The complainant had named multiple individuals, and the evidence included recordings, pen drives, and cash seizures.

The accused was alleged to have posed as a power broker and extorted ₹16.4 crores from a company by claiming that they could influence Income Tax investigations. The accused entered into a consultancy contract with the company, which was later deemed a sham. The Enforcement Directorate alleged that the accused laundered a total of ₹52.5 crores using this and similar schemes. Despite claims of extortion from multiple firms, only one formal complaint existed.

The accused was named in a co-accused's disclosure statement after 400g of heroin was recovered from three individuals. The three individuals claimed that the accused paid them ₹2.5 lakhs to collect the heroin. No recovery was made from the accused. The accused had a long history of NDPS cases, with ten FIRs pending, and multiple prior convictions under the Excise Act. The accused's prior bail application was withdrawn recently, and no new grounds were presented.

The accused was arrested along with two others near a hotel in a locality of a city. Though 1.9 kg of Methamphetamine was recovered from a bag carried by a co-accused, nothing was recovered from the accused personally. The case is based largely on retracted statements under Section 67 NDPS Act. The accused had been in custody for more than 8 years, with only a portion of the trial witnesses examined.

The accused, a person working in the information technology sector, was charged in a case under the NDPS Act following the recovery of psychotropic substances from co-accused persons. No contraband was recovered from the accused, and their implication was based on call records and financial transactions with the co-accused. The accused retracted their statement under Section 67 of the NDPS Act, claiming coercion.

The accused was apprehended in March 2017 with 300 grams of intoxicating powder allegedly containing Alprazolam. The accused claimed false implication, citing procedural violations and that they were detained illegally. The Special Judge had rejected the accused's earlier bail. The High Court considered these procedural lapses, custody length, and constitutional arguments before granting bail.

The accused, a student, was alleged to be involved in LSD trafficking via dark web networks. The accused was implicated by a co-accused, who claimed that the accused had ordered LSD blots using another person's address. The evidence included WhatsApp chats, parcel tracking IDs, and cryptocurrency transfers. The accused denied the allegations, pointing to inconsistencies in the parcel addresses, phone numbers, and weak forensic links.

The accused was arrested after being found driving a scooter containing 576 capsules of Tramadol (of two branded varieties), which were recovered during a police check. The accused claimed they were falsely implicated and that the co-accused had purchased the drugs. However, the capsules were found in the storage compartment of the scooter, which was owned and driven by the accused. The police determined the total weight of Tramadol was 337.392 grams, qualifying as a commercial quantity.

The accused was arrested with 26 grams of brown sugar and remained in custody beyond 90 days without the charge sheet being filed. The accused sought bail under Section 167(2) CrPC for default in filing the charge sheet. The Magistrate and Sessions Judge denied bail, and the accused approached the High Court under Section 439 CrPC.

The accused, listed as accused A-3, was arrested along with their sibling (accused A-2) and implicated for assisting in heroin smuggling. The accused helped collect, count, and distribute proceeds from heroin trafficking. The accused also allegedly delivered large cash amounts and was linked to the offence through surveillance and statements of co-accused. The accused was charged under various sections of the NDPS Act, the IPC, and the UAPA.

The accused was arrested after a parcel addressed to them was found to contain 10 LSD blots (0.17 grams, stated to be a commercial quantity). The parcel was seized along with 27 others based on secret information received by a central narcotics enforcement agency. The accused's name and phone number were found on the parcel. The agency linked the accused to a drug cartel on the basis of phone data and the accused's alleged voluntary statement under Section 67 of the NDPS Act.

The accused was found in possession of 288 capsules of a branded medicinal preparation containing 14.4g of Tramadol and 100 bottles (10 liters) of a branded cough syrup containing Codeine. This quantity qualifies as commercial under the NDPS Act. The accused sought bail on the basis of parity with the co-accused, but the co-accused's earlier bails were granted without reference to Section 37 NDPS.

The accused was implicated in a narcotics trafficking case after a parcel addressed to them was found to contain 25 LSD blots (0.42 grams, commercial quantity). The accused initially denied knowledge but later admitted to ordering the LSD through the dark web from a cartel, paying via cryptocurrency. Data from the accused's phone and email correspondence with the courier supported their involvement. The case is part of a broader operation in which multiple accused were identified based on 28 seized parcels.

The accused and co-accused 1 were arrested in connection with the recovery of 60 kg of ganja. They sought regular bail under Section 439 CrPC, arguing false implication, contradictions in the prosecution case, and that bail had been granted to co-accused 2. The State opposed the plea, stating that the bail granted to co-accused 2 did not consider the conditions under Section 37 NDPS. The court emphasized the mandatory twin conditions and dismissed the plea.

The accused was arrested based on call records linking them to a co-accused in a case involving 3.934 kg of charas. The charas was recovered from a bag carried by another co-accused on a motorcycle during a police trap. Viral videos and witness statements further corroborated the chain of events. The accused was implicated under Section 29 of the NDPS Act for abetment and conspiracy.

The accused was arrested after the co-accused disclosed that they had transported 16 kg of Charas from another country to a city. The accused was apprehended and 4.396 kg of Charas was recovered from the accused's bag. Both the accused and the co-accused were charged under Section 20 of the NDPS Act for possessing a commercial quantity of contraband.

The accused was arrested following a police raid at their residence based on secret information. The raid led to the recovery of 93.9 kg of dry cannabis leaves stored in plastic drums and bags. The search was conducted in the presence of a gazetted officer, a senior police officer, and other officials, with the procedure recorded and reported. The accused challenged the legality of the search under Section 42(2) of the NDPS Act.

Police recovered 289 kg of dry ganja from the house of a person, referred to here as co-accused 1, who claimed to be storing it on behalf of the accused. Further arrests were made of individuals allegedly waiting to purchase the contraband. Over time, the case expanded to implicate multiple accused in an organised narcotics trade.

The petitioner, a public representative and former leader of the opposition in a state legislature, was not initially named in the FIR registered in 2015 concerning the recovery of 1.8 kg of heroin, gold, and arms. The petitioner's name emerged later during reinvestigation. The petitioner was arrested in 2023 on the basis of new findings by a Special Investigation Team (SIT), which alleged that the petitioner had a role in funding and shielding drug traffickers.

The petitioners challenged the continued detention of individuals arrested under the NDPS Act after 90 days had lapsed without the filing of a complaint. The accused had earlier applied for bail under Section 167(2) CrPC based on this default, but their pleas were denied. The case involved international narcotic smuggling and seizure of large quantities of contraband.

The accused, a student at an educational institution, was arrested after being intercepted while receiving a courier containing 50 LSD blots, allegedly ordered by the co-accused via the dark web. The parcel was sent to the accused's college address and was recovered by authorities during an investigation into a syndicate operating through darknet purchases using cryptocurrency.

The accused was arrested in connection with an NDPS case in which 12.06 grams of heroin was recovered from the main accused. The prosecution relied on call detail records and bank transactions linking the accused to the main accused. The accused contended that they had no prior criminal history and had been implicated only on the basis of indirect evidence.

The accused was intercepted while driving a truck from which 349.250 kg of ganja was recovered from a concealed cavity. The accused and the co-accused claimed the consignment was loaded by another individual. The defence argued non-compliance with Sections 42 and 50 of the NDPS Act and lack of conscious possession. The central narcotics agency countered that procedures were followed and that the accused had knowledge and control over the contraband.

The accused was implicated in a narcotics case involving LSD blots after a parcel addressed to them was seized by a central narcotics enforcement agency. A total of 807 LSD blots and cocaine were recovered from multiple parcels. The accused was arrested on the basis of the parcel addressed in their name. No direct recovery was made from the accused, and their involvement was inferred from circumstantial evidence including phone data and courier company records.

The accused and the co-accused were convicted by the trial court under Sections 399 and 402 IPC for allegedly making preparations to commit dacoity along with another co-accused who was absconding. Police arrested them at a rest house with weapons. However, the evidence failed to show that five or more persons were involved, a necessary condition for establishing the offence of dacoity.

The accused, a former police personnel, was detained under the National Security Act (NSA) for inciting other police officials to protest and boycott duties. The accused was alleged to have given inflammatory speeches, mobilized mess strikes, and encouraged officers to defy superiors. An FIR was lodged under IPC Sections 353 and 505(1)(b), the Police Incitement Act, and IT Act provisions. The petitioner challenged the preventive detention as mala fide and argued that it was meant to frustrate bail granted in the criminal case.

The accused, a former senior government official, was arrested by a central investigating agency in a corruption and forgery case involving benami properties and forged documents. The investigating agency sought cancellation of the accused's bail, claiming that the accused had influenced witnesses and fabricated evidence. The trial court had granted bail with stringent conditions, considering the delay in arrest, the accused's prior cooperation, and the absence of violent conduct.

The accused was convicted under Section 392 IPC and sentenced to 5 years' rigorous imprisonment. The accused filed a third repeat application seeking suspension of sentence. The court noted that the accused had already served over 1.5 years and that early disposal of the appeal was unlikely, especially in the context of the Covid-19 pandemic.

The accused and their spouse were arrested by a central investigating agency in connection with a loan fraud case. The court found that the accused had cooperated throughout the investigation and that the arrest did not comply with legal mandates. The accused challenged the legality of the arrest under Sections 41 and 41-A CrPC and Article 21 of the Constitution.

The accused was convicted for armed robbery and sentenced to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment. The accused had already spent about 4 years and 3 months in custody. The looted vehicle was allegedly recovered from a third party's hut, and the identification evidence was doubtful. The accused's appeal had been pending for several years, with no early hearing in sight due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

The accused was alleged to have assembled with others in preparation to commit dacoity. The co-accused were arrested and tried, and they were acquitted due to lack of reliable evidence. The accused was arrested later and sought quashing of the proceedings on the ground that the same unreliable evidence was being used against them.

The accused was arrested for allegedly being involved in a robbery in which Rs.1,76,526/- was looted from a wholesaler. Rs.23,500/- was recovered from the accused, who was identified after more than two months, with procedural concerns noted in the identification process. The accused had been in custody since an exact date in 2018.

The accused was convicted for armed robbery in which the accused and a co-accused robbed a government official of Rs. 20 lakhs and coins worth Rs. 2.5 lakhs using a country-made pistol. Substantial recovery was made from the accused's possession, and the victim identified the accused in both the test identification parade and in court. The accused sought suspension of sentence during appeal, citing discrepancies in identification and health issues.

The accused was convicted of robbery under IPC Sections 392/34 and 397/34 and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment. The accused was alleged to have snatched a gold chain from a moving car and fled on a motorcycle. During the escape, one co-accused fired a shot. The accused, who is the appellant, was arrested shortly after the incident. No injury was caused during the robbery and no looted property was recovered from the accused.

The accused was arrested under the NDPS Act and remained in judicial custody beyond 90 days without a chargesheet being filed. The accused's bail application under Section 167(2) CrPC was initially rejected, but later accepted after it was found that the chargesheet was submitted on the 91st day. The court had to decide whether the delay, caused by the 90th day falling on a Sunday, invalidated the accused's statutory right to bail.

The accused was convicted under the NDPS Act and sentenced to 10 years' rigorous imprisonment. While the appeal was pending, the High Court granted the accused temporary bail on compassionate grounds to attend a parent's surgery and later to perform the parent's funeral rites. The case also involved deliberation over the interpretation of Section 32A of the NDPS Act regarding judicial powers of bail during appeal.

Two accused persons were arrested in connection with a murder case and were held in custody while the investigation continued. The chargesheet was filed on the 63rd day after arrest. The defense argued that under Section 167(2)(a) CrPC, detention beyond 60 days without a chargesheet is illegal. The State opposed the plea by arguing that since the bail application was pending and the challan was eventually filed, the right under Section 167(2) did not apply.

The accused faced prosecution under Section 135 of the Electricity Act. The accused had already deposited Rs. 20,000 as per an earlier court direction. The accused sought quashing of the chargesheet, but the court refused. However, applying Supreme Court guidelines laid down in earlier decisions concerning arrest and bail after a chargesheet is filed, the High Court directed that if the accused moved a surrender application before the Magistrate, the accused should not be arrested in the meantime and interim bail may be considered.

The accused was arrested in connection with a case involving the looting of two vehicles. The accused had previously withdrawn a bail application and later filed a fresh one under Section 439 CrPC. The Court noted that a co-accused, who was in similar circumstances, had already been granted bail. The accused had been in jail since an earlier date, and no criminal history was presented against them.

Applicants, including a police officer, were accused of killing two civilians in a fake encounter. A magisterial inquiry and a state investigation agency's investigation revealed that the deceased were apprehended from a railway station and later killed by the police, who fabricated an encounter narrative. Medical reports contradicted the police version. The victims were students and had no criminal background. The trial court denied bail, and the High Court also rejected the bail plea due to the seriousness of the charges.

The accused was charged in a case involving the death of the deceased, who was allegedly stabbed in the chest with a gupti (a concealed blade) by the petitioner and the co-accused. The prosecution claimed recovery of a blood-stained gupti from the accused. The defence argued that no overt act of killing or robbery was attributed directly to the accused.

The petitioner was detained under a state preventive detention law concerning dangerous activities, for allegedly engaging in multiple violent robberies targeting taxi drivers. One incident involved fatally stabbing a driver. The petitioner was in custody under Section 302 IPC, and the preventive detention was challenged on the grounds that there was no likelihood of bail and thus no necessity for preventive detention. The High Court reviewed whether the detaining authority had sufficient material to form such a belief.

The spouse of the petitioner was detained under a state preventive detention Act on the basis of four FIRs alleging chain snatching. The detainee had already been granted default bail in all four cases because the charge sheet was not filed. The detaining authority labelled the detainee a 'goonda' and invoked preventive detention, citing public fear.

The accused was arrested for allegedly snatching a mobile phone from the complainant along with other co-accused, who fled on a motorcycle. The accused had been in custody since an earlier date, and the co-accused had already been granted bail. The prosecution had no specific evidence tying the accused directly to the act.

The accused was already in judicial custody for murder and Arms Act charges when they were served with a preventive detention order under the National Security Act, 1980. The authorities did not demonstrate satisfaction that there was a real possibility of the accused being granted bail.

The accused was arrested for allegedly being involved in a robbery case in which they were accused of driving the truck used in the crime. A small amount of cash was recovered from the accused. The co-accused in the same case had already been granted bail. The accused applied for bail under Section 439 CrPC, citing parity and weak evidence.

The accused was alleged to have broken into the home of a police officer along with co-accused at night, demanded money, and carried a country-made pistol. The trial court convicted the accused under IPC Sections 458, 398 and Arms Act provisions. On appeal, the High Court found no evidence of a robbery attempt or of possession of a working weapon.

The accused was investigated by a central investigating agency, acting under orders from a government ministry, in connection with a group of companies. The accused was arrested and placed in judicial custody. Although a complaint was filed, cognizance was not taken within 60 days. The petitioners had previously been released temporarily and then surrendered in accordance with directions of the Supreme Court. Bail was claimed on the ground that the statutory 60-day limit under Section 167(2) CrPC had expired without cognizance being taken.

The petitioner was detained under a state preventive detention law concerning dangerous activities, based on two criminal cases of robbery and extortion and two in-camera witness statements alleging threats and collection of protection money. Although bail had been granted in both criminal cases, the petitioner had not availed of it. The detention was challenged as lacking justification under 'public order'.

On a certain date in 1999, six armed persons entered a shop in a locality and committed armed robbery, stealing gold jewelry and cash. The accused and others were arrested later based on disclosures made in another case. Weapons were recovered, and witnesses identified the accused. The trial court convicted all of them under Sections 452, 395 and 397 IPC. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction for robbery but removed the Section 397 IPC charge because it was unclear who had used the weapon. Juvenile co-accused were granted protection under the JJ Act, and the accused's conviction and sentence were upheld.

The petitioner was detained under the MPDA Act as a "dangerous person" due to alleged involvement in over a dozen criminal cases, including robbery and extortion. The petitioner was accused of robbing the owner of a wine shop and threatening extortion. Several in-camera statements were recorded. The detention was challenged on the grounds of non-application of mind and reliance on outdated or already quashed prior cases and detention orders.

The accused, a police officer, was alleged to have conspired with a gangster in a premeditated ambush on a police raid, which resulted in the brutal killing of 8 police personnel and injuries to others. The accused allegedly leaked the raid plan and failed to support their team, showing suspicious conduct. Multiple witness statements and call detail record evidence supported the allegation of the accused's close ties with the gangster.

The accused, an employee of a public housing authority, was accused in a fraud involving ₹26.5 lakhs related to misrepresentation and sale of premises under a fake 'Special Quota Scheme'. The complainant alleged being misled by estate agents and accused persons. After the accused's arrest, the Sessions Court denied bail. The High Court later granted bail, which was challenged before the Supreme Court by the complainant.

The juvenile appellant was accused in a case involving kidnapping for ransom and murder. Though the FIR named multiple accused and recoveries were made, nothing was recovered based on the appellant's disclosure. The appellant had already spent 2.5 years in an observation home, and the social investigation report showed no negative findings. A similarly situated co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused and a co-accused were implicated in the kidnapping of a minor child, who was originally alleged to have been taken by another person. That other person later confessed to throwing the child into a canal. The petitioners were named later, allegedly to strengthen the case. A similarly placed co-accused had already been granted bail. The child remains missing.

The accused was implicated in two FIRs related to kidnapping and human trafficking under IPC Sections 363, 368, 370, and 202. The accused's involvement was inferred from a live-in relationship with a co-accused who was allegedly involved in the sale of a child. The prosecution lacked direct evidence against the accused and relied on a supplementary witness statement alleging that the accused had assisted the co-accused.

The accused was arrested in connection with the alleged kidnapping and murder of a person and their child, whose bodies were allegedly dumped in a river. The accused's name surfaced only in the confessional statements of co-accused. The FIR did not name the accused, and the petitioner argued there was no direct or corroborated evidence against them.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a child, an incident said to have occurred several years earlier. The FIR was lodged after a delay of six days. The child was recovered in the same year, and the child's statement under Section 164 CrPC did not match the allegations in the FIR. The child claimed to have been taken away on a pretext and to have later worked in a hotel in a state. The accused alleged false implication due to a land dispute and noted that a co-accused had already received anticipatory bail.

The accused was charged in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor child. Although the accused was not named in the FIR, the implication was based on the allegation that the accused was involved in the conspiracy. The child was recovered from co-accused 1. The other co-accused, namely co-accused 1, co-accused 2 and co-accused 3, had already been granted bail by coordinate benches.

The accused was alleged to have conspired in the kidnapping and ritualistic murder of a child, allegedly by suggesting the sacrifice to their child's spouse. However, the accused was not named in the FIR, and their involvement was inferred solely from the statement of a co-accused. Other similarly placed co-accused, including the accused's spouse and others, had already been granted bail.

The accused was implicated in a case involving the alleged kidnapping and murder of a person and their child, whose bodies were allegedly thrown into a river. The accused was not named in the FIR and no specific role was attributed to them. Their name surfaced only in the confession of the deceased person's spouse. The co-accused in-laws had already been granted anticipatory bail. The accused had no criminal antecedents and had been in custody for a period of time since early in the previous year.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped and murdered a minor child for ransom. The child's body was found in the informant's field. The accused was allegedly named by a co-accused, who claimed that the kidnapping was planned for a ransom of ₹10,000 in order to repay a debt. Confessional statements and the recovery of a bloodstained brick formed the basis of the charge. The accused had been in custody since 2018.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped the complainant's in-law and grandchild under the pretext of negotiating a compromise related to a pending POCSO case against the complainant's child. The in-law and the grandchild were allegedly taken away and remained missing. The complainant later submitted a compromise document, but the Court rejected its relevance given the gravity of the accusation and the unresolved disappearance.

The accused was alleged to have assisted in the kidnapping of the informant's child, who later married the co-accused and had a child with the co-accused. There were no allegations of assault or coercion by the accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2021 and had no prior criminal record.

The accused was charged in a kidnapping and murder case in which the victim, who used to deliver food to the informant's spouse, went missing. The FIR alleged that the accused and others surrounded and kidnapped the victim. There was no eyewitness, and no recovery linking the accused to the offence. The accusation was based on the confession of a co-accused who had already been granted bail. The accused had no prior criminal record and had been in custody since a date in 2021.

The accused was convicted for kidnapping and murdering a minor. The accused was earlier granted six weeks of interim bail to care for ailing parents. Upon seeking a further extension citing health issues and COVID-19 risks, the Court refused due to allegations of the convict roaming near the complainant's residence and threatening behaviour during trial. A formal complaint was filed by the victim's parent citing fear and security concerns.

The accused was charged in a case involving the kidnapping and forced marriage of a minor, allegedly involving religious conversion. The accused's spouse and child (the main accused) had already been granted bail. The accused was present at the scene during the marriage ceremony, but no specific overt act was attributed to them. Two of the accused's other children had already received anticipatory bail.

The accused, acting as an agent of a company, allegedly misappropriated ₹7.57 crores given for land purchase in a special economic zone by executing fraudulent sale agreements with fictitious owners. Despite admitting fault and issuing two cheques (which bounced), the accused was granted anticipatory bail without disclosing a prior bail rejection in a similar fraud case. The accused was also alleged to have threatened witnesses and tampered with evidence.

The accused was charged in a case involving dacoity and attempted murder. Looted items were recovered from the accused and were identified in a Test Identification Parade. The accused's confession also led to the recovery of the motorcycle used in the robbery. Despite the informant later turning hostile, the Court refused to reconsider bail.

The accused, a managing director of a company, was accused in a money laundering case arising from an FIR under Section 420 of the IPC and a state urban development Act. The accused allegedly conspired with co-developers to fraudulently retain subsidized plots and sell them at market rates. The Directorate of Enforcement filed a complaint under the PMLA, alleging over ₹50 crores in proceeds of crime. The accused had been in custody for a period of time since a date in an earlier year and had joined the investigation multiple times. All relevant documents were already seized.

The accused, then holding the post of a revenue officer, was alleged to have fraudulently passed a mutation order in favour of the co-accused on government leasehold land belonging to a family, despite an earlier order of a senior district authority denying mutation. The mutation was carried out on the basis of an old sale deed and a report from a local revenue official, allegedly in violation of Section 165 of the state Land Revenue Code, and without the necessary permission of the senior district authority.

The case involved the alleged kidnapping and murder of a child who went missing while playing outside. The informant suspected the accused and others because of prior threats. The petitioner contended that they were falsely implicated due to past rivalry and that no substantial evidence linked them to the crime. A similarly situated co-accused had already been granted bail.

The petitioners were arrested in connection with a dacoity case. Petitioner No. 1 was not identified in the Test Identification Parade and no stolen property was recovered from them. A mobile phone was recovered from Petitioner No. 2, but it was not identified as stolen. Both petitioners had been in custody for approximately 11 months at the time of the bail hearing.

The petitioner was accused in a case involving the kidnapping and alleged child marriage of a minor. The petitioner was accused of transporting the minor on a motorcycle as part of a larger group aiding the principal accused, who married the minor in a temple. An FIR was registered against seven individuals in total. The co-accused, including the principal accused, had already been granted bail.

The accused, who is co-accused 3 in the case, was involved in a domestic dispute in which they, along with others, allegedly entered their spouse's residence, assaulted the spouse, and stole cash and valuables. The complaint stemmed from a strained marital relationship, with existing proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act and a pending divorce petition. The Court required the petitioner to cooperate with the investigation before granting bail.

The accused, who operated a service center, was alleged to have facilitated fraudulent online transactions in a loan scam. The accused accepted large sums of money through credit card transfers and provided cash to an associate, charging a 14% commission. The complainant was defrauded of ₹1.72 crores by multiple accused persons under the guise of loan processing. The applicant was not named in the FIR but was implicated during the investigation and admitted their role in such transactions.

The petitioner was accused of assaulting their spouse with a chopper, causing injuries, in violation of a protection order under the Domestic Violence Act. The alleged incident occurred on a date in January 2025. The petitioner claimed false implication due to trivial family issues. Recovery had already been made, and the petitioner sought anticipatory bail.

The accused was alleged by their spouse to have committed cruelty and attempted murder, with the incident allegedly occurring on a particular date. The FIR was lodged several months later. The accused claimed the complaint was retaliatory following the accused's divorce petition and cited multiple proceedings, including a maintenance application and a Domestic Violence Act complaint. The accused sought anticipatory bail, citing absence of custodial need and parity with co-accused relatives who had already been granted bail.

The informant, the spouse of the applicant, alleged physical and emotional abuse by the applicant and the applicant's family, including an incident where the informant's head was banged against a wall. The harassment reportedly stemmed from dissatisfaction over the birth of two children. The informant also alleged extramarital affairs and inappropriate behavior by the applicant's parent. The FIR was filed six months after the couple began living separately.

The accused was charged under Sections 498A and 304B IPC after the death of their spouse, who was reportedly suffering from depression. The marriage took place several years earlier, and no complaints of domestic violence were made until several years after the marriage. The deceased had two infant children with the accused. The Court considered these factors and granted anticipatory bail.

The accused was alleged to have trespassed into the home of the accused's estranged spouse's parent and to have abused the spouse and the spouse's in-law, in violation of a domestic violence protection order. The accused argued that they went there only to retrieve their minor child, who had gone missing from school and was later found at the complainant's house. The FIR included bailable IPC offences and one non-bailable offence under Section 31 of the DV Act.

The accused, the spouse of the complainant, applied for anticipatory bail in a case under IPC Sections 498A and 406. The complainant had left the matrimonial home, and the accused claimed the allegations were vague and that a prior domestic violence case had been filed by the accused's parent against the complainant. Streedhan articles had been returned, and the Court found no need for custodial interrogation.

The accused was the first accused in a domestic violence case, during which the accused allegedly produced forged tax receipts for sureties in order to obtain bail. A new FIR was registered after court staff discovered the forgery. The accused claimed ignorance of the fake documents and cooperated with the police interrogation.

The accused was charged under Section 498A IPC by their spouse for subjecting the spouse to cruelty. The complaint made general and omnibus allegations, and the complainant did not appear before the court despite notice. The court granted provisional anticipatory bail with specific conditions relating to possible maintenance and residence petitions under the DV Act.

The accused, along with their parent and sibling, was accused of subjecting their spouse to cruelty and torture over dowry demands. Multiple cases were filed between the parties, including under the Domestic Violence Act and divorce proceedings. The accused was ordered to pay maintenance, part of which was unpaid at the time of hearing. The accused undertook to make payments and cooperate with the case proceedings.

The accused was charged with abetting the suicide of the deceased, who was the accused's sibling-in-law. The FIR alleged that the accused and other in-laws harassed the deceased, leading the deceased to commit suicide by consuming poison. There was no suicide note. The co-accused had already been granted interim and regular bail. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2021, and the trial had not commenced.

The applicant was accused by their spouse of physical abuse and harassment after their marriage in 2019. The spouse alleged mistreatment by the applicant and the applicant's relatives, particularly over dowry. Other co-accused, including the applicant's parent and a relative, were already granted anticipatory bail. The couple had been living separately since about a year after the marriage, and proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act had already been initiated several months before the FIR was filed. The FIR was filed a few months after those proceedings were initiated.

The accused, the second accused in a crime registered at a police station, was booked under Section 31 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act. The accused filed an anticipatory bail application fearing arrest. The prosecution opposed the plea.

The accused was charged under Section 75 of the Juvenile Justice Act for allegedly mentally harassing their minor child, who is a cancer patient. The complaint arose amidst ongoing matrimonial disputes and Domestic Violence Act proceedings between the accused and their spouse. No allegations of physical assault were made, and the accused had already been granted bail in a related matrimonial cruelty case.

The accused was alleged to have committed domestic violence and was suspected of being a foreign national possibly involved in anti-national activities. However, the accused possessed valid identity documents, and no incriminating material was produced by the State. The accused complied fully with the anticipatory bail terms, including daily appearances before the investigating officer.

The accused, a branch manager of a cooperative bank, was alleged to have embezzled Rs. 16.13 crores by transferring funds from the bank's sundry account to the accounts of co-accused individuals. A co-accused had been granted bail by the Supreme Court, while the accused was identified as the main conspirator. Rs. 51 lakhs in cash and assets worth Rs. 75 lakhs were recovered from the accused. The accused had been in custody for several years.

The accused, a chartered accountant for a company, was arrested for their alleged role in a large-scale financial fraud in which the company collected money from investors by promising high returns but failed to repay them. The accused was alleged to have assured investors of high returns and misappropriated funds. The accused had been in custody for several years, since 2018, and filed a third bail application, arguing prolonged incarceration and that the securities market regulator had found no fault with them.

The accused, an Assistant Manager at a cooperative society, was alleged to have fraudulently withdrawn money in the names of depositors and not deposited collected funds. The accused was arrested and, several months later, charges were framed. Despite the framing of charges, no witness was examined for over a year. The accused applied for bail under Section 437(6) CrPC, which was initially rejected due to the gravity of the charges, but was later granted by the High Court on account of prolonged detention without progress in the trial.

The petitioner was arrested with a looted mobile phone connected to a case registered at a police station for robbery. The case was filed under IPC Section 414 and Arms Act Sections 25(1-B)(a) and 26. The Court noted the recovery and refused bail at this stage but allowed for a future bail application after framing of charge.

The petitioner, along with others, was apprehended by a police station's officers while allegedly preparing to commit a robbery. Weapons including an iron rod, knives, and chilli powder were recovered. The petitioner had 17 prior cases against them, and investigation in this case was still ongoing.

The accused, a clerk in a bank, was implicated in a multi-crore scam involving illegal transfer of public funds into the accounts of a cooperative society. The accused allegedly forged cheques and facilitated unauthorized deposits and withdrawals amounting to crores, helping conceal the fraud. The accused claimed that some transactions were personal or routine, but investigation revealed deeper involvement and association with the central figures in the scam.

The accused was alleged to have masterminded the kidnapping of a minor for a ransom of Rs. 2 crores. A threatening chit was left at the complainant's shop, and calls were made demanding ransom. The minor was rescued from the co-accused before any payment was made. The accused was arrested and remained in custody for over 9 months. The co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a minor and married them, allegedly under the influence of the accused's parent. The minor later stated in a statement under Section 164 CrPC that they went to the accused's house voluntarily to avoid a forced marriage arranged by their parent. The minor refused medical examination, and the charge-sheet had not been filed at the time of the judgment.

The accused was arrested in connection with the kidnapping of a child and had been in custody since a date in December 2020. This was the accused's second bail application. The co-accused, facing similar charges, had already been granted bail. The accused is physically disabled with 60% disability. The prosecution argued that the child was recovered from the accused's car, making the accused's role more serious. However, the Court considered the long custody period and disability while granting bail.

The accused was convicted along with three others under Section 392 IPC for robbing employees of a bank at gunpoint and snatching cash, mobile phones, and documents. The accused had been in custody for several years since the arrest. The prosecution case was based on identification by one victim and a co-accused's confession. Other co-accused had been granted bail by the High Court earlier.

The accused was arrested in a road robbery case registered under Sections 392 and 34 IPC at a police station. The accused has been in custody since an earlier date, which is more than a year before the second bail application was decided. The accused's previous bail application was rejected on the ground of seven similar criminal antecedents. In the second application, the accused sought bail citing long custody and parity with co-accused who were granted bail.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a fraud of ₹16.13 crore at a district cooperative central bank. Significant sums were transferred from the bank's Sundry account to the accused's personal bank account. The prosecution alleged that the accused acted in connivance with the bank managers. The accused had been in prolonged detention for several years and had made multiple prior bail applications. The High Court rejected the accused's fifth bail plea.

The accused was named in a robbery case registered at a police station, in which a loaded van carrying 22 quintals of live chicken and ₹70,000 in cash was allegedly looted. The vehicle's GPS data indicated that it was unloaded at a co-accused's residence. The accused claimed false implication due to enmity and pointed to the lack of any recovery from their possession. The accused also had no prior criminal record.

The accused, a director of a company, was alleged to have defrauded multiple complainants by inducing them to invest in franchise businesses under a false promise of high returns. FIRs were registered under Sections 420, 406 and 409/34 IPC. The accused denied involvement with certain companies and claimed that the disputes were civil in nature, but the court noted similar fraud complaints against the accused across several districts.

The FIR was lodged by a police officer regarding the recovery of an unidentified dead body. The accused was implicated based on witness statements suggesting their involvement in the murder of a person suspected of kidnapping a young child. There was no direct evidence linking the accused to the crime. Several co-accused had already been granted bail, and the accused had been in custody for a substantial period since an arrest in 2019.

The accused was alleged to have robbed a person at knifepoint in a moving vehicle after offering them a lift. The accused had been in custody since December of the previous year and had earlier sought bail, which was denied a few months later. The prosecution opposed bail, citing the accused's history of similar crimes and the likelihood of reoffending.

The accused was alleged to be involved in a large-scale financial fraud linked to two companies running illegal collective investment schemes. The accused allegedly facilitated the diversion of ₹4318.49 crores through 37 companies under the pretext of land development. The FIR was registered several years before the arrest, and the accused was arrested only years later, after a supplementary charge sheet was filed naming the accused.

The State sought cancellation of bail granted to several accused in a co-operative bank scam involving fraudulent overdrafts and bogus accounts. The accused were bank directors and officials alleged to have misappropriated funds through fictitious accounts and unauthorized loans. The Sessions Court had granted them bail, which the State challenged citing the seriousness of the offence and the likelihood of tampering with evidence.

The accused was extradited to India from a foreign country for allegedly acting as a middleman in a VVIP helicopter procurement deal. The accused is alleged to have received €30 million in kickbacks to influence the procurement process in favour of a particular company, including by facilitating bribes to Indian officials. The enforcement agency alleged money laundering through shell companies and bogus contracts.

The accused, the Managing Director of a real estate company, was accused of duping over 800 homebuyers through two real estate projects by collecting payments and loans worth hundreds of crores, but failing to deliver the promised flats. A forensic audit revealed misappropriation of Rs. 408.74 crores, misuse of bank loans, and fraudulent accounting. The accused also allegedly threatened the court-appointed interim resolution professional and employees cooperating with the investigation.

A juvenile petitioner was apprehended while attempting to rob a vehicle at gunpoint at a hotel, along with another accused who fled. The petitioner was caught by local residents, and a pistol with live cartridges was recovered. The petitioner had three prior criminal cases and an adverse social investigation report. The petitioner's bail plea had been rejected by both the Juvenile Justice Board and the Appellate Court.

The accused, proprietor of a factory, was accused under the CGST Act of evading duties amounting to over ₹62 crores through clandestine removal of goods without invoices. A search conducted at the accused's premises revealed incriminating documents and goods. The accused was arrested and, some time later, bail was sought. The bail was opposed on the grounds of the economic nature of the offence and the gravity of the evasion.

The accused was alleged to have trespassed into the complainant's property and falsely claimed possession using fabricated documents. The accused was charge-sheeted under multiple IPC sections, including those punishable with life imprisonment. Although bail was granted by a Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, it was cancelled by the Sessions Court for concealment of a pending bail application before a higher court. The High Court upheld the cancellation due to misuse of judicial process.

The petitioner was convicted under Sections 392/34 IPC for committing robbery and sentenced to three years' rigorous imprisonment. Though the FIR was initially registered against unknown persons, the petitioner was identified during a Test Identification Parade and later during trial by the informant. The petitioner challenged the conviction before the High Court in a criminal revision petition, seeking bail after having spent around a year in custody.

The accused, a Managing Director of a company, was arrested for alleged involvement in a fraud connected to a Merchanting Trade business, in which false financial documents were submitted to banks to secure Letters of Credit. The fraud allegedly caused an estimated loss of ₹7820 crore to public sector banks. Investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office revealed that the accused falsified financial statements, siphoned funds, and engaged in speculative currency trading. The accused had been in jail for several years, having been in custody since an arrest in 2020, and sought bail under Section 439 CrPC read with Section 212(6) of the Companies Act.

The accused and others were alleged to have committed financial fraud involving the misuse of hire-purchase loans that were meant for the purchase of four windmills, of which only two were actually bought. The accused allegedly created false documents to show that all four had been purchased and misappropriated the funds. After initially obtaining temporary protection from arrest, the accused attempted to seek regular bail without surrendering, and this was rejected by the Sessions Court.

On an earlier date, the complainant and their sibling's child, after delivering wheat and rice to a dealer, were returning on a tractor when the accused and others allegedly robbed them of ₹2000 at gunpoint. The accused persons were apprehended at the scene. They claimed false implication due to village politics and stated that a compromise was reached and nothing was recovered.

The petitioner was accused in a case involving the kidnapping of a minor for a ransom of Rs. 1 crore. The victim and the victim's parent did not name the petitioner in their statements. The petitioner was implicated based on the confessional statement of a co-accused. The petitioner has no prior criminal antecedents and has been in custody since a date in September 2020.

The accused was alleged to have committed a robbery in a case registered at a police station, in which unidentified persons allegedly robbed a person of their motorcycle, wristwatch, and silver chain. The accused was arrested on the basis of a co-accused's confession and a motorcycle recovered by the police. The accused had been in custody since an exact date in 2020, and had five prior cases involving robbery and abduction.

The applicant was arrested for allegedly kidnapping an eight-month-old child from the complainant. The applicant claimed to be unaware of the co-accused's prior marriage to the complainant and denied the allegations. The applicant's earlier temporary bail was not availed because the applicant was unable to furnish cash surety.

The accused was arrested in connection with an attempted dacoity at an ATM center in a city. The accused and their associates were found hiding and were later apprehended after a chase. The accused had nearly 13 to 14 prior cases of a similar nature. The accused was identified by three witnesses in a test identification parade. Bail was earlier rejected on two occasions, several years after the arrest and again later, even though the co-accused had been granted bail.

The accused was arrested for allegedly enticing and kidnapping a minor, who is a relative of the accused. The minor stated in their Section 164 CrPC statement that they went with the accused voluntarily. The accused had been in custody since arrest and sought regular bail.

The accused was arrested in a case involving robbery under IPC Section 392. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2019, and the trial had not progressed due to absconding co-accused and judicial delays. The accused previously applied for bail, which was rejected several months later in 2020.

The accused was alleged to have kidnapped a child, who was later recovered from the accused's house along with the accused's spouse. The accused had been in custody since December 2021, which was a substantial period before the application. The investigation was complete and no further recovery was required from the accused. The accused's spouse had already been granted bail.

The petitioner sought anticipatory bail in a case involving the robbery of a track machine by three unknown persons. Although the petitioner was not named in the FIR, they were later identified by an independent eyewitness during investigation. No recovery was made from the petitioner, and the petitioner claimed false implication.

The accused, an employee of a bank, was implicated in a Rs. 50 crore bank fraud involving multiple accused. The accused was earlier denied bail by the High Court, but subsequently secured bail from the Trial Court while concealing a pending petition. The case involved the clearance of fraudulent cheques and creation of fake companies.

The accused, along with the co-accused, allegedly committed a robbery at gunpoint, stealing cash, ATM cards, and a mobile phone from the complainant and a friend of the complainant. The FIR named the accused, and both victims identified the accused. The co-accused was apprehended soon after the incident with the stolen items.

The petitioner was accused of participating in a robbery in which Rs. 5 lakhs were snatched. CCTV footage allegedly shows the petitioner's active involvement. The petitioner's earlier bail plea was rejected. The petitioner filed for bail again, citing parity with the co-accused, who was granted bail.

The accused was alleged to have opened a fake bank account using forged documents and defrauded over Rs. 9 lakhs through RTGS transfers. The accused's first two bail applications were rejected. On the third attempt, the accused argued that there was a lack of evidence, such as no recovery, no verified photograph on the bank records, and improper investigation procedures. The accused had been in custody for a period of several years, since 2014.

The accused, a senior officer of a company, was arrested in a ₹3269 crore bank fraud and money laundering case. The accused was alleged to have procured fake invoices from shell companies, diverted funds, and siphoned money abroad. Though not named in the initial complaints, the accused was arrested after being implicated in the fourth supplementary complaint under the PMLA.

The accused was named as one of several accused in a multi-state GST fraud involving the registration of fake firms using stolen identities, including that of a journalist. The scam involved fraudulent Input Tax Credit claims amounting to over ₹2645 crore. While the FIR initially named unknown persons, the accused's name surfaced later through confessional statements. A non-bailable warrant was issued against the accused, and the investigation is ongoing under a Special Investigation Team.

The accused was alleged, in a state excise policy case, to have acted as a cash handler who received Rs. 45 crore through hawala for use in a political party's election campaign in a state. The accused was named in the sixth supplementary complaint under the PMLA after being arrested by a central investigating agency in the predicate offence, and was later arrested by an enforcement agency several months afterwards. The prosecution alleged the accused's involvement in the placement, layering, and integration of proceeds of crime.

A juvenile was involved in two robbery cases reported within two days of each other. The juvenile was detained several months later. The lower courts denied bail, citing prior similar offences and alleged criminal association. The High Court found no material to indicate negative influence or criminal association if the juvenile were released.

The accused, an adult, was arrested in a kidnapping case under Sections 363 and 370 IPC. The victim was subsequently recovered. The applicant claimed false implication and emphasized a clean record and willingness to cooperate with legal proceedings. The accused had been in custody since a date in March 2020.

The accused was alleged to have diverted over 2700 kg of gold jewellery meant for export to the domestic market and to have laundered the proceeds through multiple shell companies and bank accounts. A central revenue intelligence agency initially booked the accused, and later a central enforcement agency registered a case under the PMLA. Though the accused had earlier been released on bail in related cases, the accused was re-arrested in a later year for money laundering. The enforcement agency alleged that the accused operated through multiple firms, procured fake passports, and used over 120 bank accounts.

The accused was arrested after a kidnapped child, aged under two and a half years and therefore a minor, was recovered from the accused's possession. The child was allegedly sold to the accused by the co-accused, who had purchased the child from two persons involved in the abduction at a railway station. The accused admitted to paying ₹1,20,000 for the child, citing a personal desire to have a child of a particular sex. The co-accused had already been granted bail.

The accused was arrested in connection with a robbery in which three persons on a motorcycle snatched ₹1.3 lakhs at gunpoint. While two of the robbers fled, the accused was caught on the spot by the police with a katta (country-made pistol) and four cartridges. The accused claimed false implication and lack of conscious possession of the weapon.

The accused, already in custody, sought bail in a case involving allegations of extortion by a criminal gang. Two co-accused were arrested with firearms and named the accused as a gang member. A raid on the accused's house led to the recovery of a country-made pistol, a musket, a live cartridge, and a motorcycle key. The accused denied the charges and questioned the lack of seizure witnesses.

The accused was arrested in connection with a robbery case under Section 392 IPC, in which a looted mobile phone was recovered from their possession. The accused applied for bail in a High Court. The trial was pending before a Judicial Magistrate.

The accused, a director of a real estate company, was alleged to have orchestrated a large-scale land fraud through fake plotting schemes. It was alleged that ₹315 crore was collected from investors, but the land was not transferred to them. Multiple FIRs were filed, and witness statements indicated threats and fraud. A charge sheet was filed under provisions of the IPC and the PMLA, and further investigation was pending.

The accused, a director of a real estate company, was alleged to have cheated thousands of investors in a land fraud scam valued at over ₹315 crore. The victims alleged threats and non-allotment of promised plots. A charge sheet was filed under various sections of the IPC and under the PMLA. The Court noted that the investigation was continuing, that prior bail applications had been rejected, and that there was potential for witness intimidation.

The accused was arrested for robbery under IPC Section 392 and Sections 11 and 13 of the MPDVPK Act. Ear tops were allegedly recovered from the accused. The second bail application was filed after the first was rejected. The accused argued that the Test Identification Parade (TIP), held over a month after the arrest, diminished its probative value. The accused had been in custody for over three months.

The accused persons were arrested in a road robbery case in which the complainant was intercepted and robbed of ₹42,000 and a scooter, which was later recovered. The accused persons argued that the scooter was not recovered on the basis of their confession and that the complainant did not participate in the Test Identification Parade. The State submitted that the accused persons had prior similar criminal cases.

The accused was alleged to have participated in a robbery in which the complainant, returning from a city with ₹45,000, was attacked at night by multiple individuals on motorcycles. The complainant was beaten and the money was snatched. The accused was specifically alleged to have assaulted the complainant during the robbery. The accused previously applied for anticipatory bail and then regular bail, which was initially denied. After the charge sheet was filed, the accused applied again.

Two applicants were arrested in a case involving the kidnapping and brutal murder of a minor child. The applicants were not named in the original FIR, which named only one accused. Their names emerged during investigation on the basis of alleged confessional statements and circumstantial evidence, including testimony from witnesses who claimed to have overheard incriminating conversations.

The accused, then a police inspector at a police station, was accused of conspiracy and negligence in a mob assault on victims by vigilantes in a town. The accused was alleged to have failed to intervene or take timely action, and possibly to have conspired to misrepresent facts. The accused denied being present at the scene and cited their duties before the magistrate that day. A charge sheet was filed with over 300 witnesses.

The accused was arrested in a road robbery case under Section 394 IPC and had been in custody since a date in 2022. The accused was identified in a Test Identification Parade. A previous bail plea of the accused was rejected several months later. The accused renewed the bail application, citing that the co-accused had been granted bail and that the accused had not suppressed any facts.

The accused was arrested after police received information about a criminal gathering. Upon a raid, a loaded country-made pistol, two live cartridges, and a motorcycle were recovered from the accused. The accused had been in custody since a date in 2017. The co-accused was granted bail earlier, but only three cartridges were recovered from the co-accused.

The accused was arrested in a case of kidnapping for ransom involving a minor. The accused was not named in the FIR but was implicated based on the confessional statements of the co-accused. The minor was ultimately recovered from a child helpline. The victim did not name the accused in the statement recorded under Section 164 CrPC. Two co-accused were granted bail earlier.

The accused was arrested during a police raid where several persons suspected of unlawful activity were found assembled. A loaded country-made pistol was recovered from the accused, and another from a co-accused. The accused had been in custody since late 2017. The accused's counsel argued that there was limited evidence beyond the recovery of the weapon. The State opposed bail citing the accused's criminal history, including three prior robbery cases.

The accused was arrested in a case investigated by a state criminal investigation agency, involving a ₹60 crore fraud against a private company. The accused and other co-accused allegedly impersonated public servants, used forged documents and government seals to fabricate a fake contract and cheat the complainants. Though the charge sheet was filed and the co-accused were granted bail, the accused's role was considered central to the conspiracy. The accused was arrested after evading summons and has remained in judicial custody since then.

The accused, proprietor of a registered GST firm, was alleged to have fraudulently availed input tax credit of ₹4.28 crore and cancelled e-way bills worth ₹17.33 crore without actual movement of goods. The FIR, filed by a special police unit, alleged use of non-existent firms and fake invoices. The accused argued that the GST department had not passed any adjudication or cancellation orders, and that all purchases were made from GST-registered dealers. The accused also cited prolonged custody, pending trial, and health issues.
